title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
text:
Phase is how we measure when things happen in an oscillation: is the signal at its peak, its trough, or somewhere in between? If you want to know whether two brain regions are coordinating their activity, you need to compare their phases. Are they peaking at the same time (in phase)? Are they alternating (in anti-phase)? Is the relationship consistent or drifting?
The Hilbert transform is the mathematical tool that extracts instantaneous phase from a signal. It is the foundation for all phase-based connectivity measures: phase-locking value (PLV), the phase alignment matrix, and metastability. Understanding how it works, and where it can go wrong, is critical for Natalia’s project on resting-state EEG dynamics in Parkinson’s disease.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
text:
The analytic signal
Given a real-valued signal \(x(t)\), the Hilbert transform produces a new signal \(\hat{x}(t)\) that is the “90-degree shifted” version of \(x(t)\). For a pure cosine, the Hilbert transform gives a sine; for a sine, it gives a negative cosine.
The analytic signal combines the original signal and its Hilbert transform:
\[z(t) = x(t) + i \, \hat{x}(t)\]
This is a complex-valued signal. You can think of \(x(t)\) as the “real part” and \(\hat{x}(t)\) as the “imaginary part”. The analytic signal has a useful property: its negative-frequency components are zero. This means it contains only forward-rotating phasors, which gives a clean definition of instantaneous phase and amplitude.
In polar form:
\[z(t) = A(t) \, e^{i\phi(t)}\]
where:

\(A(t) = |z(t)| = \sqrt{x(t)^2 + \hat{x}(t)^2}\) is the instantaneous amplitude (or envelope). It tells you how large the oscillation is at each moment.
\(\phi(t) = \arg(z(t)) = \arctan\!\big(\hat{x}(t) / x(t)\big)\) is the instantaneous phase. It tells you where in the oscillatory cycle the signal is at each moment.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
section: How the Hilbert transform works in the frequency domain
text:
How the Hilbert transform works in the frequency domain
The Hilbert transform can be defined in the frequency domain. It multiplies the positive-frequency components of the signal by \(-i\) and the negative-frequency components by \(+i\). This shifts each frequency component by 90 degrees without changing its amplitude.
In practice, Python computes the Hilbert transform using the FFT:

Compute the FFT of \(x(t)\).
Set the negative-frequency components to zero.
Double the positive-frequency components.
Take the inverse FFT.

The result is the analytic signal \(z(t)\), from which you extract phase and amplitude.
from scipy.signal import hilbert
import numpy as np

# The function returns the analytic signal, not the Hilbert transform itself
analytic = hilbert(x)

# Extract phase and amplitude
phase = np.angle(analytic)       # radians, range [-pi, pi]
amplitude = np.abs(analytic)     # instantaneous envelope
Note that scipy.signal.hilbert returns the full analytic signal \(z(t) = x(t) + i\hat{x}(t)\), not just the Hilbert transform \(\hat{x}(t)\). The naming is a common source of confusion.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
text:
Phase wrapping
The instantaneous phase returned by np.angle() is wrapped to the interval \([-\pi, \pi]\). This means that as the oscillation progresses, the phase increases from \(-\pi\) towards \(\pi\), then jumps back to \(-\pi\) at the start of the next cycle.
These jumps are not a problem for computing phase differences (which is what connectivity measures use), because:
\[\cos(\phi_i - \phi_j)\]
and
\[e^{i(\phi_i - \phi_j)}\]
both handle wrapped phases correctly. The cosine and complex exponential are periodic, so jumps cancel out.
However, if you want to compute a cumulative phase (e.g., to count the number of oscillatory cycles or to compute instantaneous frequency as \(f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi}\frac{d\phi}{dt}\)), you need to unwrap the phase first:
phase_unwrapped = np.unwrap(phase)

# Instantaneous frequency (Hz)
inst_freq = np.diff(phase_unwrapped) / (2 * np.pi) * sfreq
np.unwrap() detects jumps larger than \(\pi\) and adds \(\pm 2\pi\) to remove them, producing a continuous phase trace.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
text:
Why band-pass filtering comes first
The Hilbert transform gives a meaningful instantaneous phase only for narrowband signals, that is, signals whose frequency content is concentrated in a relatively narrow range.
If you apply the Hilbert transform to a broadband EEG signal (containing everything from delta to gamma), the instantaneous phase will fluctuate erratically and will not correspond to any single oscillation. The concept of “the phase of this signal” simply does not make sense when the signal contains many different oscillations superimposed.
The solution is to band-pass filter the signal to the frequency band of interest before applying the Hilbert transform. For example, if you want the phase of alpha oscillations, filter to 8–13 Hz first.
The width of the filter band matters:

Too narrow (e.g., 9.5–10.5 Hz): you lose temporal resolution because the filter output changes slowly. The instantaneous frequency is forced to stay near the centre frequency.
Too wide (e.g., 2–30 Hz): the signal is not narrowband enough for the phase to be meaningful.
Just right (e.g., 8–13 Hz for alpha): a band that covers the physiological range of the oscillation you are studying.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
section: Working example: phase extraction from a sinusoid and from EEG-like data
text:
Working example: phase extraction from a sinusoid and from EEG-like data
The code below demonstrates the Hilbert transform in two settings: first with a clean sinusoid (where the result is exactly predictable), and then with a noisy, band-pass-filtered EEG-like signal.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 2
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Part 1: Clean sinusoid
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
freq = 10.0  # Hz
sinusoid = np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * times)

# Hilbert transform
analytic_sin = hilbert(sinusoid)
phase_sin = np.angle(analytic_sin)
amplitude_sin = np.abs(analytic_sin)

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Part 2: Noisy EEG-like signal
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Pink noise background
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink_noise = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)

# Alpha oscillation embedded in noise
alpha = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times + 0.3 * np.cumsum(
    rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
eeg_signal = pink_noise + alpha

# Band-pass filter to alpha band (8-13 Hz)
b, a = butter(4, [8, 13], btype="band", fs=sfreq)
eeg_alpha = filtfilt(b, a, eeg_signal)

# Hilbert transform on the filtered signal
analytic_eeg = hilbert(eeg_alpha)
phase_eeg = np.angle(analytic_eeg)
amplitude_eeg = np.abs(analytic_eeg)

# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
# Visualisation
# ═══════════════════════════════════════════════════════════════
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7))

# ── Top left: sinusoid + envelope ──────────────────────────────
ax = axes[0, 0]
ax.plot(times, sinusoid, color="#2c3e50", linewidth=0.8, label="Signal")
ax.plot(times, amplitude_sin, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.2,
        linestyle="--", label="Envelope (amplitude)")
ax.plot(times, -amplitude_sin, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.2,
        linestyle="--")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Clean sinusoid (10 Hz)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)

# ── Top right: sinusoid phase ─────────────────────────────────
ax = axes[0, 1]
ax.plot(times, phase_sin, color="#8e44ad", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Phase (radians)")
ax.set_title("Instantaneous phase (sinusoid)")
ax.set_ylim(-np.pi - 0.3, np.pi + 0.3)
ax.axhline(np.pi, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(-np.pi, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_yticks([-np.pi, -np.pi/2, 0, np.pi/2, np.pi])
ax.set_yticklabels([r"$-\pi$", r"$-\pi/2$", "0", r"$\pi/2$", r"$\pi$"])
ax.set_xlim(0, 1)

# ── Bottom left: EEG signal + filtered + envelope ─────────────
ax = axes[1, 0]
# Normalise the raw EEG for display
eeg_norm = eeg_signal / np.max(np.abs(eeg_signal))
ax.plot(times, eeg_norm, color="#bdc3c7", linewidth=0.4,
        label="Raw EEG (normalised)")
ax.plot(times, eeg_alpha / np.max(np.abs(eeg_alpha)),
        color="#2c3e50", linewidth=0.8, label="Alpha-filtered")
env_norm = amplitude_eeg / np.max(np.abs(eeg_alpha))
ax.plot(times, env_norm, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.2,
        linestyle="--", label="Envelope")
ax.plot(times, -env_norm, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.2, linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (normalised)")
ax.set_title("EEG-like signal filtered to alpha (8\u201313 Hz)")
ax.legend(fontsize=8)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2)

# ── Bottom right: EEG phase ──────────────────────────────────
ax = axes[1, 1]
ax.plot(times, phase_eeg, color="#8e44ad", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Phase (radians)")
ax.set_title("Instantaneous phase (alpha-filtered EEG)")
ax.set_ylim(-np.pi - 0.3, np.pi + 0.3)
ax.axhline(np.pi, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(-np.pi, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_yticks([-np.pi, -np.pi/2, 0, np.pi/2, np.pi])
ax.set_yticklabels([r"$-\pi$", r"$-\pi/2$", "0", r"$\pi/2$", r"$\pi$"])
ax.set_xlim(0, 2)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Instantaneous phase extraction using the Hilbert transform. Top row: a clean 10 Hz sinusoid, where the phase increases linearly. Bottom row: a noisy EEG-like signal filtered to the alpha band, where the phase still tracks the oscillatory cycles despite the noise.




In the top row, the clean sinusoid has a constant envelope (the amplitude never changes) and a phase that increases linearly with sawtooth-like wrapping at \(\pm\pi\). This is exactly what we expect: a pure sine wave has a constant frequency and constant amplitude, so the phase grows at a steady rate.
In the bottom row, the EEG-like signal is noisier. The raw signal (grey) contains multiple frequency components. After band-pass filtering to the alpha band (blue), the oscillatory structure becomes visible. The envelope (red dashed) now varies over time, reflecting fluctuations in alpha power. The instantaneous phase (purple) still follows the sawtooth pattern, but with slight irregularities from the noise and the natural variability of the oscillation.

title: The Hilbert transform and instantaneous phase
text:
Key takeaways

The Hilbert transform converts a real signal into an analytic signal, from which you can extract the instantaneous phase and instantaneous amplitude at every time point.
In Python, scipy.signal.hilbert() returns the analytic signal (not just the Hilbert transform). Use np.angle() for phase and np.abs() for amplitude.
You must band-pass filter the signal to a narrow frequency band before applying the Hilbert transform. Broadband signals do not have a meaningful instantaneous phase.
Phase values are wrapped to \([-\pi, \pi]\). This is fine for computing phase differences and connectivity measures. Use np.unwrap() if you need cumulative phase or instantaneous frequency.
The instantaneous phase is the input to all phase-based connectivity measures: PLV, phase alignment matrices, and metastability. Getting clean phase estimates (good filtering, adequate signal-to-noise ratio) is the foundation that everything else depends on.

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
text:
Not every electrode in an EEG recording works perfectly. Gel dries out, electrodes lose contact with the scalp, cables pick up interference, and amplifiers sometimes misbehave. The result is one or more channels that record something other than brain activity. If you leave these channels in your data, they will contaminate your averages, distort your topographic maps, and throw off algorithms like ICA that assume all channels carry meaningful signal.
A bad channel typically shows one (or more) of these patterns:

Excessive noise: the channel is much noisier than its neighbours, with large, rapid voltage fluctuations that do not resemble brain activity.
Flat signal: the channel records little or no variation, either because the electrode lost contact or because the amplifier is saturated.
Slow drift: the channel shows a large, gradual shift in baseline voltage, usually from electrode polarisation or sweat bridging.
Uncorrelated activity: the channel’s signal does not resemble the signals at nearby electrodes. Since neighbouring electrodes should pick up similar brain activity (because of volume conduction), a channel that looks completely different from its neighbours is suspect.

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
text:
Manual detection
The most direct way to identify bad channels is to look at the data. MNE-Python provides interactive plotting tools for this.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Create simulated data with one bad channel ────────────────
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4",
            "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=256, ch_types="eeg")

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n_samples = 256 * 30  # 30 seconds

# Normal channels: pink-ish noise
data = rng.standard_normal((10, n_samples)) * 5e-6

# Make channel "F4" (index 3) excessively noisy
data[3, :] *= 10  # 10x the amplitude of other channels

# Make channel "O2" (index 9) flat
data[9, :] = 0.1e-6 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)  # near-zero signal

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# ── Interactive plot (scroll through and click bad channels) ──
# In an interactive session, this opens a window where you can
# click on channel names to mark them as bad
# raw.plot(scalings="auto", n_channels=10)

When you click on a channel name in the interactive plot, MNE marks it as bad and adds it to raw.info['bads']. You can also set bad channels programmatically:

# Mark channels as bad manually
raw.info["bads"] = ["F4", "O2"]
print(f"Bad channels: {raw.info['bads']}")

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
text:
Automated detection
For large datasets or when you want a reproducible pipeline, you can detect bad channels automatically. The two most common approaches are variance-based and correlation-based detection.

Variance-based detection
A noisy channel has much higher variance than a normal channel. A flat channel has much lower variance. You can flag channels whose variance falls outside a reasonable range.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Compute the variance of each channel ──────────────────────
data_array = raw.get_data()
channel_vars = np.var(data_array, axis=1)

# Compute the median and median absolute deviation (MAD) of variances
median_var = np.median(channel_vars)
mad_var = np.median(np.abs(channel_vars - median_var))

# Flag channels whose variance is more than 5 MADs from the median
threshold_high = median_var + 5 * mad_var
threshold_low = median_var - 5 * mad_var

bads_by_variance = []
for i, ch_name in enumerate(raw.ch_names):
    if channel_vars[i] > threshold_high:
        bads_by_variance.append(ch_name)
        print(f"{ch_name}: HIGH variance ({channel_vars[i]:.2e})")
    elif channel_vars[i] < max(threshold_low, 0):
        bads_by_variance.append(ch_name)
        print(f"{ch_name}: LOW variance ({channel_vars[i]:.2e})")

print(f"\nBad channels (variance): {bads_by_variance}")



Correlation-based detection
A channel that carries genuine brain signal will be correlated with its neighbours (because of volume conduction). A bad channel will show low correlation with nearby channels. This approach requires electrode locations (a montage) so that MNE can determine which channels are neighbours.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Compute pairwise correlations between channels ────────────
data_array = raw.get_data()
n_channels = data_array.shape[0]

# Correlation matrix
corr_matrix = np.corrcoef(data_array)

# For each channel, compute its mean correlation with all other channels
mean_corr = np.zeros(n_channels)
for i in range(n_channels):
    # Exclude self-correlation
    other_corrs = np.delete(corr_matrix[i, :], i)
    mean_corr[i] = np.mean(np.abs(other_corrs))

# Flag channels with very low mean correlation
corr_threshold = 0.4  # channels below this are suspicious
bads_by_corr = []
for i, ch_name in enumerate(raw.ch_names):
    if mean_corr[i] < corr_threshold:
        bads_by_corr.append(ch_name)
        print(f"{ch_name}: low correlation ({mean_corr[i]:.3f})")

print(f"\nBad channels (correlation): {bads_by_corr}")



Using RANSAC (via the autoreject package)
The autoreject package provides a more sophisticated approach called RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus). It predicts each channel’s signal from its neighbours using spherical spline interpolation, then flags channels where the prediction and the actual signal disagree. This is more robust than simple variance or correlation checks.

# Install autoreject if needed: pip install autoreject
# from autoreject import Ransac
#
# ransac = Ransac(verbose=True)
# epochs_clean = ransac.fit_transform(epochs)
# print(f"Bad channels (RANSAC): {ransac.bad_chs_}")

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
text:
Interpolation via spherical splines
Once you have identified bad channels, you have two options: exclude them or interpolate them. Interpolation estimates what the bad channel should have recorded, based on the signals at surrounding channels. MNE uses spherical spline interpolation (Perrin et al., 1989), which fits a smooth surface over the scalp and reads off the estimated value at the bad channel’s location.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Set up data with a standard montage ───────────────────────
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4",
            "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=256, ch_types="eeg")

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
data = rng.standard_normal((10, 256 * 10)) * 5e-6

# Make F4 noisy
data[3, :] *= 10

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Set a standard montage (needed for interpolation)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Mark the bad channel
raw.info["bads"] = ["F4"]

# Interpolate
raw_interp = raw.copy().interpolate_bads(reset_bads=True)

# After interpolation, the bad channel is replaced with an estimate
# and removed from the bads list (because reset_bads=True)
print(f"Bad channels after interpolation: {raw_interp.info['bads']}")

Spherical spline interpolation works by fitting a smooth surface across the scalp using the good channels as anchor points. The interpolated value at a bad channel is a weighted average of the surrounding channels, with weights that depend on the distance between electrodes. Channels that are closer contribute more.

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
section: When to interpolate vs when to exclude
text:
When to interpolate vs when to exclude
The decision between interpolation and exclusion depends on what you plan to do with the data.

Interpolate when:

You need all channels for topographic maps or source localisation. Missing channels leave gaps in the spatial coverage.
You want to use the average reference. Dropping channels changes the average and can introduce bias.
Only a few channels are bad (say, 1–3 out of 64). The interpolated values will be reliable because there are plenty of good neighbours.



Exclude when:

Many channels are bad (more than 10–15% of the total). Interpolation becomes unreliable when there are not enough good neighbours to estimate the missing signals.
The bad channels are at the edge of the array (e.g., the outermost ring), where there are few neighbours on one side.
You are doing a channel-level analysis (e.g., comparing specific channels across conditions) and do not want to include estimated data.



A general guideline
A common approach is:

Mark bad channels before any other preprocessing.
Keep them marked (but present in the data) during filtering and ICA, so that ICA does not try to decompose their noise.
Interpolate after ICA, just before computing Epochs or ERPs.
If a recording has too many bad channels (more than about 10–15% of the total), consider excluding that participant from the study rather than interpolating.


import mne

# ── Recommended workflow ──────────────────────────────────────
# 1. Load data and mark bad channels
# raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)
# raw.info["bads"] = ["F4", "T8"]

# 2. Filter (bad channels are ignored automatically)
# raw.filter(1, 40)

# 3. Run ICA (bad channels are excluded automatically)
# ica = mne.preprocessing.ICA(n_components=20)
# ica.fit(raw)
# ica.apply(raw)

# 4. Interpolate bad channels
# raw.interpolate_bads(reset_bads=True)

# 5. Re-reference (now with all channels restored)
# raw.set_eeg_reference("average", projection=False)

# 6. Epoch
# epochs = mne.Epochs(raw, events, event_id, tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8)

title: Detecting and interpolating bad channels
text:
Key takeaways

A bad channel is one that records something other than brain activity: excessive noise, flat signal, slow drifts, or activity uncorrelated with its neighbours.
Manual detection by scrolling through the data is the most reliable method for small datasets. Mark bad channels by adding their names to raw.info['bads'].
Automated detection using variance and correlation metrics provides a reproducible way to flag bad channels in larger datasets. The RANSAC method from the autoreject package is a more sophisticated option.
Spherical spline interpolation estimates the signal at a bad channel from its neighbours. It requires a montage (electrode locations) and works best when only a few channels are bad.
Interpolate when you need complete spatial coverage (for topographic maps, source localisation, or average referencing). Exclude when too many channels are bad or when the bad channels are at the edges of the array.
Mark bad channels early in the pipeline, but interpolate late (after ICA). This way, ICA does not waste components on channel noise, and the interpolated values are based on cleaned data.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Raw time-frequency power tells you how strong a particular oscillation is at a given moment, but it does not tell you whether that power level is unusual. Is 5 \(\mu V^2\) of alpha power at 300 ms post-stimulus a lot or a little? The answer depends on how much alpha power was present before the stimulus arrived. ERSP (event-related spectral perturbation) answers this question by expressing power at each time-frequency point relative to a baseline period.
ERSP is the time-frequency counterpart of the event-related potential (ERP). Where the ERP shows how average voltage changes after an event, ERSP shows how average oscillatory power changes. It reveals phenomena that ERPs cannot capture, such as alpha desynchronisation during visual processing or beta rebound after a movement. These oscillatory dynamics are central to modern EEG research on perception, motor control, attention, and clinical disorders.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
What ERSP measures
ERSP quantifies the change in spectral power at each frequency and time point, averaged across trials, relative to a pre-event baseline. The procedure is:

Epoch the continuous data around events (e.g., stimulus onset).
Compute a time-frequency representation (TFR) for each epoch, typically using Morlet wavelets.
Average the power across epochs. This gives you an AverageTFR object in MNE.
Apply baseline correction: express each time-frequency point as a change from the pre-stimulus baseline.

The baseline correction step is what transforms raw power into ERSP. Without it, you are looking at absolute power, which varies enormously across participants and frequencies (low frequencies have much more power than high frequencies, simply because of the 1/f spectrum).

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Baseline correction modes
There are several ways to express power relative to baseline. Each has advantages and trade-offs.

Percent change
\[\text{ERSP}(t, f) = \frac{P(t, f) - \bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)}{\bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)} \times 100\]
where \(P(t, f)\) is the power at time \(t\) and frequency \(f\), and \(\bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)\) is the average power at frequency \(f\) during the baseline window.
Percent change is intuitive: a value of -50 means power dropped by half compared to baseline. It is easy to interpret, but it can give very large values at frequencies where baseline power is low (because you are dividing by a small number).
In MNE: power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent")


Ratio
\[\text{ERSP}(t, f) = \frac{P(t, f)}{\bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)}\]
The ratio mode divides power by the baseline mean without subtracting first. A value of 1.0 means no change, values above 1.0 indicate an increase, and values below 1.0 indicate a decrease. This is less commonly used in publications but can be convenient for multiplicative comparisons.
In MNE: power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="ratio")


Log-ratio (decibels)
\[\text{ERSP}(t, f) = 10 \cdot \log_{10}\!\left(\frac{P(t, f)}{\bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)}\right)\]
The decibel (dB) scale compresses the dynamic range and makes increases and decreases symmetric. A doubling of power is about +3 dB, and a halving is about -3 dB. This symmetry is useful for visualisation: on a linear scale, a doubling (+100%) looks much larger than a halving (-50%), even though they represent the same magnitude of change in opposite directions.
The dB scale also reduces the influence of the 1/f spectrum, making it easier to compare effects across frequencies. This is probably the most widely used baseline correction mode in the literature.
In MNE: power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="logratio")


Z-score
\[\text{ERSP}(t, f) = \frac{P(t, f) - \bar{P}_{\text{base}}(f)}{\sigma_{\text{base}}(f)}\]
where \(\sigma_{\text{base}}(f)\) is the standard deviation of power at frequency \(f\) during the baseline window.
Z-scoring normalises by the variability of the baseline, not just its mean. A z-score of 2.0 means the power is two standard deviations above the baseline mean. This is useful when you want to know whether a change is “unusual” relative to the natural fluctuations in baseline power. It also puts all frequencies on the same scale, since each frequency is normalised by its own variability.
In MNE: power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="zscore")


Which mode should you use?
There is no single best answer. Here are some guidelines:

Percent change is good for presentations and talks because it is immediately interpretable.
dB (logratio) is the most common choice in publications. It treats increases and decreases symmetrically and compresses the dynamic range.
Z-score is useful when you want to account for baseline variability, or when you plan to compare effects across frequencies that have very different baseline power levels.
Ratio is occasionally useful but less common.

Whatever mode you choose, report it clearly in your methods section. Different modes can produce different visual impressions from the same data.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
ERD and ERS
Two of the most important patterns in ERSP are event-related desynchronisation (ERD) and event-related synchronisation (ERS).

Event-related desynchronisation (ERD)
ERD is a decrease in oscillatory power relative to baseline. It appears as negative values (blue regions) on ERSP maps. The term “desynchronisation” comes from the idea that when neurons in a cortical area become engaged in processing, they stop oscillating in synchrony and instead fire more independently. The synchronous oscillation breaks down, and the measured power drops.
The best-known examples:

Alpha ERD over occipital cortex when the eyes open or a visual stimulus appears. The posterior alpha rhythm suppresses because visual cortex becomes active.
Beta ERD over motor cortex during movement preparation and execution. Beta power drops about 500-1000 ms before movement onset and stays low during the movement.
Mu ERD (the sensorimotor alpha rhythm, ~10 Hz) over central electrodes during movement or even during observation of someone else’s movement.



Event-related synchronisation (ERS)
ERS is an increase in oscillatory power relative to baseline. It appears as positive values (red regions) on ERSP maps. ERS indicates that a population of neurons has become more synchronised.
Common examples:

Beta ERS (beta rebound) over motor cortex after a movement ends. Beta power increases above baseline levels for several hundred milliseconds. This is one of the most reliable ERS findings.
Gamma ERS in sensory cortices during stimulus processing. Brief bursts of gamma synchronisation are associated with active perceptual processing.
Theta ERS over frontal midline electrodes during working memory tasks and error processing.

The combination of ERD during a task and ERS after the task is a typical pattern. For a motor task, you see beta ERD from about -500 ms to +500 ms around movement, followed by a beta rebound (ERS) peaking around 500-1000 ms after movement ends.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Computing ERSP in MNE
In MNE, the standard workflow is:
import mne
import numpy as np

# Assume `epochs` is your preprocessed Epochs object
# with a baseline period from -0.5 to 0 s

# 1. Compute time-frequency representation with Morlet wavelets
freqs = np.arange(4, 40, 1)  # 4 to 39 Hz
power = mne.time_frequency.tfr_morlet(
    epochs, freqs=freqs, n_cycles=freqs / 2,
    return_itc=False, average=True
)

# 2. Apply baseline correction
power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent")

# 3. Plot the ERSP
power.plot([0], title="ERSP: percent change from baseline")
You can swap mode="percent" for any of the other modes described above.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Choosing the baseline window
The baseline window is the time period you treat as “normal” (pre-event activity). Choosing it well is important:

Use a pre-stimulus interval. The baseline should come before the event of interest, so it is not contaminated by the event-related response. A common choice is -500 ms to 0 ms (i.e., the half-second before stimulus onset).
Avoid edge artefacts. Wavelet convolution produces artefacts at the edges of the epoch. If your epoch starts at -1.0 s, the first 200-300 ms might be unreliable (depending on the wavelet length). Start your baseline after the edge artefact zone.
Make sure the baseline is clean. If the baseline period contains artefacts, transient responses to previous stimuli, or anticipatory activity, the baseline estimate will be wrong, and the ERSP will be distorted. With short inter-trial intervals, the baseline may overlap with the response to the previous trial.
Use the same baseline for all conditions. If you compare ERSP between conditions, the baseline window should be the same. Otherwise, differences might reflect baseline differences rather than genuine post-event effects.

A practical tip: compute ERSP with and without baseline correction, and inspect both. If you see something odd in the ERSP, checking the raw power map can help you determine whether the problem is in the post-event activity or in the baseline.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Statistical testing of ERSP
ERSP maps are rich but also high-dimensional: you have values at every combination of time point and frequency. Testing each pixel independently would involve thousands of comparisons, leading to massive multiple-comparison problems.
The standard approach is cluster-based permutation testing (Maris and Oostenveld, 2007). The idea is:

At each time-frequency point, compute a test statistic (e.g., a t-value comparing two conditions).
Threshold the map to find points that exceed a critical value.
Group adjacent supra-threshold points into clusters.
Sum the test statistics within each cluster to get a cluster-level statistic.
Build a null distribution by permuting condition labels across participants and repeating steps 1-4 many times.
Compare the observed cluster statistics to the null distribution.

This approach controls the family-wise error rate across the entire time-frequency map without being overly conservative. MNE implements it in mne.stats.permutation_cluster_test() and related functions.
from mne.stats import permutation_cluster_1samp_test

# Assume `ersp_data` is an array of shape (n_subjects, n_freqs, n_times)
# containing ERSP values (e.g., percent change from baseline)
t_obs, clusters, cluster_pv, H0 = permutation_cluster_1samp_test(
    ersp_data, n_permutations=1000, threshold=2.0, tail=0
)
The threshold parameter sets the initial t-value threshold for forming clusters. The tail parameter controls whether you test for increases only (1), decreases only (-1), or both (0).

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Working example: simulated alpha desynchronisation
The code below simulates epochs where alpha power drops between 200 and 500 ms after an event. It computes the time-frequency representation using Morlet wavelets from scipy, applies baseline correction, and plots the ERSP map. We use numpy, scipy, and matplotlib directly rather than MNE’s tfr_morlet, since that function requires MNE Epochs objects.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert

# Parameters
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sfreq = 256
n_epochs = 80
epoch_duration = 1.5  # seconds: -0.5 to 1.0 s
n_samples = int(sfreq * epoch_duration)
times = np.linspace(-0.5, 1.0, n_samples, endpoint=False)

# Frequencies for the time-frequency decomposition
freqs = np.arange(4, 36, 0.5)
n_freqs = len(freqs)

# Number of wavelet cycles (scales with frequency)
n_cycles = freqs / 2.0

# Generate simulated epochs
epochs_data = np.zeros((n_epochs, n_samples))

for ep in range(n_epochs):
    # Pink noise background
    white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1.0 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1.0
    pink_filter = 1.0 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std() * 0.8

    # Alpha oscillation (10 Hz) present throughout the epoch
    phase = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    alpha = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times + phase)

    # Create a suppression window: alpha drops between 200 and 500 ms
    suppression = np.ones(n_samples)
    mask_suppress = (times >= 0.2) & (times <= 0.5)
    # Smooth suppression using a raised cosine taper
    suppress_idx = np.where(mask_suppress)[0]
    n_suppress = len(suppress_idx)
    taper = 0.5 * (1 - np.cos(np.pi * np.arange(n_suppress) / n_suppress))
    # Suppress to 30% of original amplitude
    suppression[suppress_idx] = 1.0 - 0.7 * np.sin(
        np.pi * np.arange(n_suppress) / n_suppress
    )

    alpha_suppressed = alpha * suppression
    epochs_data[ep] = pink + alpha_suppressed

# Compute time-frequency representation using Morlet wavelets
# We convolve each epoch with wavelets at each frequency
tfr_power = np.zeros((n_epochs, n_freqs, n_samples))

def make_morlet(sfreq, freq, n_cycles):
    """Create a complex Morlet wavelet."""
    sigma_t = n_cycles / (2.0 * np.pi * freq)
    t_len = int(6 * sigma_t * sfreq)
    if t_len % 2 == 0:
        t_len += 1
    t = np.arange(-t_len // 2, t_len // 2 + 1) / sfreq
    wavelet = np.exp(2j * np.pi * freq * t) * np.exp(-t**2 / (2 * sigma_t**2))
    wavelet /= np.sqrt(np.sum(np.abs(wavelet) ** 2))
    return wavelet

for fi, (freq, nc) in enumerate(zip(freqs, n_cycles)):
    wavelet = make_morlet(sfreq, freq, nc)

    for ep in range(n_epochs):
        # Convolve signal with wavelet
        analytic = np.convolve(epochs_data[ep], wavelet, mode="same")
        tfr_power[ep, fi, :] = np.abs(analytic) ** 2

# Average across epochs
avg_power = tfr_power.mean(axis=0)  # shape: (n_freqs, n_samples)

# Apply baseline correction (percent change)
# Baseline: -0.4 to -0.1 s (avoiding very edges)
baseline_mask = (times >= -0.4) & (times <= -0.1)
baseline_power = avg_power[:, baseline_mask].mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
ersp = (avg_power - baseline_power) / baseline_power * 100

# Plot the ERSP
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

# Determine symmetric colour limits
vlim = np.percentile(np.abs(ersp), 97)
im = ax.pcolormesh(
    times, freqs, ersp,
    cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-vlim, vmax=vlim,
    shading="auto"
)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("ERSP: percent change from baseline")
ax.axvline(0, color="k", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8, label="Event onset")
ax.axhline(8, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(13, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.6, alpha=0.7)
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)

cbar = fig.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Power change (%)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Simulated ERSP showing alpha desynchronisation (200-500 ms post-event) as a blue region in the 8-13 Hz range.




The plot should show a blue region (negative percent change) in the alpha range (8-13 Hz) between approximately 200 and 500 ms after event onset. This is the simulated alpha desynchronisation: the 10 Hz oscillation was suppressed during that window, and the ERSP captures this as a power decrease relative to the pre-event baseline.
The rest of the time-frequency map should be close to zero (white or light colours), because we did not inject any other systematic power changes. Some noise is expected, especially at the edges of the epoch where the wavelet convolution produces artefacts.

title: Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
text:
Key takeaways

ERSP expresses oscillatory power relative to a pre-event baseline, revealing event-related power changes that raw power maps cannot show.
Baseline correction mode matters: percent change is intuitive, dB (logratio) is symmetric and widely used, z-score accounts for baseline variability. Report your choice in the methods.
ERD (power decrease) and ERS (power increase) are the two main patterns. Alpha ERD during stimulation and beta rebound after movement are classic examples.
Choose a clean pre-stimulus baseline window, and use the same window for all conditions.
For statistical testing of ERSP, cluster-based permutation tests control the multiple-comparison problem across the time-frequency map.
Always inspect both the raw power map and the ERSP. If the ERSP looks odd, the baseline might be contaminated.

title: Re-referencing EEG data
text:
Every EEG channel measures a voltage difference between two points on the scalp: the electrode of interest and a reference electrode. The reference electrode is chosen during recording (often Cz, the nose, or one mastoid), and its activity is subtracted from every other channel. This means that the waveform you see at any channel is not the “true” brain activity at that location. It is the difference between that location and the reference.
This matters because the reference electrode picks up its own brain activity, and that activity contaminates every channel. If the reference is at Cz, then any brain signal near Cz is partially subtracted from all other channels. If you are studying central brain activity, this is a problem.
Re-referencing changes the reference point after recording. You cannot undo the physics (you always need a reference), but you can choose a reference scheme that minimises bias for your analysis.

title: Re-referencing EEG data
text:
Every EEG channel measures a voltage difference between two points on the scalp: the electrode of interest and a reference electrode. The reference electrode is chosen during recording (often Cz, the nose, or one mastoid), and its activity is subtracted from every other channel. This means that the waveform you see at any channel is not the “true” brain activity at that location. It is the difference between that location and the reference.
This matters because the reference electrode picks up its own brain activity, and that activity contaminates every channel. If the reference is at Cz, then any brain signal near Cz is partially subtracted from all other channels. If you are studying central brain activity, this is a problem.
Re-referencing changes the reference point after recording. You cannot undo the physics (you always need a reference), but you can choose a reference scheme that minimises bias for your analysis.

title: Re-referencing EEG data
text:
Common reference schemes

Average reference
The average reference subtracts the mean of all EEG channels from each channel. The idea is that if you have enough electrodes spread evenly across the scalp, the average signal approximates zero (because positive and negative voltages across the head roughly cancel out).
When to use it: this is the most common choice for studies with dense electrode arrays (32 or more channels). It reduces the influence of any single reference location and works well for topographic mapping.
Limitations: the average reference assumes that the electrodes cover the entire head evenly. With a sparse array (e.g., 16 channels) or an array that covers only part of the scalp, the average can be biased. It also reduces the data rank by one (because the average is now zero by definition), which matters for ICA and some statistical methods.


Linked mastoids
Linked mastoids use the average of the two mastoid electrodes (the bony prominences behind the ears, typically labelled M1 and M2, or TP9 and TP10) as the reference. You compute this by averaging the two mastoid channels and subtracting the result from all EEG channels.
When to use it: this is a traditional choice in ERP research, especially for auditory and language studies. It places the reference at a relatively neutral location that is away from most cortical sources.
Limitations: the mastoids are not electrically neutral. They pick up temporal lobe activity and can introduce an asymmetry if one mastoid is noisier than the other.


Cz reference
Some recordings use Cz (the vertex) as the online reference. Cz is a common recording reference because it is easy to locate and produces stable impedances.
When to use it: you typically do not re-reference to Cz, because it is already the recording reference. But if your data was recorded with a different reference and you want to compare with older studies that used Cz, you can re-reference to it.
Limitations: Cz sits directly over the motor and somatosensory cortex. Any brain activity near Cz is subtracted from all channels, which can distort motor-related potentials and central alpha rhythms.


REST (Reference Electrode Standardisation Technique)
REST is a mathematical technique that estimates what the EEG would look like with a reference at infinity (i.e., no reference influence at all). It uses a head model to compute the transformation from the current reference to the theoretical infinity reference.
When to use it: REST is useful when you need a reference-free representation of the data, particularly for source-level analyses or when comparing data recorded with different reference schemes.
Limitations: REST requires a head model and accurate electrode locations. The result depends on the quality of these inputs. It is also computationally more involved than a simple re-referencing.

title: Re-referencing EEG data
text:
Re-referencing in MNE-Python
MNE provides the set_eeg_reference() method on Raw, Epochs, and Evoked objects. There are two ways it can handle re-referencing: the projection approach and the data approach.

The data approach (recommended for most uses)
The data approach modifies the data in place. The new reference is subtracted from every EEG channel immediately.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Create simulated data ──────────────────────────────────────
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4",
            "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2", "M1", "M2"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=256, ch_types="eeg")

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
data = rng.standard_normal((12, 256 * 10)) * 1e-6
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# ── Average reference ──────────────────────────────────────────
# Setting projection=False applies it directly to the data
raw_avg = raw.copy().set_eeg_reference("average", projection=False)
print("After average reference:")
print(raw_avg.info["custom_ref_applied"])


# ── Linked mastoids reference ──────────────────────────────────
# Re-reference to the average of M1 and M2
raw_mastoids = raw.copy().set_eeg_reference(["M1", "M2"], projection=False)
print("After linked mastoids reference:")
print(raw_mastoids.info["custom_ref_applied"])


# ── Single channel reference (e.g., Cz) ───────────────────────
# If Cz were in the data, you would do:
# raw_cz = raw.copy().set_eeg_reference(["Cz"], projection=False)



The projection approach
The projection approach does not modify the data immediately. Instead, it adds a projector to the data that is applied on the fly whenever you access the data (e.g., for plotting or computing). The raw data stored in memory remains unchanged.

# Average reference as a projection
raw_proj = raw.copy().set_eeg_reference("average", projection=True)

# The projector is stored but not yet applied
print(f"Projectors: {raw_proj.info['projs']}")

# Data is modified only when you access it:
# data_with_proj = raw_proj.get_data()  # projector applied here

The projection approach is useful when you want to:

Delay the decision about when to apply the reference
Combine the reference projector with other projectors (e.g., SSP for artifact removal)
Preserve the original data for comparison

For most analyses, the data approach (projection=False) is simpler and more transparent. You see exactly what the data looks like after re-referencing, with no hidden transformations.


REST in MNE-Python
MNE supports REST re-referencing through the same set_eeg_reference() method. You need a forward model, which MNE can compute if you have electrode locations and a head model:

# REST re-referencing (requires electrode locations and a forward model)
# This is a simplified example; in practice you would compute the
# forward model from a BEM (boundary element model) or sphere model

# raw_rest = raw.copy().set_eeg_reference("REST", projection=False)
# Note: REST requires that the Raw object has a valid montage set
# and that a forward solution is available or can be computed

REST is less commonly used in routine preprocessing, but it is valuable in studies that compare data across different recording setups.

title: Re-referencing EEG data
section: A practical note on reference and ICA
text:
A practical note on reference and ICA
If you plan to run ICA, re-reference to average before fitting ICA. The average reference reduces the data rank by one, so set the number of ICA components to n_channels - 1 to avoid numerical issues. If you re-reference after ICA, the ICA solution may not be valid because the spatial patterns were learned under a different reference.

import mne

# Re-reference to average before ICA
raw.set_eeg_reference("average", projection=False)

# Set number of ICA components to account for the rank reduction
n_components = len(raw.ch_names) - 1  # one less than the number of channels

title: Re-referencing EEG data
text:
Key takeaways

Every EEG channel measures a voltage difference relative to a reference. The choice of reference affects the shape and amplitude of your data.
Average reference is the most common choice for studies with dense arrays (32+ channels). It minimises the influence of any single reference location but reduces the data rank by one.
Linked mastoids are a traditional choice for ERP studies. They provide a relatively neutral reference for many cortical sources but are not truly inactive.
REST estimates the data as if recorded with a reference at infinity. It is useful for source-level analyses but requires electrode locations and a head model.
In MNE, use set_eeg_reference() with projection=False to modify the data directly (the data approach), or projection=True to add a projector that is applied on the fly (the projection approach). The data approach is simpler for most workflows.
Re-reference before running ICA. If you use the average reference, set the number of ICA components to n_channels - 1 to account for the rank reduction.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Most measures of brain connectivity give you a static picture: region A is connected to region B with strength 0.6. But the brain is not static. Its coordination patterns change constantly, shifting between different configurations as you think, rest, move, or sleep. Some transitions happen in milliseconds; others unfold over seconds.
Metastability captures this dynamic quality. It quantifies how much a brain region’s role in the network changes over time. A region with high metastability is flexible, moving between different coordination states. A region with low metastability is rigid, stuck in one configuration. This distinction has direct clinical relevance: several neurological conditions, including Parkinson’s disease, are characterised by abnormal rigidity in brain dynamics.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Most measures of brain connectivity give you a static picture: region A is connected to region B with strength 0.6. But the brain is not static. Its coordination patterns change constantly, shifting between different configurations as you think, rest, move, or sleep. Some transitions happen in milliseconds; others unfold over seconds.
Metastability captures this dynamic quality. It quantifies how much a brain region’s role in the network changes over time. A region with high metastability is flexible, moving between different coordination states. A region with low metastability is rigid, stuck in one configuration. This distinction has direct clinical relevance: several neurological conditions, including Parkinson’s disease, are characterised by abnormal rigidity in brain dynamics.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
What metastability means
The word “metastability” comes from physics, where it describes a system that is neither fully stable nor fully unstable. A ball sitting in a shallow dip on a hilltop is metastable: it rests there for a while, but a small push sends it rolling to a new position.
In neuroscience, Tognoli and Kelso (2014) proposed that the healthy brain operates in a metastable regime. This means that the brain does not settle into a single, fixed coordination pattern. Instead, it dwells temporarily in one pattern, transitions to another, dwells again, and so on. Each temporary dwelling state is like the ball sitting in a shallow dip: stable enough to persist for a while, but not so stable that the system cannot move on.
This framework provides a natural language for describing brain dynamics:

High metastability indicates flexible, adaptive dynamics. The brain transitions between different coordination states, which may support cognitive flexibility, attention switching, and adaptive behaviour.
Low metastability indicates rigid dynamics. The brain is locked into one coordination pattern and does not explore alternatives. This rigidity may underlie the motor and cognitive symptoms of Parkinson’s disease, the reduced awareness of disorders of consciousness, and certain features of other neurological conditions.


The energy landscape analogy
Imagine the brain’s state as a marble rolling on a hilly landscape, where each valley represents a coordination pattern (a “state”):

In a high-metastability landscape, the valleys are shallow and the barriers between them are low. The marble moves easily from one valley to another, spending some time in each but never getting trapped.
In a low-metastability landscape, the valleys are deep and the barriers are high. The marble settles into one valley and stays there. It takes a large perturbation to push it to a different state.
In a zero-metastability landscape, there is only one deep valley. The marble sits at the bottom and never moves. This is complete synchrony or complete desynchrony, with no dynamics.

The healthy brain is thought to occupy a landscape with moderate-depth valleys, supporting flexible yet structured dynamics. Disease may alter this landscape, deepening some valleys (creating rigidity) or flattening others (creating instability).

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Computing metastability from EEG
The computation of metastability from EEG data follows the approach described by Hancock et al. (2025). The pipeline has five steps:

Step 1: Band-pass filter and extract phase
Filter the EEG data to the frequency band of interest (e.g., 8–13 Hz for alpha) and apply the Hilbert transform to obtain the instantaneous phase \(\phi_k(t)\) for each channel \(k\) at each time point \(t\).


Step 2: Build the phase alignment matrix
At each time point, compute the pairwise phase alignment matrix:
\[A_{ij}(t) = \cos\!\big(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t)\big)\]
This is an \(N \times N\) symmetric matrix with ones on the diagonal, where \(N\) is the number of channels.


Step 3: Extract the dominant eigenvector
Compute the eigendecomposition of \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) and take the eigenvector corresponding to the largest eigenvalue. This dominant eigenvector \(\mathbf{v}(t)\) captures the primary coordination pattern at time \(t\).
Each element \(v_k(t)\) describes how channel \(k\) participates in the dominant pattern:

Channels with the same sign are in phase with each other.
Channels with opposite signs are in anti-phase.
The magnitude indicates how strongly the channel participates.

A sign convention is needed because eigenvectors can flip sign arbitrarily. At each time point, check whether \(\mathbf{v}(t) \cdot \mathbf{v}(t-1) < 0\) and flip if necessary, so that the eigenvector varies smoothly over time.


Step 4: Compute regional metastability
Regional metastability for channel \(k\) is the temporal variance of its eigenvector element:
\[\text{MS}_k = \text{Var}_t\!\big(v_k(t)\big)\]
A channel with high \(\text{MS}_k\) changes its role in the coordination pattern frequently (flexible). A channel with low \(\text{MS}_k\) maintains a consistent role (rigid).


Step 5: Compute global metastability (optional)
Global metastability uses the Kuramoto order parameter instead:
\[R(t) = \frac{1}{N} \left| \sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{i\phi_k(t)} \right|\]
\[\text{MS}_{\text{global}} = \text{Var}_t\!\big(R(t)\big)\]
Global metastability tells you how much the overall level of synchrony fluctuates. It is a single number for the entire recording, whereas regional metastability gives one value per channel.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Regional vs global metastability
Global metastability answers the question: “Does the overall level of synchrony change over time?” It is useful as a summary statistic, but it can miss regionally specific effects. Two groups might have similar global metastability but differ in which brain regions are flexible or rigid.
Regional metastability answers the question: “Which brain regions change their coordination role over time, and which stay fixed?” This is more informative for understanding the spatial organisation of brain dynamics and for comparing clinical populations.
For Natalia’s project, regional metastability is the primary outcome variable. The hypothesis is that Parkinson’s patients (especially those with Freezing of Gait) will show reduced regional metastability in frontal and motor regions, reflecting the rigidity of their neural dynamics. Global metastability will be reported as a complementary measure.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Interpreting high vs low values
There is no universal threshold for “high” or “low” metastability. The values depend on the frequency band, the number of channels, the recording duration, and the noise level. What matters is the comparison between groups or conditions.
That said, some guidelines:

Very low metastability (near zero for all channels) suggests that the coordination pattern is essentially static. This could mean the signal is dominated by noise (no real oscillatory structure), or the brain is in a deeply synchronised state (e.g., during a seizure).
Moderate metastability suggests healthy, flexible dynamics with transitions between coordination states.
Very high metastability could indicate instability or noise-driven fluctuations rather than meaningful state transitions. Check whether the phase estimates are reliable (is the signal-to-noise ratio in the filtered band adequate?).

When comparing groups, effect sizes and confidence intervals are more informative than raw metastability values. A difference of 0.001 in metastability between groups might be large or small depending on the overall scale.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Clinical relevance: Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease is characterised by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurones in the substantia nigra, which disrupts the basal ganglia circuits that regulate movement and cognitive flexibility.
At the level of brain dynamics, PD is associated with:

Excessive beta synchrony: abnormally strong and persistent 13–30 Hz oscillations in the basal ganglia-thalamocortical circuits. This pathological synchrony is thought to “freeze” the motor system.
Reduced flexibility: the brain’s ability to switch between coordination states is impaired. This maps directly onto the metastability framework as reduced temporal variance of the dominant eigenvector.
Dopaminergic modulation: levodopa and other dopaminergic medications reduce pathological beta synchrony and may restore some flexibility. Comparing patients ON vs OFF medication can reveal the effect of dopamine on metastability.

Freezing of Gait (FoG) is an episodic symptom where patients suddenly become unable to step forward. It may represent an extreme case of reduced metastability: the brain becomes trapped in a coordination state that prevents the initiation of the stepping motor programme.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Working example
The code below implements the full metastability pipeline on simulated data. It creates two groups of channels (flexible and rigid), computes regional metastability, and shows that the pipeline correctly recovers the difference.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── 1. Simulation parameters ──────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 12
sfreq = 256
duration = 60  # seconds (need enough data for stable variance)
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

freq_osc = 10.0  # alpha frequency

# Define two groups of channels:
# - "Rigid" channels (0-5): strongly coupled, low metastability
# - "Flexible" channels (6-11): weakly coupled, high metastability
coupling = np.array([
    0.92, 0.90, 0.88, 0.91, 0.89, 0.93,  # rigid group
    0.30, 0.25, 0.35, 0.28, 0.32, 0.22,  # flexible group
])

channel_labels = (
    ["F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "P3", "P4"]     # "rigid" (frontal/central/parietal)
    + ["T7", "T8", "O1", "O2", "Fp1", "Fp2"]  # "flexible" (temporal/occipital/frontal-pole)
)

# ── 2. Generate coupled oscillatory data ──────────────────────
# Common reference oscillation
ref_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
             + 0.3 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
ref_signal = np.sin(ref_phase)

data = np.zeros((n_channels, n_samples))
for ch in range(n_channels):
    ind_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
                 + 2.0 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
    ind_signal = np.sin(ind_phase)
    data[ch] = (coupling[ch] * ref_signal
                + (1 - coupling[ch]) * ind_signal
                + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples))

# ── 3. Band-pass filter and Hilbert transform ─────────────────
b, a = butter(4, [8, 13], btype="band", fs=sfreq)
phases = np.zeros_like(data)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    filtered = filtfilt(b, a, data[ch])
    phases[ch] = np.angle(hilbert(filtered))

# ── 4. Dominant eigenvector at each time point ────────────────
step = max(1, sfreq // 100)  # compute every 10 ms
time_indices = np.arange(0, n_samples, step)
n_timepoints = len(time_indices)

eigvec_series = np.zeros((n_channels, n_timepoints))

for ti, t in enumerate(time_indices):
    phi = phases[:, t]
    phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
    A = np.cos(phase_diff)

    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
    dominant = eigenvectors[:, -1]

    # Sign continuity
    if ti > 0 and np.dot(dominant, eigvec_series[:, ti - 1]) < 0:
        dominant = -dominant

    eigvec_series[:, ti] = dominant

# ── 5. Regional metastability ─────────────────────────────────
regional_ms = np.var(eigvec_series, axis=1)

# ── 6. Global metastability (Kuramoto) ────────────────────────
R = np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * phases[:, time_indices]), axis=0))
global_ms = np.var(R)

# ── Print results ─────────────────────────────────────────────
print("Regional metastability:")
print("-" * 45)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    group = "rigid" if ch < 6 else "flexible"
    print(f"  {channel_labels[ch]:>4s} (coupling={coupling[ch]:.2f}, "
          f"{group:>8s}):  MS = {regional_ms[ch]:.6f}")

print(f"\nMean MS (rigid group):    {regional_ms[:6].mean():.6f}")
print(f"Mean MS (flexible group): {regional_ms[6:].mean():.6f}")
print(f"Global metastability:     {global_ms:.6f}")

# ── 7. Visualisation ──────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 8))

# Panel A: Eigenvector dynamics for selected channels
ax = axes[0, 0]
t_plot = time_indices / sfreq
for ch, colour, ls in [(1, "#2c3e50", "-"), (3, "#34495e", "--"),
                        (7, "#e67e22", "-"), (9, "#e74c3c", "--")]:
    label = f"{channel_labels[ch]} ({'rigid' if ch < 6 else 'flexible'})"
    ax.plot(t_plot, eigvec_series[ch], linewidth=0.5,
            color=colour, linestyle=ls, alpha=0.8, label=label)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel(r"$v_k(t)$")
ax.set_title("A. Dominant eigenvector over time")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")
ax.set_xlim(0, 20)  # first 20 seconds

# Panel B: Regional metastability bar chart
ax = axes[0, 1]
colours = ["#2c3e50"] * 6 + ["#e67e22"] * 6
bars = ax.bar(range(n_channels), regional_ms, color=colours,
              edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Channel")
ax.set_ylabel("Regional metastability (variance)")
ax.set_title("B. Regional metastability by channel")
ax.set_xticks(range(n_channels))
ax.set_xticklabels(channel_labels, rotation=45, ha="right", fontsize=8)
# Group labels
ax.text(2.5, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "Rigid group",
        ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#2c3e50", fontstyle="italic")
ax.text(8.5, ax.get_ylim()[1] * 0.9, "Flexible group",
        ha="center", fontsize=9, color="#e67e22", fontstyle="italic")

# Panel C: Kuramoto order parameter
ax = axes[1, 0]
ax.plot(t_plot, R, linewidth=0.4, color="#8e44ad", alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(np.mean(R), color="#8e44ad", linestyle="--", linewidth=1.2,
           label=f"Mean R = {np.mean(R):.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Kuramoto R(t)")
ax.set_title("C. Global synchrony over time")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

# Panel D: Group comparison box plot
ax = axes[1, 1]
group_data = [regional_ms[:6], regional_ms[6:]]
bp = ax.boxplot(group_data, labels=["Rigid\n(strongly coupled)",
                                     "Flexible\n(weakly coupled)"],
                patch_artist=True, widths=0.5)
bp["boxes"][0].set_facecolor("#2c3e50")
bp["boxes"][0].set_alpha(0.6)
bp["boxes"][1].set_facecolor("#e67e22")
bp["boxes"][1].set_alpha(0.6)
for median in bp["medians"]:
    median.set_color("black")
    median.set_linewidth(1.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Regional metastability")
ax.set_title("D. Group comparison")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Regional metastability:
---------------------------------------------
    F3 (coupling=0.92,    rigid):  MS = 0.000023
    F4 (coupling=0.90,    rigid):  MS = 0.000014
    C3 (coupling=0.88,    rigid):  MS = 0.000014
    C4 (coupling=0.91,    rigid):  MS = 0.000024
    P3 (coupling=0.89,    rigid):  MS = 0.000020
    P4 (coupling=0.93,    rigid):  MS = 0.000023
    T7 (coupling=0.30, flexible):  MS = 0.000040
    T8 (coupling=0.25, flexible):  MS = 0.000805
    O1 (coupling=0.35, flexible):  MS = 0.000370
    O2 (coupling=0.28, flexible):  MS = 0.000037
   Fp1 (coupling=0.32, flexible):  MS = 0.000177
   Fp2 (coupling=0.22, flexible):  MS = 0.000060

Mean MS (rigid group):    0.000020
Mean MS (flexible group): 0.000248
Global metastability:     0.000304
