  bp = ax.boxplot(group_data, labels=["Rigid\n(strongly coupled)",





Regional metastability computed from simulated EEG. Weakly coupled channels (simulating flexible regions) show higher metastability than strongly coupled channels (simulating rigid regions). This is the pattern we expect to see reversed in Parkinson’s disease: motor and frontal regions may show abnormally low metastability.





Reading the output
Panel A shows the dominant eigenvector element \(v_k(t)\) for four channels over the first 20 seconds. The rigid channels (dark blue tones) hold a relatively steady value, meaning their role in the coordination pattern does not change much. The flexible channels (orange/red tones) fluctuate considerably, indicating that their coordination role keeps shifting.
Panel B is the main result. The bar chart shows regional metastability for each channel. The six rigid channels (left, dark) have low metastability, while the six flexible channels (right, orange) have high metastability. This matches the coupling strengths we set in the simulation.
Panel C shows the Kuramoto order parameter \(R(t)\) over time. It fluctuates around a moderate value, reflecting the mix of strongly and weakly coupled channels.
Panel D compares the two groups as a box plot. The separation is clear, demonstrating that the metastability pipeline can distinguish between regions with different dynamic properties.

title: Metastability: theory and computation
text:
Key takeaways

Metastability quantifies how much a brain region’s coordination role changes over time. It is computed as the temporal variance of the dominant eigenvector of the phase alignment matrix.
The concept comes from dynamical systems theory (Tognoli and Kelso, 2014). A metastable brain dwells temporarily in coordination patterns but transitions flexibly between them.
The computation follows five steps: (1) band-pass filter, (2) Hilbert transform for phase, (3) phase alignment matrix, (4) dominant eigenvector extraction, (5) temporal variance.
Regional metastability gives one value per channel, telling you which brain regions are flexible and which are rigid. This is more informative than global metastability, which gives a single summary number.
In Parkinson’s disease, the hypothesis is that motor and frontal regions show reduced metastability (excessive rigidity), especially in patients with Freezing of Gait.
Metastability values are meaningful only in comparison (between groups, conditions, or frequency bands). There is no universal threshold for “high” or “low”.
Practical considerations: use enough data (at least 30–60 seconds of clean recording) for stable variance estimates, and choose the frequency band based on the research question (beta for motor-related hypotheses, alpha for resting-state).

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
The ICA theory page explains what ICA does and why it works. This page is about the mechanics: how to run ICA in MNE-Python, inspect the results, decide which components to remove, and apply the correction to your data. Think of this as the hands-on companion to the conceptual page.
MNE wraps everything into the mne.preprocessing.ICA class. You create an ICA object, fit it to your data, inspect and label artifact components, and then apply the correction. The class keeps track of the unmixing matrix, component topographies, and your exclusion decisions, so you can save and reload the full solution later.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
The ICA theory page explains what ICA does and why it works. This page is about the mechanics: how to run ICA in MNE-Python, inspect the results, decide which components to remove, and apply the correction to your data. Think of this as the hands-on companion to the conceptual page.
MNE wraps everything into the mne.preprocessing.ICA class. You create an ICA object, fit it to your data, inspect and label artifact components, and then apply the correction. The class keeps track of the unmixing matrix, component topographies, and your exclusion decisions, so you can save and reload the full solution later.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Creating the ICA object
The first step is to create an ICA instance and set a few parameters.

import mne
from mne.preprocessing import ICA

# Create the ICA object
ica = ICA(
    n_components=20,       # number of components to extract
    method="infomax",      # ICA algorithm
    fit_params=dict(extended=True),  # use extended infomax
    random_state=42,       # for reproducibility
    max_iter=500           # maximum iterations for convergence
)


Choosing n_components
The n_components parameter controls how many independent components ICA extracts. You have three main options:

n_components = None (default): uses the number of channels. This gives ICA maximum freedom to separate sources. It is the right choice when your data has full rank.
n_components = n (an integer): extracts exactly n components. Useful if your data rank is reduced (for example, after average re-referencing or removing bad channels). You can check the data rank with mne.compute_rank(raw).
n_components = 0.99 (a float between 0 and 1): retains enough PCA components to explain that fraction of the variance. This is a convenient way to let MNE figure out the right number automatically.

A practical rule: check the data rank first, and set n_components to match it.

# Check the data rank
rank = mne.compute_rank(raw, rank="info")
print(f"Data rank: {rank}")

# Set n_components to match the rank
n_comp = list(rank.values())[0]
ica = ICA(n_components=int(n_comp), method="infomax",
          fit_params=dict(extended=True), random_state=42)

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Algorithm options
MNE supports three ICA algorithms. Each finds independent components through a different mathematical strategy, but in practice they all produce similar results for typical EEG data.










Algorithm
method=
Speed
Stability
Notes




FastICA
"fastica"
Fast
Moderate
Default in MNE. Can vary between runs.


Infomax
"infomax"
Moderate
High
Gold standard for EEG. Use extended=True.


Picard
"picard"
Fast
High
Requires python-picard package. Combines speed and stability.



For research analysis, extended Infomax is the safest choice. It handles both sub-Gaussian and super-Gaussian sources (which matters because blink artifacts have a super-Gaussian distribution while muscle artifacts tend to be sub-Gaussian). FastICA is fine for quick exploration or teaching.
Picard is a newer option that converges faster than Infomax while maintaining comparable stability. If you install the python-picard package (pip install python-picard), you can use it by setting method="picard".

# FastICA (default, fast but less stable)
ica_fast = ICA(n_components=20, method="fastica", random_state=42)

# Extended Infomax (recommended for EEG)
ica_infomax = ICA(n_components=20, method="infomax",
                  fit_params=dict(extended=True), random_state=42)

# Picard (fast and stable, needs python-picard)
ica_picard = ICA(n_components=20, method="picard", random_state=42)

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Fitting ICA
Once you have created the ICA object, you fit it to your data using ica.fit(). ICA learns the unmixing matrix from the data, so the quality of the fit depends on the data you give it.

# Fit ICA on the raw data
ica.fit(raw)

# You can also fit on epochs
# ica.fit(epochs)


Filtering before fitting
ICA works best on data that has been high-pass filtered at 1 Hz or higher. Slow drifts (below 1 Hz) violate the stationarity assumption and can produce unreliable decompositions. If your main analysis requires a lower high-pass cutoff (say, 0.1 Hz), create a copy of your data filtered at 1 Hz just for fitting ICA, then apply the ICA solution to the original data.

# Filter a copy at 1 Hz for ICA fitting
raw_for_ica = raw.copy().filter(l_freq=1.0, h_freq=None)

# Fit ICA on the filtered copy
ica.fit(raw_for_ica)

# Apply the solution to the original (less aggressively filtered) data
ica.apply(raw)  # modifies raw in-place



Excluding bad segments
If your data contains annotations starting with “BAD” (from visual inspection or automated rejection), ICA will skip those segments during fitting. This is the intended behaviour: you do not want ICA to learn from corrupted data.

# ICA automatically excludes BAD-annotated segments
print(f"Annotations: {raw.annotations}")
ica.fit(raw)  # BAD segments are skipped

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Plotting and inspecting components
After fitting, you need to inspect the components to decide which ones are artifacts. MNE provides several plotting methods for this.

Component topographies
ica.plot_components() shows the scalp topography of each component. This is usually the first thing you look at, because the spatial pattern is the most reliable indicator of what a component represents.

# Plot topographies of all components
ica.plot_components()

# Plot only the first 10 components
ica.plot_components(picks=range(10))

Blink components have a strong frontal pattern (concentrated at Fp1/Fp2). Muscle components show peripheral patterns at temporal or frontal edges. Brain components typically have smooth, focal spatial patterns.


Component time courses
ica.plot_sources() shows the time course of each component, similar to scrolling through raw data. This lets you see the temporal structure: blinks appear as intermittent sharp deflections, heartbeat components show a regular rhythm, and muscle components look like bursts of high-frequency noise.

# Plot component time courses (interactive viewer)
ica.plot_sources(raw)

# You can also plot sources for epochs
# ica.plot_sources(epochs)



Detailed component properties
ica.plot_properties() shows a comprehensive view of a single component: its topography, time course, power spectrum, and epoch image (if epochs are provided). This is the most informative view for making a decision about a specific component.

# Detailed properties of component 0
ica.plot_properties(raw, picks=[0])

# Properties of multiple components
ica.plot_properties(raw, picks=[0, 1, 2])

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Excluding components
Once you have identified artifact components, you mark them for exclusion by adding their indices to ica.exclude.

# Mark components 0 and 3 as artifacts
ica.exclude = [0, 3]

# Or add to the existing list
ica.exclude.append(5)

print(f"Components to exclude: {ica.exclude}")

You can also mark components interactively. When you click on a component in the plot_components() or plot_sources() viewer, MNE adds or removes it from ica.exclude.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Applying ICA
ica.apply() reconstructs the data without the excluded components. This is the step that actually cleans your data.

# Apply ICA correction (modifies raw in-place)
ica.apply(raw)

# To keep the original data, work on a copy
raw_clean = raw.copy()
ica.apply(raw_clean)

A note about what happens under the hood: ica.apply() does not simply zero out the excluded component time courses. It projects the data into the ICA space, removes the excluded components, and projects back. This is mathematically equivalent but handles the PCA reduction step correctly.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Saving and loading ICA solutions
You can save an ICA solution to disk and reload it later. This is useful when you want to review or modify your component selections without re-fitting ICA (which takes time and, for non-deterministic algorithms, might give different results).

# Save the ICA solution (including exclude list)
ica.save("subject01-ica.fif", overwrite=True)

# Load it back
ica_loaded = mne.preprocessing.read_ica("subject01-ica.fif")
print(f"Excluded components: {ica_loaded.exclude}")

# Apply the loaded solution to data
ica_loaded.apply(raw)

The saved file contains the unmixing matrix, the mixing matrix, the PCA components, and the exclude list. It does not contain the original data, so the file is small.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Working example
The code below demonstrates the full ICA workflow using simulated data. We create multi-channel data with a clear blink artifact, fit ICA using scikit-learn’s FastICA (to avoid requiring an interactive MNE session), identify the blink component by its frontal projection, remove it, and compare the data before and after correction.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Simulation parameters ──────────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 8
sfreq = 256
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

channel_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"]

# ── Create source signals ─────────────────────────────────────
# Source 1: Alpha oscillation (10 Hz, brain)
alpha = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
alpha += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# Source 2: Theta oscillation (6 Hz, brain)
theta = 0.7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 6 * times + 1.0)
theta += 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# Source 3: Blink artifact (intermittent sharp peaks)
blink = np.zeros(n_samples)
for bt in [1.0, 2.8, 4.5, 6.2, 7.9, 9.5]:
    idx = int(bt * sfreq)
    width = int(0.15 * sfreq)
    if idx + width < n_samples:
        t_b = np.arange(width) / sfreq
        blink[idx:idx + width] = 5 * np.sin(np.pi * t_b / (width / sfreq))

# Source 4: Background noise
noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── Mixing matrix (channels x sources) ────────────────────────
# Blink projects strongly to Fp1, Fp2 and weakly to posterior channels
mixing = np.array([
    [0.4, 0.3, 1.0, 0.4],   # Fp1
    [0.4, 0.3, 0.95, 0.4],  # Fp2
    [0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.3],   # F3
    [0.7, 0.5, 0.25, 0.3],  # F4
    [0.9, 0.4, 0.05, 0.3],  # C3
    [0.9, 0.4, 0.05, 0.3],  # C4
    [1.0, 0.2, 0.02, 0.2],  # O1
    [1.0, 0.2, 0.02, 0.2],  # O2
])

sources = np.vstack([alpha, theta, blink, noise])
data = mixing @ sources
data *= 30e-6 / data.std()  # scale to realistic amplitude

# ── Fit ICA ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ica = FastICA(n_components=4, random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
components = ica.fit_transform(data.T).T
ica_mixing = ica.mixing_

# ── Identify the blink component ──────────────────────────────
# Blink component has the largest loading on frontal channels
frontal_loading = np.abs(ica_mixing[:2, :]).mean(axis=0)
blink_ic = np.argmax(frontal_loading)
print(f"Blink component: IC {blink_ic} "
      f"(frontal loading = {frontal_loading[blink_ic]:.4f})")

# ── Remove the blink component ────────────────────────────────
clean_components = components.copy()
clean_components[blink_ic] = 0
data_clean = ica_mixing @ clean_components

# ── Plot results ───────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(13, 9))

# Original data
ax = axes[0]
offset = 0
for ch in [0, 1, 6, 7]:
    trace = data[ch] / np.max(np.abs(data)) + offset
    ax.plot(times, trace, lw=0.5, label=channel_names[ch])
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Original data (with blink artifact)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

# ICA components
ax = axes[1]
offset = 0
for i in range(4):
    trace = components[i] / np.max(np.abs(components)) + offset
    colour = "#e74c3c" if i == blink_ic else "#2c3e50"
    lw = 1.0 if i == blink_ic else 0.5
    label = f"IC {i}" + (" (blink)" if i == blink_ic else "")
    ax.plot(times, trace, lw=lw, color=colour, label=label)
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Independent components")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

# Cleaned data
ax = axes[2]
offset = 0
for ch in [0, 1, 6, 7]:
    trace = data_clean[ch] / np.max(np.abs(data_clean)) + offset
    ax.plot(times, trace, lw=0.5, label=channel_names[ch])
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Cleaned data (blink component removed)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Blink component: IC 3 (frontal loading = 0.0000)





Full ICA workflow on simulated data. Top: original data with blink artifacts visible at frontal channels. Middle: extracted ICA components, with the blink component highlighted in red. Bottom: cleaned data after removing the blink component.




The top panel shows the original data. Notice the large blink deflections at Fp1 and Fp2, with smaller deflections propagating to other channels. The middle panel shows the four extracted components: one of them (highlighted in red) captures the blink artifact with its characteristic sharp, intermittent peaks. The bottom panel shows the data after removing the blink component. The frontal channels are now clean, while the brain oscillations at all channels are preserved.

title: ICA in MNE-Python
text:
Key takeaways

MNE’s mne.preprocessing.ICA class handles the full ICA workflow: fitting, inspection, component exclusion, and correction.
Set n_components to match your data rank. Check the rank with mne.compute_rank(), especially after average re-referencing or bad channel removal.
Extended Infomax (method="infomax" with fit_params=dict(extended=True)) is the recommended algorithm for EEG. Picard is a faster alternative with comparable stability.
Always high-pass filter at 1 Hz before fitting ICA. If your analysis requires a lower cutoff, filter a copy for ICA fitting and apply the solution to the original data.
Use ica.plot_components() for topographies, ica.plot_sources() for time courses, and ica.plot_properties() for a detailed view of individual components.
Mark artifact components in ica.exclude and call ica.apply() to reconstruct clean data. Work on a copy if you want to preserve the original.
Save your ICA solution with ica.save(). The file stores the full decomposition and your exclusion decisions, so you can reload and modify them without re-fitting.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
EEG electrodes pick up electrical activity from the brain, but they also pick up electrical activity from other sources: eye movements, muscle contractions, the heartbeat, and physical movement of the electrodes. These non-brain signals are called artifacts. They can be much larger than the brain signals you care about (a single eye blink can be 10 times the amplitude of an alpha oscillation), and they can distort your analysis if you do not recognise and handle them.
Before you can remove artifacts, you need to know what they look like. Each type has a characteristic signature in the time domain, a typical frequency range, and a predictable spatial distribution across the scalp. Learning to recognise these patterns is the first step in any preprocessing pipeline.

text:

Before you can remove artifacts, you need to know what they look like. Each type has a characteristic signature in the time domain, a typical frequency range, and a predictable spatial distribution across the scalp. Learning to recognise these patterns is the first step in any preprocessing pipeline.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Ocular artifacts

Eye blinks
Eye blinks are the most common and most recognisable EEG artifact. When you blink, the eyelid slides over the positively charged cornea, creating a large electrical potential change that propagates across the scalp.
What it looks like: a sharp, positive-going deflection lasting about 200 to 400 milliseconds, followed by a return to baseline. The waveform has a roughly triangular or bell-shaped appearance.
Which channels are affected: blink artifacts are largest at frontal electrodes, especially Fp1 and Fp2 (the frontopolar sites, right above the eyes). The amplitude decreases as you move towards the back of the head. Central electrodes (Cz, C3, C4) show a moderate effect, and occipital electrodes (O1, O2) are usually unaffected.
Frequency characteristics: the energy is concentrated below 5 Hz, mostly in the delta range. This means that blinks overlap spectrally with slow brain oscillations, and you cannot remove them by simple low-pass filtering without also destroying delta and theta activity.


Saccades (horizontal and vertical eye movements)
When you move your eyes, the corneal-retinal dipole (the eye acts like a small battery, positive at the front and negative at the back) rotates. This creates a sustained potential shift in the EEG.
What it looks like: a step-like shift in the signal that lasts as long as the eye is in its new position. Horizontal saccades produce opposite-polarity deflections on the left and right sides of the scalp: if F7 goes positive, F8 goes negative, and vice versa. Vertical eye movements produce a bilateral frontal deflection similar to blinks, but smaller and more sustained.
Which channels are affected: horizontal saccades affect lateral frontal channels (F7, F8, AF7, AF8) most strongly. Vertical eye movements affect midline frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2, Fpz). Both types diminish towards posterior electrodes.
Frequency characteristics: the frequency content depends on the speed of the eye movement, but most of the energy is below 8 Hz.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Muscular artifacts (EMG)
Muscles produce electrical activity when they contract. Any muscle near the head (jaw, forehead, neck, scalp) can inject artifact into EEG electrodes. Common sources include jaw clenching (temporalis and masseter muscles), teeth grinding (bruxism), frowning, and neck tension.
What it looks like: EMG artifact has a distinctive high-frequency, spiky appearance. It looks like a burst of rapid, irregular oscillations superimposed on the EEG. In mild cases, it adds a “fuzzy” quality to the signal. In severe cases, it can completely obscure the underlying brain activity.
Which channels are affected: temporal electrodes (T7, T8, FT9, FT10) are most susceptible because they sit directly over the temporalis muscle. Frontal electrodes pick up forehead muscle activity. Posterior channels can be affected by neck muscles, especially during head movements.
Frequency characteristics: EMG energy is concentrated above 20 Hz, with a broad spectral bump that can extend up to 200 Hz or higher. This overlaps with beta and gamma bands, making it a serious concern for any analysis involving high-frequency brain activity. At the same time, very strong muscle contractions can also inject energy into lower frequencies (down to about 10 Hz).

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Cardiac artifacts (ECG)
The heart is a powerful electrical generator. Its electrical field can propagate through the body and reach the scalp, appearing as a periodic artifact in the EEG.
What it looks like: a regular, repeating waveform that follows the heart rate (typically 60 to 100 beats per minute). The artifact looks like a small, sharp spike (corresponding to the QRS complex of the ECG) followed by a slower wave. The shape is consistent across heartbeats, which helps distinguish it from random noise.
Which channels are affected: the cardiac artifact is typically diffuse, affecting many channels at once. It is often most visible at temporal and mastoid electrodes, and it can be particularly prominent in recordings with linked-ear references. Its amplitude is usually small compared to blinks and muscle artifacts, but it can become noticeable in high-density recordings or when other noise sources have been removed.
Frequency characteristics: the heart rate determines the fundamental frequency (about 1 to 1.7 Hz for rates of 60 to 100 bpm), but the sharp QRS complex introduces harmonics that can extend into the alpha and beta ranges (up to about 30 Hz). This means the cardiac artifact can contaminate spectral analyses across a wide range of frequencies.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Movement artifacts
Physical movement of the electrodes, the cable, or the participant’s head creates artifacts through two mechanisms: changes in the electrode-skin impedance and changes in the static charge on the electrode.
What it looks like: large, slow, irregular deflections that do not follow any rhythmic pattern. Movement artifacts are often asymmetric (one side of the head shifts more than the other if the participant turns their head) and can include sudden jumps or baseline shifts. In severe cases, one or more channels may “rail”, meaning they hit the amplifier’s maximum or minimum voltage and saturate.
Which channels are affected: movement artifacts tend to be widespread, affecting many or all channels at once. The specific pattern depends on the type of movement. Head rotations affect channels on the side the participant turns towards. Cable movement tends to affect the channels nearest to the disturbed cable. Electrode pops (brief losses of skin contact) typically affect a single channel with a sharp, vertical spike.
Frequency characteristics: the energy is concentrated at very low frequencies, mostly below 2 Hz, because the movements are slow compared to brain oscillations. Single-channel electrode pops, however, can produce broadband artifacts that extend across all frequencies.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Working example
The code below simulates all four artifact types and plots them side by side so you can see how each one appears in a time series. We add each artifact to a common alpha oscillation background so you can see how it distorts the underlying brain signal.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Simulation parameters ─────────────────────────────────────
sfreq = 256
duration = 4
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# ── Clean alpha oscillation (shared background) ──────────────
alpha = 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
alpha += 2e-6 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── 1. Eye blink artifact ────────────────────────────────────
blink = np.zeros(n_samples)
blink_times = [0.8, 2.0, 3.2]
for bt in blink_times:
    idx = int(bt * sfreq)
    width = int(0.2 * sfreq)
    if idx + width < n_samples:
        t_bl = np.arange(width) / sfreq
        blink[idx:idx + width] = 80e-6 * np.sin(np.pi * t_bl / (width / sfreq))

signal_blink = alpha + blink

# ── 2. Muscle artifact (EMG) ─────────────────────────────────
emg = np.zeros(n_samples)
emg_start = int(1.2 * sfreq)
emg_end = int(2.5 * sfreq)
emg_burst = 15e-6 * rng.standard_normal(emg_end - emg_start)
# Add high-frequency content (30-80 Hz)
for freq in np.arange(30, 80, 5):
    emg_burst += 5e-6 * np.sin(
        2 * np.pi * freq * np.arange(emg_end - emg_start) / sfreq
        + rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    )
# Taper the onset and offset
taper_len = int(0.05 * sfreq)
taper = np.ones(emg_end - emg_start)
taper[:taper_len] = np.linspace(0, 1, taper_len)
taper[-taper_len:] = np.linspace(1, 0, taper_len)
emg[emg_start:emg_end] = emg_burst * taper

signal_emg = alpha + emg

# ── 3. Cardiac artifact (ECG) ────────────────────────────────
ecg = np.zeros(n_samples)
heart_rate = 72  # bpm
beat_interval = sfreq * 60 / heart_rate
beat_positions = np.arange(0, n_samples, beat_interval).astype(int)
for bp in beat_positions:
    # QRS complex: sharp spike lasting about 80 ms
    qrs_width = int(0.04 * sfreq)
    if bp + qrs_width < n_samples:
        t_qrs = np.arange(qrs_width) / sfreq
        qrs = 8e-6 * np.sin(np.pi * t_qrs / (qrs_width / sfreq))
        ecg[bp:bp + qrs_width] += qrs
    # T-wave: slower, broader bump about 200 ms after QRS
    t_offset = int(0.2 * sfreq)
    t_width = int(0.12 * sfreq)
    if bp + t_offset + t_width < n_samples:
        t_tw = np.arange(t_width) / sfreq
        t_wave = 3e-6 * np.sin(np.pi * t_tw / (t_width / sfreq))
        ecg[bp + t_offset:bp + t_offset + t_width] += t_wave

signal_ecg = alpha + ecg

# ── 4. Movement artifact ─────────────────────────────────────
# Slow baseline drift with a sudden shift
movement = np.zeros(n_samples)
# Slow sinusoidal drift (0.3 Hz)
movement += 30e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.3 * times)
# Sudden baseline shift at t = 2.5 s
shift_start = int(2.5 * sfreq)
shift_duration = int(0.3 * sfreq)
if shift_start + shift_duration < n_samples:
    movement[shift_start:shift_start + shift_duration] += np.linspace(
        0, 50e-6, shift_duration
    )
    movement[shift_start + shift_duration:] += 50e-6

signal_movement = alpha + movement

# ── Visualisation ─────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(13, 7), sharex=True)
scale = 1e6  # convert to microvolts

titles = [
    "Eye blink artifact (Fp1)",
    "Muscle artifact / EMG (T7)",
    "Cardiac artifact / ECG (T8)",
    "Movement artifact (Cz)"
]
signals = [signal_blink, signal_emg, signal_ecg, signal_movement]
artifacts = [blink, emg, ecg, movement]
colours = ["#e74c3c", "#e67e22", "#8e44ad", "#27ae60"]

for ax, title, sig, art, col in zip(
    axes.flat, titles, signals, artifacts, colours
):
    ax.plot(times, sig * scale, color="#2c3e50", linewidth=0.5,
            label="Signal + artifact")
    ax.plot(times, alpha * scale, color="#bdc3c7", linewidth=0.4,
            label="Clean alpha", alpha=0.7)
    ax.fill_between(times, (alpha * scale), (sig * scale),
                     color=col, alpha=0.15, label="Artifact contribution")
    ax.set_title(title, fontsize=10)
    ax.set_ylabel(r"Amplitude ($\mu$V)")
    ax.legend(fontsize=7, loc="upper right")

axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Four common EEG artifact types, each shown alongside a clean alpha oscillation for comparison. Top left: eye blink (sharp frontal deflection). Top right: muscle artifact (high-frequency burst). Bottom left: cardiac artifact (regular QRS-like spikes). Bottom right: movement artifact (slow baseline drift).




Each panel shows the clean alpha oscillation (grey) alongside the contaminated signal (dark blue). The shaded region highlights the artifact contribution. Notice how the blink artifact dwarfs the alpha rhythm, the muscle artifact adds high-frequency fuzz, the cardiac artifact produces regularly spaced small spikes, and the movement artifact creates a slow drift that shifts the baseline.

title: Types of EEG artifacts
text:
Key takeaways

Eye blinks are the largest and most common artifact. They produce sharp, positive deflections at frontal electrodes, with energy below 5 Hz. Saccades (eye movements) produce step-like shifts, strongest at lateral frontal sites.
Muscle artifacts (EMG) look like high-frequency bursts and affect temporal and frontal electrodes. Their energy is above 20 Hz, which overlaps with beta and gamma bands.
Cardiac artifacts (ECG) produce regular, small spikes at the heart rate. They are diffuse across the scalp and contain harmonics that extend into the alpha and beta ranges.
Movement artifacts cause slow baseline drifts and sudden shifts. They are widespread and concentrated below 2 Hz, though electrode pops can produce broadband spikes.
Each artifact type has a characteristic time-domain shape, spatial distribution, and frequency range. Learning to recognise these patterns is the first step in deciding how to handle them (filtering, ICA, rejection, or a combination).

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
When neuroscientists talk about brain activity, they often talk in terms of frequency bands: “alpha power increased when participants closed their eyes” or “theta oscillations were stronger during memory encoding.” These frequency bands are the vocabulary of EEG research, and understanding them is essential for interpreting both your own data and the published literature.
The brain produces electrical activity across a wide range of frequencies, from below 1 Hz to above 100 Hz. Early EEG researchers noticed that activity in different frequency ranges tended to appear under different behavioural conditions, and they gave these ranges Greek letter names. The boundaries between bands are somewhat arbitrary (different sources use slightly different cutoffs), but the conventional divisions have been stable for decades.

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
When neuroscientists talk about brain activity, they often talk in terms of frequency bands: “alpha power increased when participants closed their eyes” or “theta oscillations were stronger during memory encoding.” These frequency bands are the vocabulary of EEG research, and understanding them is essential for interpreting both your own data and the published literature.
The brain produces electrical activity across a wide range of frequencies, from below 1 Hz to above 100 Hz. Early EEG researchers noticed that activity in different frequency ranges tended to appear under different behavioural conditions, and they gave these ranges Greek letter names. The boundaries between bands are somewhat arbitrary (different sources use slightly different cutoffs), but the conventional divisions have been stable for decades.

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
The five classical bands

Delta (1–4 Hz)
Delta waves are the slowest EEG oscillations. They are large, high-amplitude waves that dominate the EEG during deep (stage 3) sleep. In waking adults, prominent delta activity is unusual and can indicate brain pathology (e.g., focal brain lesions, encephalopathy) or drowsiness.
Delta activity is also studied in the context of slow oscillations during sleep, where it plays a role in memory consolidation. The “up states” and “down states” of cortical neurons during deep sleep cycle at delta frequencies.


Theta (4–8 Hz)
Theta oscillations are associated with memory processes, spatial navigation, and drowsiness. In the hippocampus (measured with intracranial electrodes or estimated from scalp EEG), theta is linked to memory encoding and retrieval. Frontal midline theta (strongest at Fz) increases during tasks that require sustained attention or working memory.
In clinical settings, excessive theta in the waking EEG can indicate drowsiness, cognitive decline, or certain neurological conditions. Theta is also prominent during light sleep (stage 1) and in the transition from wakefulness to sleep.


Alpha (8–13 Hz)
Alpha is the most studied EEG rhythm and was the first to be identified by Hans Berger in 1929. It is strongest over the posterior scalp (O1, O2, Oz, P3, P4, Pz) and increases when participants close their eyes and relax. It decreases (or “desynchronises”) when participants open their eyes, engage in mental calculation, or attend to a visual stimulus.
Alpha is widely interpreted as reflecting cortical “idling” or active inhibition of task-irrelevant regions. If you are not using the visual cortex, alpha power increases over occipital electrodes. If you are not using the motor cortex, a similar rhythm (called the mu rhythm, also in the alpha range) increases over central electrodes.


Beta (13–30 Hz)
Beta oscillations are associated with active cognitive processing, motor planning, and sustained attention. Over the motor cortex (C3, C4, Cz), beta decreases before and during movement (event-related desynchronisation) and increases after movement ends (beta rebound).
Pharmacologically, beta activity increases with drugs that enhance GABAergic inhibition (such as benzodiazepines and barbiturates) and with alertness-promoting agents. In clinical EEG, excessive fast (beta) activity is sometimes seen with sedative medications or anxiety.


Gamma (30–100+ Hz)
Gamma oscillations are the fastest rhythms studied in scalp EEG. They are associated with perception, attention, consciousness, and the “binding” of features into coherent percepts. For example, gamma power increases when participants perceive a meaningful visual object compared to a scrambled version of the same stimulus.
Gamma is the most difficult band to study with scalp EEG because it overlaps with the frequency range of muscle artifact (EMG). A burst of jaw clenching or forehead tension can produce broadband activity in the 20–100 Hz range that looks like gamma. Careful artifact handling is essential when working with gamma, and some researchers argue that scalp-recorded gamma should be interpreted with caution unless EMG contamination has been ruled out.

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
Sub-bands
Each band can be divided into sub-bands that have somewhat different functional profiles.

Alpha sub-bands

Low alpha (8–10 Hz): associated with general arousal and attention. Tends to show widespread desynchronisation during cognitive tasks.
High alpha (10–13 Hz): associated with more specific, task-related processing. Desynchronises more selectively (e.g., only over the cortical region engaged by the task).

The split at 10 Hz is approximate. Some researchers use each participant’s individual alpha frequency (IAF) as the boundary: low alpha is IAF minus 2 Hz to IAF, and high alpha is IAF to IAF plus 2 Hz.


Beta sub-bands

Low beta (13–20 Hz): sometimes called beta-1. Associated with relaxed but alert states and light motor activity.
High beta (20–30 Hz): sometimes called beta-2. Associated with active problem-solving, anxiety, and intense concentration.



Theta sub-bands
Some researchers distinguish between slow theta (4–6 Hz) and fast theta (6–8 Hz), with slow theta being more associated with drowsiness and fast theta with cognitive processes. This distinction is less established than the alpha and beta sub-bands.

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
Computing band power
Band power is the amount of energy in a specific frequency range. There are several ways to compute it, but the most common approach is to estimate the power spectral density (PSD) and then integrate over the frequency range of interest.

Using Welch’s method

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import welch

# Assume 'signal' is a 1D numpy array and sfreq is the sampling rate
sfreq = 256
freqs, psd = welch(signal, fs=sfreq, nperseg=2 * sfreq)

# Define band boundaries
bands = {
    "delta": (1, 4),
    "theta": (4, 8),
    "alpha": (8, 13),
    "beta":  (13, 30),
    "gamma": (30, 45)
}

# Compute absolute power in each band
band_power = {}
for band_name, (low, high) in bands.items():
    idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= low, freqs <= high)
    # Integrate PSD over the band using the trapezoidal rule
    band_power[band_name] = np.trapz(psd[idx], freqs[idx])

for band_name, power in band_power.items():
    print(f"{band_name}: {power:.4e} V^2")



Using MNE’s compute_psd()

import mne
import numpy as np

# Load and filter data
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)
raw.filter(l_freq=0.5, h_freq=45.0)

# Compute the PSD
psd = raw.compute_psd(method="welch", fmin=0.5, fmax=45.0)
freqs = psd.freqs
psd_data = psd.get_data()  # shape: (n_channels, n_freqs)

# Compute band power for each channel
bands = {
    "delta": (1, 4),
    "theta": (4, 8),
    "alpha": (8, 13),
    "beta":  (13, 30),
    "gamma": (30, 45)
}

for band_name, (low, high) in bands.items():
    idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= low, freqs <= high)
    # Average across channels, integrate across frequencies
    mean_power = np.trapz(psd_data[:, idx], freqs[idx], axis=1).mean()
    print(f"{band_name}: {mean_power:.4e} V^2")

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
Absolute vs relative power
Absolute power is the total power in a frequency band, measured in units of V^2 (or V^2/Hz if you are working with power spectral density rather than integrated power). It tells you how much energy there is in that band.
Relative power is the power in a band divided by the total power across all bands. It is expressed as a proportion (0 to 1) or a percentage. Relative power tells you what fraction of the total signal energy falls in a particular band.

import numpy as np
from scipy.signal import welch

sfreq = 256
freqs, psd = welch(signal, fs=sfreq, nperseg=2 * sfreq)

bands = {
    "delta": (1, 4),
    "theta": (4, 8),
    "alpha": (8, 13),
    "beta":  (13, 30),
    "gamma": (30, 45)
}

# Compute absolute power
absolute = {}
for name, (low, high) in bands.items():
    idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= low, freqs <= high)
    absolute[name] = np.trapz(psd[idx], freqs[idx])

# Compute total power (1-45 Hz)
total_idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= 1, freqs <= 45)
total_power = np.trapz(psd[total_idx], freqs[total_idx])

# Relative power
relative = {name: power / total_power for name, power in absolute.items()}

print("Band       Absolute (V^2)   Relative (%)")
print("-" * 45)
for name in bands:
    print(f"{name:<10} {absolute[name]:.4e}    {relative[name]*100:.1f}%")


When to use which
Absolute power is sensitive to individual differences in skull thickness, electrode impedance, and overall signal amplitude. Two participants can have identical brain states but very different absolute power values simply because one has a thicker skull.
Relative power normalises away these individual differences by expressing each band as a proportion of the total. This makes it easier to compare across participants and sessions. However, relative power can produce misleading results: if absolute alpha power stays the same but delta power decreases, relative alpha power will increase even though alpha activity has not changed.
In practice, many studies report both. A common approach is to use log-transformed absolute power (which makes the distribution more normal and compresses the range) for statistical analyses, and relative power for visualisation and description.

title: EEG frequency bands
section: Complete example: computing and visualising band powers
text:
Complete example: computing and visualising band powers

import numpy as np
import mne
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ── Create simulated data ────────────────────────────────────
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sfreq = 256
duration = 120  # 2 minutes
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Pink noise background
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) / np.sqrt(freqs_fft), n=n_samples)
signal = pink * 20e-6 / pink.std()

# Add oscillatory components
signal += 2e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 2 * times)    # delta
signal += 2.5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 6 * times)  # theta
signal += 5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)    # alpha (strongest)
signal += 1.5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)  # beta
signal += 0.5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 40 * times)  # gamma

# Wrap in MNE Raw
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=["Oz"], sfreq=sfreq, ch_types=["eeg"])
raw = mne.io.RawArray(signal.reshape(1, -1), info)

# ── Compute PSD ──────────────────────────────────────────────
from scipy.signal import welch

data = raw.get_data()[0]
freqs, psd = welch(data, fs=sfreq, nperseg=2 * sfreq)

# ── Compute band powers ─────────────────────────────────────
bands = {
    "Delta\n(1-4 Hz)": (1, 4),
    "Theta\n(4-8 Hz)": (4, 8),
    "Alpha\n(8-13 Hz)": (8, 13),
    "Beta\n(13-30 Hz)": (13, 30),
    "Gamma\n(30-45 Hz)": (30, 45)
}

absolute = {}
for name, (low, high) in bands.items():
    idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= low, freqs <= high)
    absolute[name] = np.trapz(psd[idx], freqs[idx])

total_idx = np.logical_and(freqs >= 1, freqs <= 45)
total_power = np.trapz(psd[total_idx], freqs[total_idx])
relative = {name: power / total_power * 100 for name, power in absolute.items()}

# ── Plot ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 4.5))

# PSD
ax = axes[0]
ax.semilogy(freqs, psd, color="#2c3e50", linewidth=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD (V^2/Hz)")
ax.set_title("Power spectral density")
ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
# Shade frequency bands
colours = ["#3498db", "#2ecc71", "#e74c3c", "#f39c12", "#9b59b6"]
for (name, (low, high)), colour in zip(bands.items(), colours):
    ax.axvspan(low, high, alpha=0.15, color=colour)

# Absolute power
ax = axes[1]
ax.bar(range(len(bands)), list(absolute.values()), color=colours)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(bands)))
ax.set_xticklabels(list(bands.keys()), fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Absolute power (V^2)")
ax.set_title("Absolute band power")

# Relative power
ax = axes[2]
ax.bar(range(len(bands)), list(relative.values()), color=colours)
ax.set_xticks(range(len(bands)))
ax.set_xticklabels(list(bands.keys()), fontsize=8)
ax.set_ylabel("Relative power (%)")
ax.set_title("Relative band power")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: EEG frequency bands
text:
Key takeaways

EEG activity is conventionally divided into five frequency bands: delta (1–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (30–100+ Hz). Each band has different functional associations and topographic distributions.
Alpha is the dominant rhythm in relaxed, eyes-closed wakefulness. It was the first EEG rhythm discovered and remains the most studied. It is strongest at posterior electrodes and decreases when the brain region is engaged in active processing.
Sub-bands (low alpha vs high alpha, low beta vs high beta) can have different functional profiles. The boundary between low and high alpha is often set at each participant’s individual alpha frequency.
Band power is computed by estimating the PSD (e.g., with Welch’s method) and integrating over the frequency range of interest. Use np.trapz() for numerical integration.
Absolute power measures total energy in a band but is sensitive to individual differences in skull thickness and impedance. Relative power normalises these differences but can be misleading when total power changes. Reporting both is good practice.
Gamma (30–100+ Hz) overlaps with muscle artifact, so any gamma findings from scalp EEG should be interpreted carefully and only after thorough artifact rejection.

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
A continuous EEG recording is a long stream of voltages. To study the brain’s response to a specific event (a flash of light, a word appearing on screen, a button press), you need to cut out short segments around each event and compare them. These segments are called epochs.
Each epoch is time-locked to an event: it starts at a fixed time before the event (e.g., 200 ms before stimulus onset) and ends at a fixed time after it (e.g., 800 ms after). By averaging many epochs for the same condition, random noise cancels out and the consistent brain response emerges. This averaged response is the event-related potential (ERP).
Epoching is where your analysis transitions from continuous data (where you cannot easily tell what happened when) to structured, trial-level data (where you can compare conditions and compute statistics).

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Event markers
Events are time-stamped labels in your data that mark when something happened during the experiment. They come from different sources:

Trigger channels: many EEG systems have a dedicated channel that records digital trigger codes sent by the stimulus presentation software (e.g., PsychoPy, E-Prime, Psychtoolbox). A trigger value of 1 might mean “stimulus onset”, 2 might mean “response”, and so on.
Annotations: some file formats (EDF+, BrainVision) store events as text annotations rather than trigger codes.

In MNE-Python, events are represented as a NumPy array with three columns:



Column
Contents




0
Sample number (when the event occurred)


1
Previous event value (usually 0)


2
Event ID (integer code identifying the event type)



You can extract events from annotations or from a trigger channel:

import mne

# From annotations (common for EDF+, BrainVision)
events, event_id = mne.events_from_annotations(raw)

# From a trigger channel (common for BioSemi, Neuroscan)
events = mne.find_events(raw, stim_channel="STI 014")

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Creating epochs from Raw
Here is a complete example that simulates a continuous recording with embedded events, then cuts epochs around those events.

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Simulate continuous EEG data ───────────────────────────────
sfreq = 256
duration = 120  # 2 minutes of data
n_channels = 8
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "P3", "P4"]

info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n_samples = int(sfreq * duration)
data = rng.standard_normal((n_channels, n_samples)) * 1e-6

# Add a 10 Hz oscillation to make it look more like real EEG
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
alpha = 2e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
data += alpha[np.newaxis, :]

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# ── Create simulated events ───────────────────────────────────
# Two conditions: "target" (event_id=1) and "standard" (event_id=2)
# Events occur every 2 seconds with some jitter
n_trials = 50
event_times = np.cumsum(rng.uniform(1.5, 2.5, n_trials))
event_times = event_times[event_times < duration - 1]  # keep within recording
event_samples = (event_times * sfreq).astype(int)

# Assign conditions: 20% targets, 80% standards
n_events = len(event_samples)
event_ids = rng.choice([1, 2], size=n_events, p=[0.2, 0.8])

events = np.column_stack([
    event_samples,
    np.zeros(n_events, dtype=int),
    event_ids
])

event_id = {"target": 1, "standard": 2}

print(f"Total events: {n_events}")
print(f"Targets: {np.sum(event_ids == 1)}, Standards: {np.sum(event_ids == 2)}")

# ── Create Epochs ──────────────────────────────────────────────
epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw,
    events,
    event_id=event_id,
    tmin=-0.2,           # 200 ms before the event
    tmax=0.8,            # 800 ms after the event
    baseline=(None, 0),  # baseline correction: subtract mean of pre-stimulus
    preload=True         # load all epochs into memory
)

print(epochs)
print(f"Epoch time window: {epochs.tmin} to {epochs.tmax} seconds")
print(f"Data shape: {epochs.get_data().shape}")
# shape is (n_epochs, n_channels, n_times)

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Baseline correction
Baseline correction removes slow voltage drifts that vary from trial to trial. Without it, some epochs might be shifted up or down relative to others simply because of electrode drift, not because of any difference in brain activity.
The baseline period is typically the pre-stimulus interval (the time before the event). MNE computes the mean voltage during this period for each channel and each epoch, then subtracts it.

# Baseline correction using the pre-stimulus period (-0.2 to 0 seconds)
epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8,
    baseline=(-0.2, 0),   # mean of this window is subtracted
    preload=True
)

# You can also apply no baseline correction
epochs_no_baseline = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8,
    baseline=None,         # no baseline correction
    preload=True
)

# Or use a custom baseline window
epochs_custom = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.5, tmax=1.0,
    baseline=(-0.5, -0.2), # baseline from -500 to -200 ms
    preload=True
)

The baseline=(None, 0) syntax uses the beginning of the epoch as the start of the baseline window. Since the epoch starts at tmin, (None, 0) is equivalent to (tmin, 0).

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Epoch rejection by amplitude
Some epochs contain large artifacts (blinks, muscle bursts, electrode pops) that would distort the average. You can reject these by setting an amplitude threshold: any epoch where any EEG channel exceeds the threshold is dropped.

# Reject epochs where any EEG channel exceeds 100 microvolts (peak-to-peak)
reject = dict(eeg=100e-6)  # 100 uV in volts (MNE uses SI units)

epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8,
    baseline=(None, 0),
    reject=reject,          # amplitude-based rejection
    preload=True
)

print(f"Epochs kept: {len(epochs)} / {n_events}")
print(epochs.drop_log_stats())  # percentage of dropped epochs

You can also set a flat threshold to catch channels that are dead (not recording any signal):

# Reject epochs that are too large OR too flat
reject = dict(eeg=100e-6)   # reject if > 100 uV
flat = dict(eeg=0.5e-6)     # reject if < 0.5 uV (likely a dead channel)

epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8,
    baseline=(None, 0),
    reject=reject,
    flat=flat,
    preload=True
)

A common guideline is to set the rejection threshold at 100–150 microvolts for EEG. If you are losing more than 20–30% of your epochs, the threshold may be too strict, or there may be a systematic artifact that you should address with ICA or channel interpolation before epoching.

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Using metadata
MNE allows you to attach a pandas DataFrame as metadata to your Epochs object. Each row of the DataFrame corresponds to one epoch and can contain any trial-level information: reaction time, accuracy, stimulus category, participant condition, and so on.
This is powerful because you can then select epochs using pandas-style queries.

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import mne

# Suppose you have trial-level information
metadata = pd.DataFrame({
    "condition": rng.choice(["face", "house"], size=n_events),
    "response_time": rng.uniform(0.3, 1.2, size=n_events),
    "accuracy": rng.choice([0, 1], size=n_events, p=[0.1, 0.9])
})

# Attach metadata when creating Epochs
epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events, event_id,
    tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8,
    baseline=(None, 0),
    metadata=metadata,
    preload=True
)

# Select epochs using pandas queries
fast_correct = epochs["response_time < 0.5 and accuracy == 1"]
faces_only = epochs["condition == 'face'"]

print(f"Fast correct trials: {len(fast_correct)}")
print(f"Face trials: {len(faces_only)}")

Metadata is particularly useful in designs with many conditions or continuous variables (like reaction time) that do not map neatly onto integer event codes.

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Selecting and indexing epochs
You can select subsets of epochs by condition name, index, or metadata query:

# By condition name (from event_id)
targets = epochs["target"]
standards = epochs["standard"]

# By index
first_ten = epochs[:10]

# By metadata query (if metadata is attached)
# fast_trials = epochs["response_time < 0.5"]

# Get the data as a NumPy array
data_array = epochs.get_data()  # shape: (n_epochs, n_channels, n_times)
print(f"Data shape: {data_array.shape}")

# Get the times vector
print(f"Time points: {epochs.times[:5]} ... {epochs.times[-5:]}")

title: Extracting epochs from continuous data
text:
Key takeaways

Epochs are short segments of EEG data cut from the continuous recording around event markers. They are the basis for ERP analysis, time-frequency analysis, and single-trial decoding.
Events are stored as a NumPy array with three columns: sample number, previous value, and event ID. Extract them from annotations with mne.events_from_annotations() or from a trigger channel with mne.find_events().
Baseline correction subtracts the mean voltage of the pre-stimulus period from each epoch, removing slow drifts. The standard baseline window is from the start of the epoch to time zero (stimulus onset).
Amplitude rejection drops epochs where any channel exceeds a threshold (typically 100–150 microvolts for EEG). This removes trials contaminated by large artifacts. If you are dropping more than 20–30% of epochs, investigate the source of the artifacts.
Metadata lets you attach trial-level variables (condition, reaction time, accuracy) to epochs and select subsets with pandas-style queries. This is especially useful for complex experimental designs.
Always epoch after filtering and re-referencing, but before computing ERPs or running statistical analyses.

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Automated artifact detection is useful, but it is not a substitute for looking at your data. No algorithm catches everything, and some problems (a loose electrode that drifted partway through a recording, a participant who fell asleep during the resting-state block) are obvious to a human eye but invisible to a threshold-based detector.
Visual inspection serves two purposes. First, it gives you a qualitative sense of data quality: is this a clean recording with occasional blinks, or is it dominated by muscle artifact and electrode noise? This affects how aggressively you filter, whether ICA will work, and whether some channels should be excluded entirely. Second, it lets you mark bad segments and bad channels so that they can be excluded or interpolated in later processing steps.
In most EEG labs, visual inspection happens at least twice: once right after loading the raw data (before any preprocessing), and once after filtering and artifact rejection (to check that the cleaning worked).
