title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Using raw.plot() interactively
MNE’s raw.plot() method opens an interactive viewer that lets you scroll through the data, zoom in and out, and mark bad segments and channels.

import mne

# Load data
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)

# Set channel types and montage (good practice before plotting)
raw.set_montage(mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020"),
                on_missing="warn")

# Open the interactive viewer
raw.plot(
    duration=10,           # show 10 seconds at a time
    n_channels=20,         # show 20 channels at a time
    scalings="auto",       # automatic scaling per channel type
    block=True             # block execution until the window is closed
)


Keyboard and mouse controls
The interactive viewer has several useful controls:



Action
Key/mouse




Scroll forward in time
Right arrow or scroll wheel


Scroll backward in time
Left arrow or scroll wheel


Page forward
Page Down


Page backward
Page Up


Zoom in (time)
+


Zoom out (time)
-


Zoom in (amplitude)
=


Zoom out (amplitude)
- (with shift)


Scroll channels down
Down arrow


Scroll channels up
Up arrow


Mark bad channel
Click on channel name


Mark bad segment
Click and drag on the data


Toggle annotation mode
a


Show/hide event markers
e





Adjusting the display

# Show more time per screen with fewer channels
raw.plot(duration=30, n_channels=10)

# Custom scaling (useful if auto-scaling is not right)
raw.plot(
    duration=10,
    n_channels=20,
    scalings={"eeg": 50e-6, "eog": 150e-6}  # 50 uV for EEG, 150 uV for EOG
)

# Highpass filter the display only (does not modify the data)
raw.plot(duration=10, n_channels=20, highpass=1.0)

# Show butterfly plot (all channels overlaid)
raw.plot(duration=10, n_channels=20, butterfly=True)

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Identifying common artifacts
Learning to recognise artifacts is a skill that improves with practice. Here are the most common ones and what they look like.

Eye blinks
Blinks produce large, slow, positive deflections lasting 200–400 ms. They are strongest at the frontal electrodes (Fp1, Fp2) and decrease in amplitude toward posterior electrodes. In a multi-channel view, you will see a synchronous upward deflection at the front of the head that is nearly absent at the back.
Blinks are easy to spot because they are large (often 50–100 microvolts at Fp1/Fp2) and have a characteristic rounded shape. They occur every few seconds in most recordings.
What to do: blinks are usually removed with ICA rather than by rejecting entire segments, because they are so frequent that rejecting every blink would discard too much data.


Saccadic eye movements
Saccades (rapid eye movements) produce step-like deflections in the horizontal EOG channels (or in F7/F8 if no dedicated EOG channels are present). The deflection is positive on one side and negative on the other, reflecting the change in the corneo-retinal dipole as the eyes move left or right.
Saccades are shorter than blinks (50–100 ms) and have a more rectangular shape. In vertical eye movements, they look similar to blinks but are smaller and often have a different time course.
What to do: like blinks, saccades are best handled with ICA. If your task requires participants to fixate and they are making frequent saccades, that is also worth noting as a data quality concern.


Muscle artifacts (EMG)
Muscle artifacts come from tension in the scalp, jaw, neck, or forehead muscles. They appear as bursts of high-frequency activity (typically above 20 Hz) that last from a fraction of a second to many seconds. In the time domain, they look like rapid, irregular oscillations superimposed on the EEG.
Muscle artifact is most common at temporal electrodes (T7, T8, F7, F8) because the temporalis muscle (used for chewing) runs directly beneath these electrodes. Jaw clenching produces especially large bursts across most channels.
What to do: brief muscle bursts can sometimes be removed with ICA. Sustained muscle tension is harder to handle and may require rejecting entire segments. If a participant has persistent muscle artifact, consider whether the recording conditions can be improved (e.g., asking them to relax their jaw).


Movement artifacts
Head or body movements produce slow, large-amplitude drifts that affect multiple channels simultaneously. They often look like low-frequency waves (below 1 Hz) and may coincide with EMG bursts if the participant moved their head.
Cable movements produce similar artifacts: a brief, sharp deflection followed by a slow return to baseline, often affecting a single channel.
What to do: mark these segments as bad and exclude them from analysis. Movement artifacts are usually too large and too variable for ICA to handle well.


Electrode pops
An electrode pop occurs when the electrode briefly loses contact with the scalp. It produces a sudden, very large deflection (sometimes hundreds of microvolts) on a single channel, often followed by a slow drift back to baseline. The key distinguishing feature is that it affects only one channel: if you see a massive deflection on one channel but all neighbouring channels look normal, it is likely an electrode pop.
What to do: if pops are infrequent, mark the affected segments as bad. If a channel has frequent pops throughout the recording, mark it as a bad channel and interpolate it later.


Line noise
Power line interference appears as a continuous, regular oscillation at 50 Hz (in Europe, South America, and most of Asia) or 60 Hz (in North America and parts of Asia). It is easier to see in the frequency domain than the time domain, but in the time domain it looks like a fine, regular “fuzz” on the signal.
What to do: line noise is removed with a notch filter or with the band-pass filter (if your low-pass cutoff is below the line frequency). It does not usually need to be handled during visual inspection.

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Marking bad segments
When you spot a bad segment during visual inspection, you can mark it as an annotation in MNE. This tells downstream processing steps (epoching, averaging) to exclude that time period.

In the interactive viewer
Click and drag on the data to highlight a bad segment. This creates a “BAD_” annotation. You can change the annotation label by pressing “a” to toggle annotation mode and typing a new label.


Programmatically

import mne

# Create annotations for known bad segments
bad_annots = mne.Annotations(
    onset=[12.5, 45.0, 102.3],        # start times in seconds
    duration=[2.0, 3.5, 1.0],         # durations in seconds
    description=["BAD_movement", "BAD_muscle", "BAD_electrode_pop"]
)

# Add to the raw object (preserving any existing annotations)
raw.set_annotations(raw.annotations + bad_annots)

# Verify
print(raw.annotations)

Annotations whose description starts with “BAD” or “bad” are automatically excluded by MNE when you create epochs. Any other prefix is treated as a regular annotation (e.g., an event marker).

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Marking bad channels
If a channel is noisy throughout the entire recording, you should mark it as bad rather than trying to fix it segment by segment.

# Mark channels as bad
raw.info["bads"] = ["F3", "T8"]

# Or add to the existing list
raw.info["bads"].extend(["P7"])

# Check which channels are marked as bad
print(f"Bad channels: {raw.info['bads']}")

Bad channels are excluded from most analyses by default (e.g., they are not included in the average reference calculation). Later, you can interpolate them using the montage:

# Interpolate bad channels using neighbouring channels
raw.interpolate_bads(reset_bads=True)

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
A practical inspection workflow
Here is a suggested workflow for visual inspection of a new dataset:

import mne

# 1. Load and set up the data
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("subject01.edf", preload=True)
raw.set_montage(mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020"),
                on_missing="warn")

# 2. First pass: get an overview
#    Plot the power spectrum to check for line noise and overall quality
raw.compute_psd(fmax=80).plot()

# 3. Second pass: scroll through the data
#    Look at 10-second windows, marking bad segments and channels
raw.plot(duration=10, n_channels=20, block=True)

# 4. After closing the viewer, check what was marked
print(f"Bad channels: {raw.info['bads']}")
print(f"Annotations: {raw.annotations}")

# 5. Save the inspection results
#    The bad channel and annotation information is preserved when you save
raw.save("subject01_inspected_raw.fif", overwrite=True)

title: Visual inspection of EEG data
text:
Key takeaways

Visual inspection is not optional. Look at your data before and after preprocessing. Automated methods miss things that are obvious to a human.
Use raw.plot() to scroll through the data interactively. Learn the keyboard shortcuts; they make the process much faster.
Learn the visual signatures of common artifacts: blinks (large, slow, frontal), saccades (step-like, lateral), muscle (high-frequency bursts, temporal), movement (slow drifts, multi-channel), and electrode pops (sudden deflection, single channel).
Mark bad segments with annotations starting with “BAD”. MNE excludes these automatically during epoching.
Mark consistently noisy channels as bad with raw.info["bads"] and interpolate them later using raw.interpolate_bads().
Save your inspection results by writing the data to a FIF file. This preserves your bad channel and annotation markings for later processing steps.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
The Hilbert transform gives you the instantaneous phase of each EEG channel. But phase at a single channel, on its own, does not tell you much about how brain regions communicate. What matters is the relationship between phases at different channels. Are two regions oscillating together? Are they systematically out of step? And does this relationship hold steady or keep changing?
Phase alignment measures answer these questions. They turn raw phase values into connectivity matrices that describe the pattern of coordination across the entire scalp at each moment in time. These matrices are the input to metastability analysis and other network-level measures of brain dynamics.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
The Hilbert transform gives you the instantaneous phase of each EEG channel. But phase at a single channel, on its own, does not tell you much about how brain regions communicate. What matters is the relationship between phases at different channels. Are two regions oscillating together? Are they systematically out of step? And does this relationship hold steady or keep changing?
Phase alignment measures answer these questions. They turn raw phase values into connectivity matrices that describe the pattern of coordination across the entire scalp at each moment in time. These matrices are the input to metastability analysis and other network-level measures of brain dynamics.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Phase-locking value (PLV)
The phase-locking value (PLV; Lachaux et al., 1999) is the most widely used phase-based connectivity measure. It quantifies how consistent the phase difference between two signals is over a time window.
For two channels \(i\) and \(j\) with instantaneous phases \(\phi_i(t)\) and \(\phi_j(t)\), the PLV is:
\[\text{PLV}_{ij} = \left| \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} e^{i(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))} \right|\]
The complex exponential \(e^{i\Delta\phi}\) represents the phase difference as a unit vector on the complex plane. If the phase difference is constant over time, all these vectors point in the same direction, and their average has magnitude close to 1. If the phase difference varies randomly, the vectors point in different directions and their average cancels out towards 0.
PLV ranges from 0 (no phase locking; phase difference is random) to 1 (perfect phase locking; phase difference is constant). In real EEG data, PLV values between 0.2 and 0.5 typically indicate meaningful synchronisation.

Limitations of PLV
PLV is computed over a time window, so it summarises the average synchronisation within that window. It does not tell you what is happening at individual time points. If synchronisation changes within the window (e.g., the first half is synchronised and the second half is not), PLV reports a moderate value that masks the dynamics.
PLV is also sensitive to volume conduction: nearby electrodes record overlapping signals from the same cortical sources, which inflates PLV artificially. This is a general problem for all phase-based measures at the sensor level.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
The cosine of phase difference
An alternative to PLV that operates at individual time points is the cosine of the phase difference:
\[c_{ij}(t) = \cos\!\big(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t)\big)\]
This gives an instantaneous measure of phase alignment between channels \(i\) and \(j\) at time \(t\). Its values range from \(-1\) to \(+1\):

\(c_{ij}(t) = 1\): channels are perfectly in phase (peaks coincide).
\(c_{ij}(t) = -1\): channels are perfectly in anti-phase (one peaks while the other troughs).
\(c_{ij}(t) = 0\): channels are a quarter-cycle apart (orthogonal).

The cosine measure has a useful property: it is symmetric (\(c_{ij} = c_{ji}\)) and it varies smoothly as the phase difference changes. Unlike PLV, it does not require averaging over a time window. You get a value at every single time point.
The trade-off is that the cosine measure is noisier than PLV, precisely because it does not average over time. A single time point of \(c_{ij}(t) = 0.9\) does not mean much on its own; it could just be a moment when two independent oscillations happened to line up. The power of this measure comes from looking at how the entire matrix of \(c_{ij}(t)\) values evolves over time.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Building the instantaneous connectivity matrix
At each time point \(t\), you can compute \(c_{ij}(t) = \cos(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))\) for every pair of channels. This produces an \(N \times N\) matrix:
\[\mathbf{A}(t) = \begin{bmatrix} 1 & \cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2) & \cdots & \cos(\phi_1 - \phi_N) \\ \cos(\phi_2 - \phi_1) & 1 & \cdots & \cos(\phi_2 - \phi_N) \\ \vdots & \vdots & \ddots & \vdots \\ \cos(\phi_N - \phi_1) & \cos(\phi_N - \phi_2) & \cdots & 1 \end{bmatrix}\]
Properties of this matrix:

Symmetric: \(A_{ij}(t) = A_{ji}(t)\), because \(\cos(\alpha) = \cos(-\alpha)\).
Diagonal entries are 1: each channel is perfectly aligned with itself.
Real-valued: all entries are between \(-1\) and \(+1\).
Changes every time point: the matrix captures the instantaneous pattern of coordination.

In matrix notation, if \(\boldsymbol{\phi}(t)\) is the vector of phases at time \(t\), then:
\[A_{ij}(t) = \cos\!\big(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t)\big)\]
This is very efficient to compute. For \(N\) channels you only need to compute the pairwise phase differences and take their cosine.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Interpreting positive and negative values
The sign of \(A_{ij}(t)\) tells you the type of phase relationship:
Positive values (\(A_{ij} > 0\)): channels \(i\) and \(j\) are within a quarter-cycle of each other. The closer to \(+1\), the more tightly synchronised they are. In neuroscience terms, these regions are likely part of the same functional network at that moment.
Negative values (\(A_{ij} < 0\)): channels \(i\) and \(j\) are more than a quarter-cycle apart, with \(-1\) meaning exact anti-phase. Anti-phase relationships are not “bad” or “disconnected”. They can reflect legitimate neural coordination. For example, two regions might be in a reciprocal inhibitory relationship, where one is active while the other is suppressed.
Values near zero: channels are roughly a quarter-cycle apart. This is sometimes interpreted as a “transitional” relationship, neither clearly in-phase nor anti-phase.
The dominant eigenvector of \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) captures the primary partition: channels with the same sign in the eigenvector tend to be in phase with each other, while channels with opposite signs tend to be in anti-phase. This partition defines the “coordination pattern” at time \(t\).

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Sliding-window vs instantaneous approaches
There are two strategies for using phase alignment:

Instantaneous (time-point-by-time-point)
Compute \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) at every time point (or at regular intervals, e.g., every 10 ms). Extract the dominant eigenvector at each time point. Compute metastability as the temporal variance of the eigenvector elements.
This is the approach used in the metastability pipeline (Hancock et al., 2025). It provides maximum temporal resolution: you can track changes in coordination on a millisecond timescale.


Sliding window
Compute PLV (or average \(\mathbf{A}(t)\)) within a moving time window (e.g., 500 ms wide, sliding by 50 ms). This smooths out the moment-to-moment noise and gives more stable connectivity estimates, at the cost of temporal resolution.
Sliding-window PLV is more appropriate when you want to track slower changes in connectivity (e.g., over seconds) or when you need a connectivity measure that is robust to noise.
For the metastability analysis in Natalia’s project, the instantaneous approach is preferred because metastability is specifically about the variability of coordination over time. Averaging within a window would smooth out some of that variability.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Working example
The code below simulates two channels with a known phase relationship, computes the connectivity matrix over time, and visualises how the phase alignment changes.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Simulation parameters ──────────────────────────────────────
sfreq = 256
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
freq = 10.0  # Hz (alpha)

# ── Create two channels with a time-varying phase relationship ─
# Channel 1: stable 10 Hz oscillation with slight drift
phase_drift_1 = 0.2 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq)
signal_1 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * times + phase_drift_1)
signal_1 += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)  # add noise

# Channel 2: same frequency, but with an extra slow phase offset
# that makes the channels go in and out of alignment
slow_offset = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.3 * times)  # 0.3 Hz modulation
phase_drift_2 = 0.2 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq)
signal_2 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * times + phase_drift_2 + slow_offset)
signal_2 += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── Band-pass filter to alpha band ────────────────────────────
b, a = butter(4, [8, 13], btype="band", fs=sfreq)
filtered_1 = filtfilt(b, a, signal_1)
filtered_2 = filtfilt(b, a, signal_2)

# ── Hilbert transform: extract phase ─────────────────────────
phase_1 = np.angle(hilbert(filtered_1))
phase_2 = np.angle(hilbert(filtered_2))

# ── Compute instantaneous phase alignment ─────────────────────
# cosine of phase difference (the A_ij(t) matrix element for 2 channels)
cos_diff = np.cos(phase_1 - phase_2)

# ── Compute sliding-window PLV for comparison ────────────────
window_samples = int(0.5 * sfreq)  # 500 ms window
plv_times = []
plv_values = []
for start in range(0, n_samples - window_samples, int(0.05 * sfreq)):
    end = start + window_samples
    phase_diff_window = phase_1[start:end] - phase_2[start:end]
    plv = np.abs(np.mean(np.exp(1j * phase_diff_window)))
    plv_times.append(times[start + window_samples // 2])
    plv_values.append(plv)

# ── Build the full 2x2 connectivity matrix at one time point ──
t_example = int(2.5 * sfreq)  # at t = 2.5 seconds
phi = np.array([phase_1[t_example], phase_2[t_example]])
phase_diff_matrix = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
A_example = np.cos(phase_diff_matrix)

print("Phase alignment matrix at t = 2.5 s:")
print(f"  A = [[{A_example[0,0]:+.3f}, {A_example[0,1]:+.3f}],")
print(f"       [{A_example[1,0]:+.3f}, {A_example[1,1]:+.3f}]]")
print(f"  Phase difference: {np.degrees(phase_1[t_example] - phase_2[t_example]):.1f} degrees")

# ── Visualisation ─────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(13, 8), sharex=True)

# Panel 1: Filtered signals
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, filtered_1, linewidth=0.5, color="#2c3e50",
        label="Channel 1", alpha=0.8)
ax.plot(times, filtered_2, linewidth=0.5, color="#e67e22",
        label="Channel 2", alpha=0.8)
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Alpha-filtered signals (8\u201313 Hz)")
ax.legend(fontsize=9, loc="upper right")

# Panel 2: Instantaneous phase alignment (cosine of phase difference)
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(times, cos_diff, linewidth=0.5, color="#27ae60", alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5, linestyle=":")
ax.axhline(1, color="grey", linewidth=0.5, linestyle=":")
ax.axhline(-1, color="grey", linewidth=0.5, linestyle=":")
ax.fill_between(times, cos_diff, 0, where=(cos_diff > 0),
                color="#27ae60", alpha=0.15)
ax.fill_between(times, cos_diff, 0, where=(cos_diff < 0),
                color="#e74c3c", alpha=0.15)
ax.set_ylabel(r"$\cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2)$")
ax.set_title("Instantaneous phase alignment")
ax.set_ylim(-1.2, 1.2)

# Panel 3: Sliding-window PLV
ax = axes[2]
ax.plot(plv_times, plv_values, linewidth=1.2, color="#8e44ad")
ax.set_ylabel("PLV")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_title("Phase-locking value (500 ms sliding window)")
ax.set_ylim(0, 1.05)
ax.axhline(0.5, color="grey", linewidth=0.5, linestyle=":",
           label="PLV = 0.5")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Phase alignment matrix at t = 2.5 s:
  A = [[+1.000, +0.003],
       [+0.003, +1.000]]
  Phase difference: 89.9 degrees





Phase alignment between two simulated EEG channels. The two channels start in phase, drift apart, and then re-align, illustrating how the cosine measure tracks changes in instantaneous connectivity.




The top panel shows the two alpha-filtered signals. You can see periods where they oscillate together (peaks aligned) and periods where they drift apart.
The middle panel shows the instantaneous phase alignment, \(\cos(\phi_1 - \phi_2)\). When it is near \(+1\) (green shading), the channels are in phase. When it is near \(-1\) (red shading), they are in anti-phase. The slow modulation reflects the 0.3 Hz phase offset we built into the simulation: the channels cycle between being aligned and being out of alignment roughly every 3 seconds.
The bottom panel shows the sliding-window PLV, which is always positive (because PLV measures the consistency of the phase difference, not its sign). It is high when the phase difference is stable (either in-phase or anti-phase) and low when the phase relationship is changing rapidly.

title: Phase alignment and connectivity matrices
text:
Key takeaways

PLV measures how consistent the phase difference between two channels is over a time window. It ranges from 0 (random) to 1 (perfectly locked) and is the most widely used phase connectivity measure.
The cosine of the phase difference, \(\cos(\phi_i - \phi_j)\), gives an instantaneous measure of alignment at each time point. It ranges from \(-1\) (anti-phase) to \(+1\) (in-phase).
The instantaneous connectivity matrix \(A_{ij}(t) = \cos(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))\) captures the full pattern of pairwise phase relationships across all channels at each moment. It is symmetric, with ones on the diagonal.
Positive values mean the channels are within a quarter-cycle of each other; negative values mean they are more than a quarter-cycle apart. Both can reflect real neural coordination.
For metastability analysis, the instantaneous approach (computing \(\mathbf{A}(t)\) at every time point) is preferred over sliding-window PLV, because metastability is about temporal variability in coordination patterns.
All phase-based connectivity measures at the sensor level are affected by volume conduction, which inflates apparent connectivity between nearby electrodes. Source-space analysis or the imaginary part of coherence can mitigate this, but they add complexity.

title: MNE data structures
text:
When you work with EEG data in MNE-Python, you do not deal with plain NumPy arrays (though you can always extract the underlying array if you need to). Instead, MNE wraps your data in specialised objects that carry metadata alongside the numbers: channel names, sampling frequency, channel types, montage information, event markers, and more.
Understanding these objects is important because every MNE function expects a specific type of input. You cannot pass a Raw object to a function that expects Epochs, or vice versa. Knowing which object to use at each stage of your analysis pipeline saves time and prevents confusing error messages.

title: MNE data structures
text:
When you work with EEG data in MNE-Python, you do not deal with plain NumPy arrays (though you can always extract the underlying array if you need to). Instead, MNE wraps your data in specialised objects that carry metadata alongside the numbers: channel names, sampling frequency, channel types, montage information, event markers, and more.
Understanding these objects is important because every MNE function expects a specific type of input. You cannot pass a Raw object to a function that expects Epochs, or vice versa. Knowing which object to use at each stage of your analysis pipeline saves time and prevents confusing error messages.

title: MNE data structures
text:
The four main objects
MNE-Python organises EEG data into four main objects. They form a natural progression from raw recording to statistical summary:
Raw  ──>  Epochs  ──>  Evoked
                 │
              (Info is attached to all three)

Raw: continuous data
A Raw object holds the continuous EEG recording as it comes off the amplifier. It is a two-dimensional array of shape (n_channels, n_times), paired with metadata about the channels, sampling rate, and recording parameters.
You use Raw when you are:

Loading data from a file
Filtering
Re-referencing
Inspecting the continuous recording
Running ICA

Raw is your starting point. Almost every analysis begins by creating or loading a Raw object.


Epochs: segmented data
An Epochs object contains segments of data cut from the continuous recording around events of interest. Each segment (epoch) has the same duration and is time-locked to an event marker (e.g., stimulus onset, button press).
The underlying array has three dimensions: (n_epochs, n_channels, n_times). If you recorded 200 trials with 64 channels and each epoch spans 1 second at 256 Hz, your Epochs object contains 200 x 64 x 256 numbers.
You use Epochs when you are:

Computing event-related potentials (ERPs)
Doing time-frequency analysis on single trials
Running statistical tests across trials
Decoding stimulus conditions from brain activity



Evoked: averaged data
An Evoked object is the average of a set of epochs for one experimental condition. It has shape (n_channels, n_times), like Raw, but it represents an averaged response rather than continuous data.
Evoked objects are what you typically see in ERP publications: a waveform showing the average brain response to a stimulus, with clear components like the N170 (a negative peak at about 170 ms for face stimuli) or the P300 (a positive peak at about 300 ms for rare target stimuli).
You use Evoked when you are:

Plotting ERPs
Comparing conditions (e.g., faces vs. houses)
Running sensor-level statistics across participants
Identifying ERP components



Info: metadata container
An Info object is not a data container itself but a dictionary-like structure that holds all the metadata about a recording. Every Raw, Epochs, and Evoked object has an .info attribute.
The Info object stores:

Channel names and types (EEG, EOG, ECG, etc.)
Sampling frequency
Channel locations (montage)
Bad channels
Reference scheme
Recording date and subject information

You create an Info object explicitly when building data from scratch (e.g., from a NumPy array). When loading data from a file, MNE creates the Info object automatically from the file header.

title: MNE data structures
section: How the objects relate to each other
text:
How the objects relate to each other
The typical flow is:

Load or create Raw from a file or array.
Preprocess the Raw (filter, re-reference, run ICA).
Extract Epochs by cutting segments around events.
Average Epochs to get Evoked for each condition.

Each step produces a new object, and the Info metadata travels along:
Raw (continuous, 2D)
 │
 │  find events, cut segments
 ▼
Epochs (segmented, 3D)
 │
 │  average across trials
 ▼
Evoked (averaged, 2D)
You can always go back and access the underlying NumPy array with .get_data() (for Raw and Epochs) or .data (for Evoked). But working with the MNE objects is usually easier because the metadata stays attached.

title: MNE data structures
text:
Code examples

Creating Raw from scratch

import numpy as np
import mne

# Create metadata
info = mne.create_info(
    ch_names=["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"],
    sfreq=256,
    ch_types="eeg"
)

# Simulate 10 seconds of data (8 channels x 2560 samples)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
n_channels = 8
n_samples = 256 * 10
data = rng.standard_normal((n_channels, n_samples)) * 1e-6

# Create Raw object
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
print(raw)
print(f"Duration: {raw.times[-1]:.1f} seconds")
print(f"Channels: {raw.ch_names}")



Creating Epochs from Raw

import numpy as np
import mne

# ── Set up simulated continuous data ───────────────────────────
info = mne.create_info(
    ch_names=["Fz", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"],
    sfreq=256,
    ch_types="eeg"
)

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
duration = 60  # 60 seconds of data
n_samples = 256 * duration
data = rng.standard_normal((4, n_samples)) * 1e-6

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# ── Create events (every 2 seconds, alternating between two types) ──
n_events = 25
event_samples = np.arange(256, n_events * 2 * 256, 2 * 256)
event_ids = np.tile([1, 2], n_events)[:len(event_samples)]
events = np.column_stack([
    event_samples,
    np.zeros(len(event_samples), dtype=int),
    event_ids
])

event_id = {"stimulus_A": 1, "stimulus_B": 2}

# ── Create Epochs ──────────────────────────────────────────────
epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw,
    events,
    event_id=event_id,
    tmin=-0.2,         # 200 ms before event
    tmax=0.8,          # 800 ms after event
    baseline=(None, 0) # baseline correct using pre-stimulus period
)

print(epochs)
print(f"Number of epochs: {len(epochs)}")
print(f"Epoch shape: {epochs.get_data().shape}")



Creating Evoked from Epochs

# Continuing from the Epochs example above

# Average all epochs for condition "stimulus_A"
evoked_A = epochs["stimulus_A"].average()
print(evoked_A)
print(f"Evoked shape: {evoked_A.data.shape}")

# Average all epochs for condition "stimulus_B"
evoked_B = epochs["stimulus_B"].average()
print(evoked_B)

# You can also get a list of Evoked objects for all conditions at once
all_evoked = [epochs[cond].average() for cond in event_id]



Inspecting the Info object

# The Info object is attached to Raw, Epochs, and Evoked
print(raw.info)

# Access specific fields
print(f"Sampling frequency: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"Channel names: {raw.info['ch_names']}")
print(f"Number of channels: {raw.info['nchan']}")
print(f"Bad channels: {raw.info['bads']}")

# You can also create an Info object directly
info = mne.create_info(
    ch_names=["Fz", "Cz", "Pz"],
    sfreq=512,
    ch_types=["eeg", "eeg", "eeg"]
)
print(info)

title: MNE data structures
text:
Key takeaways

MNE-Python uses four main objects: Raw (continuous data), Epochs (trial segments), Evoked (averaged responses), and Info (metadata).
Raw is two-dimensional (channels x time), Epochs is three-dimensional (trials x channels x time), and Evoked is two-dimensional again (channels x time, after averaging).
The Info object carries metadata (channel names, sampling rate, montage) and is attached to all three data objects.
The typical workflow is Raw -> Epochs -> Evoked, with preprocessing applied to the Raw object before epoching.
You can always extract the underlying NumPy array with .get_data(), but working with MNE objects keeps your metadata intact and lets you use MNE’s built-in functions.

title: Visual inspection and manual rejection
text:
Automated methods for artifact removal (ICA, threshold-based rejection) are powerful, but they are not infallible. Sometimes they miss subtle artifacts, and sometimes they flag clean data as bad. Visual inspection is the quality-control step that catches what automation misses. Even in a fully automated pipeline, you should look at your data at some point to check that nothing has gone wrong.
Manual rejection is also the most appropriate strategy when you have a small number of clearly contaminated segments. If three out of two hundred epochs contain a large muscle burst, it is faster and more reliable to mark those three epochs as bad by eye than to tune an automated algorithm to catch them.
