title: The BIDS format for EEG
section: The BIDS folder hierarchy for EEG
text:
The BIDS folder hierarchy for EEG
A BIDS dataset has a fixed directory structure. At the top level you have a root folder (the dataset name). Inside it, each participant gets a folder named sub-XX, where XX is a label you choose (often a zero-padded number like 01, 02, etc.). Inside each participant folder, data is organised by modality. For EEG, the subfolder is called eeg/.
Here is a minimal example with two participants:
my-experiment/
├── dataset_description.json
├── participants.tsv
├── participants.json
├── sub-01/
│   └── eeg/
│       ├── sub-01_task-rest_eeg.edf
│       ├── sub-01_task-rest_eeg.json
│       ├── sub-01_task-rest_channels.tsv
│       └── sub-01_task-rest_events.tsv
└── sub-02/
    └── eeg/
        ├── sub-02_task-rest_eeg.edf
        ├── sub-02_task-rest_eeg.json
        ├── sub-02_task-rest_channels.tsv
        └── sub-02_task-rest_events.tsv
If your experiment has multiple sessions (e.g., baseline and follow-up), you add a ses-XX level between the subject folder and the modality folder: sub-01/ses-01/eeg/.
The dataset_description.json file at the root describes the dataset as a whole (name, BIDS version, license). The participants.tsv file lists all participants and can include columns for age, sex, group, or any other relevant variable.

title: The BIDS format for EEG
text:
File naming conventions
BIDS file names follow a strict pattern of key-value pairs separated by underscores. For EEG, a typical file name looks like this:
sub-01_ses-01_task-auditory_run-02_eeg.edf
Each part has a specific meaning:



Key
Meaning
Required?




sub-XX
Participant label
Yes


ses-XX
Session label
Only if multiple sessions


task-YY
Task name (e.g., rest, oddball, motor)
Yes


run-XX
Run number within a session
Only if multiple runs


eeg
Modality suffix
Yes



The file extension indicates the format: .edf, .bdf, .vhdr (BrainVision), .set (EEGLAB), or .fif (MNE native format). BIDS supports all of these.
The naming convention is what makes BIDS machine-readable. A script can parse the file name to extract the subject, task, and run without needing a lookup table or custom code.

title: The BIDS format for EEG
text:
Metadata sidecar files
Each EEG recording has a set of companion files that provide metadata. These sidecars are what make BIDS self-documenting.

JSON sidecar (*_eeg.json)
This file contains recording-level metadata: sampling frequency, power line frequency, reference electrode, and task description. A minimal example:
{
    "TaskName": "rest",
    "TaskDescription": "Five minutes of eyes-closed resting state",
    "SamplingFrequency": 256,
    "PowerLineFrequency": 50,
    "EEGReference": "Cz",
    "SoftwareFilters": {
        "HighpassFilter": {"CutoffFrequency": 0.1},
        "LowpassFilter": {"CutoffFrequency": 100}
    }
}


Channels file (*_channels.tsv)
A tab-separated file listing every channel, its type, units, and sampling frequency. This is where you document which channels are EEG, EOG, ECG, or EMG.
name    type    units   sampling_frequency  status
Fp1 EEG uV  256 good
Fp2 EEG uV  256 good
EOG1    EOG uV  256 good
Cz  EEG uV  256 bad
The status column is useful for marking channels that were noisy during recording.


Events file (*_events.tsv)
This file lists every event (stimulus onset, response, etc.) with its timing and a human-readable description.
onset   duration    trial_type  value
1.5 0.0 stimulus/face   1
2.1 0.0 response/correct    2
4.0 0.0 stimulus/house  3
The onset column is in seconds, and trial_type gives a meaningful label rather than just a numeric code.


Participants file (participants.tsv)
This file lives at the dataset root and lists all participants with demographic or grouping variables.
participant_id  age sex group
sub-01  25  F   control
sub-02  30  M   patient

title: The BIDS format for EEG
section: Using mne-bids to work with BIDS datasets
text:
Using mne-bids to work with BIDS datasets
The mne-bids package bridges MNE-Python and the BIDS standard. It can read BIDS datasets into MNE objects, write MNE objects into BIDS format, and validate that a dataset follows the specification.

Installation
pip install mne-bids
If you need to read or write BrainVision files, also install pybv:
pip install pybv


The BIDSPath object
BIDSPath is the central object in mne-bids. It encodes all the BIDS entities (subject, session, task, run) and the root directory. You use it to point to a specific file in a BIDS dataset.

import mne_bids

bids_path = mne_bids.BIDSPath(
    subject="01",
    task="rest",
    datatype="eeg",
    root="/path/to/my-experiment"
)
print(bids_path)
# Output: /path/to/my-experiment/sub-01/eeg/sub-01_task-rest_eeg



Reading a BIDS dataset
Once you have a BIDSPath, reading the data is a single function call. read_raw_bids() returns an MNE Raw object with the montage, channel types, and event annotations already set from the BIDS metadata.

raw = mne_bids.read_raw_bids(bids_path)
print(raw.info)
print(raw.annotations)  # events from *_events.tsv are loaded as annotations

This is one of the biggest practical benefits of BIDS: you do not need to manually set the montage, fix channel types, or parse event files. The BIDS metadata takes care of all of that.


Writing data to BIDS format
write_raw_bids() takes an MNE Raw object and saves it in BIDS format, creating the folder structure and sidecar files automatically.

import mne
import mne_bids

# Load your data as usual
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("original_recording.edf", preload=True)

# Set channel types if needed
raw.set_channel_types({"EOG1": "eog", "EOG2": "eog"})

# Create a BIDSPath for the output
bids_path = mne_bids.BIDSPath(
    subject="01",
    task="rest",
    datatype="eeg",
    root="/path/to/bids-dataset"
)

# Write to BIDS
mne_bids.write_raw_bids(raw, bids_path, overwrite=True)

After running this, mne-bids will create the full directory tree, rename the data file according to BIDS conventions, and generate the JSON sidecar and channels TSV automatically from the information in raw.info.

title: The BIDS format for EEG
section: Converting an existing dataset to BIDS
text:
Converting an existing dataset to BIDS
If you have a collection of EEG files in an ad-hoc folder structure, the conversion process is a loop over participants. The pattern is:

Load each participant’s raw file with MNE.
Set the correct channel types and montage.
Create a BIDSPath with the right subject label and task name.
Call write_raw_bids().


import mne
import mne_bids
from pathlib import Path

# Suppose your original data is in: data/raw/subjectXX.edf
raw_dir = Path("data/raw")
bids_root = Path("data/bids")

subjects = {"subject01": "01", "subject02": "02", "subject03": "03"}

for original_name, bids_label in subjects.items():
    # Load
    raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf(raw_dir / f"{original_name}.edf", preload=True)

    # Set montage and channel types
    raw.set_montage(mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020"))
    raw.set_channel_types({"EOG1": "eog", "EOG2": "eog"})

    # Define BIDS path
    bids_path = mne_bids.BIDSPath(
        subject=bids_label,
        task="rest",
        datatype="eeg",
        root=bids_root
    )

    # Write
    mne_bids.write_raw_bids(raw, bids_path, overwrite=True)

print(f"BIDS dataset written to {bids_root}")

After the loop, the data/bids/ folder will have the standard BIDS structure. You can validate it with the BIDS Validator to check for missing files or naming errors.

title: The BIDS format for EEG
section: Creating BIDS structure manually with Python
text:
Creating BIDS structure manually with Python
You do not always need mne-bids. If you want to understand what BIDS looks like under the hood, or if you need to set up the folder structure before you have any data, you can create it with pure Python.

import json
from pathlib import Path

bids_root = Path("my-experiment")

# Create the directory tree
subjects = ["01", "02", "03"]
for sub in subjects:
    eeg_dir = bids_root / f"sub-{sub}" / "eeg"
    eeg_dir.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)

# Write dataset_description.json
description = {
    "Name": "My EEG Experiment",
    "BIDSVersion": "1.9.0",
    "License": "CC-BY-4.0",
    "Authors": ["Alice Researcher", "Bob Scientist"]
}
with open(bids_root / "dataset_description.json", "w") as f:
    json.dump(description, f, indent=4)

# Write participants.tsv
participants_header = "participant_id\tage\tsex\tgroup\n"
participants_rows = [
    "sub-01\t25\tF\tcontrol\n",
    "sub-02\t30\tM\tpatient\n",
    "sub-03\t28\tF\tcontrol\n",
]
with open(bids_root / "participants.tsv", "w") as f:
    f.write(participants_header)
    f.writelines(participants_rows)

# Write a JSON sidecar template for one subject
sidecar = {
    "TaskName": "rest",
    "SamplingFrequency": 256,
    "PowerLineFrequency": 50,
    "EEGReference": "Cz"
}
sidecar_path = bids_root / "sub-01" / "eeg" / "sub-01_task-rest_eeg.json"
with open(sidecar_path, "w") as f:
    json.dump(sidecar, f, indent=4)

print(f"BIDS skeleton created at {bids_root}")

This gives you the folder structure and metadata files. You would then copy or convert your actual EEG recordings into the appropriate locations, following the naming convention described above.

title: The BIDS format for EEG
text:
Key takeaways

BIDS is a folder and naming convention that makes EEG datasets self-documenting and machine-readable.
The structure is simple: sub-XX/eeg/ folders with consistently named data files and metadata sidecars.
JSON sidecars store recording parameters, TSV files store channel information, events, and participant demographics.
The mne-bids package automates reading from and writing to BIDS format, including folder creation and sidecar generation.
Converting an existing dataset to BIDS is a loop: load each file, set metadata, and call write_raw_bids().
Starting your project in BIDS from the beginning is easier than converting later. Even if you never share your data, the consistent structure will save you time when you return to the project months later.

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
A montage is a mapping from channel names to physical locations on the scalp. It tells MNE-Python where each electrode sits in three-dimensional space. Without a montage, MNE can still filter, epoch, and average your data, but it cannot produce topographic maps, interpolate bad channels, or estimate source locations, because all of these operations need to know where the electrodes are.
Most EEG file formats do not store electrode locations, or store them in a non-standard way. So setting the montage is usually something you do manually after loading your data. This page explains the standard montage systems, how to apply them, and how to handle non-standard setups.

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
A montage is a mapping from channel names to physical locations on the scalp. It tells MNE-Python where each electrode sits in three-dimensional space. Without a montage, MNE can still filter, epoch, and average your data, but it cannot produce topographic maps, interpolate bad channels, or estimate source locations, because all of these operations need to know where the electrodes are.
Most EEG file formats do not store electrode locations, or store them in a non-standard way. So setting the montage is usually something you do manually after loading your data. This page explains the standard montage systems, how to apply them, and how to handle non-standard setups.

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
Standard montage systems

The 10-20 system
The original 10-20 system, introduced by Jasper in 1958, places 21 electrodes on the scalp using anatomical landmarks: the nasion (bridge of the nose), the inion (bump at the back of the skull), and the left and right preauricular points (in front of each ear). Electrodes are spaced at intervals of 10% and 20% of the distance between these landmarks.
The channel names follow a convention: letters indicate the brain region (F for frontal, C for central, P for parietal, O for occipital, T for temporal) and numbers indicate laterality (odd numbers on the left, even numbers on the right, z for the midline). So Fp1 is the left frontopolar electrode, O2 is the right occipital electrode, and Cz is the central midline electrode.
The 10-20 system has 21 positions: Fp1, Fp2, F7, F3, Fz, F4, F8, T3 (or T7), C3, Cz, C4, T4 (or T8), T5 (or P7), P3, Pz, P4, T6 (or P8), O1, O2, A1, A2.


The 10-10 and 10-05 systems
The 10-10 system (also called the extended 10-20 system) adds electrodes between the 10-20 positions, giving about 75 locations. It uses the same naming convention but with more positions filled in. This is the most common system for research-grade EEG caps with 32 or 64 channels.
The 10-05 system goes even further, filling in positions at 5% intervals, producing over 300 possible electrode sites. This is used for high-density arrays (128 or 256 channels).


Available montages in MNE
MNE-Python includes many standard montages. You can see the full list with:

import mne

# List all built-in montages
print(mne.channels.get_builtin_montages())

The most commonly used ones are:



Montage name
System
Channels




standard_1020
10-20
94 positions (includes 10-10 extensions)


standard_1005
10-05
343 positions


biosemi16
BioSemi 16-channel
16


biosemi32
BioSemi 32-channel
32


biosemi64
BioSemi 64-channel
64


biosemi128
BioSemi 128-channel
128


biosemi256
BioSemi 256-channel
256


easycap-M1
EasyCap M1 layout
74


GSN-HydroCel-129
EGI 128-channel + Cz
129


GSN-HydroCel-257
EGI 256-channel + Cz
257

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
Setting a montage in MNE-Python

Basic usage

import mne

# Load your data
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)

# Create a standard montage
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")

# Apply it to the data
raw.set_montage(montage)



Handling mismatched channel names
Your data may use channel names that do not exactly match the montage. For example, the montage uses “T7” but your data has “T3” (an older naming convention for the same electrode). MNE will raise an error by default when channel names do not match.
You have several options:

# Option 1: warn instead of raising an error
raw.set_montage(montage, on_missing="warn")

# Option 2: ignore missing channels entirely
raw.set_montage(montage, on_missing="ignore")

# Option 3: rename channels before setting the montage
raw.rename_channels({"T3": "T7", "T4": "T8", "T5": "P7", "T6": "P8"})
raw.set_montage(montage)

Option 3 is usually the best approach, because it solves the problem at the source rather than hiding it.


Checking what happened
After setting a montage, you can verify that it worked by inspecting the channel positions:

# Check that channels have positions
for ch in raw.info["chs"][:5]:
    print(f"{ch['ch_name']}: {ch['loc'][:3]}")

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
Plotting channel locations
Once a montage is set, you can visualise the electrode positions. This is useful for verifying that the montage was applied correctly and for generating figures.

2D topographic view

import mne

montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")

# Plot the montage directly
montage.plot(kind="topomap", show_names=True)



3D view

# 3D scatter plot of electrode positions
montage.plot(kind="3d", show_names=True)



Plotting from a Raw object

# Plot the sensor layout from an existing Raw object
raw.plot_sensors(kind="topomap", show_names=True)

# Or in 3D
raw.plot_sensors(kind="3d", show_names=True)

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
Custom montages from CSV
If your recording system uses electrode positions that do not match any standard montage (for example, a custom cap or intracranial electrodes), you can create a montage from a CSV file containing the channel names and their coordinates.

CSV format
Your CSV file should have columns for the channel name and the x, y, z coordinates (in metres). For example:
name,x,y,z
Fp1,-0.0309,0.0838,0.0415
Fp2,0.0309,0.0838,0.0415
F3,-0.0549,0.0571,0.0694
F4,0.0549,0.0571,0.0694
C3,-0.0684,0.0,0.0753
C4,0.0684,0.0,0.0753


Loading and applying a custom montage

import numpy as np
import mne

# Read the CSV file
data = np.genfromtxt(
    "electrode_positions.csv",
    delimiter=",",
    names=True,
    dtype=None,
    encoding="utf-8"
)

# Build a dictionary of channel positions
ch_pos = {}
for row in data:
    name = str(row["name"])
    ch_pos[name] = np.array([row["x"], row["y"], row["z"]])

# Create a custom montage
montage = mne.channels.make_dig_montage(
    ch_pos=ch_pos,
    coord_frame="head"
)

print(montage)

# Apply to your data
raw.set_montage(montage)



Using digitised positions
Some labs use a 3D digitiser (such as a Polhemus) to measure the exact position of each electrode on each participant’s head. MNE can read several digitiser formats:

# Read positions from a Polhemus .elp file
montage = mne.channels.read_dig_polhemus_isotrak("digitisation.elp")

# Read positions from a .hsp file
montage = mne.channels.read_dig_polhemus_isotrak("headshape.hsp")

# Read from BESA .elp format
montage = mne.channels.read_custom_montage("positions.elp")

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
When does the montage matter?
The montage affects several downstream analyses:

Topographic plots (mne.viz.plot_topomap, evoked.plot_topomap): the montage determines where each channel’s value is plotted on the scalp map.
Bad channel interpolation (raw.interpolate_bads): interpolation uses the spatial distances between channels to estimate what a bad channel should look like. Without a montage, interpolation will fail.
Source localisation: estimating brain sources from scalp data requires accurate electrode positions. Errors in the montage translate directly into errors in source estimates.
Average reference: the quality of an average reference depends on electrode coverage. The montage helps you judge whether your coverage is sufficient.

If you are only doing temporal analyses (filtering, epoching, averaging, time-frequency) without any spatial component, you can technically skip the montage. But setting it takes one line of code and prevents errors later, so there is little reason not to.

title: Setting channel locations (montages)
text:
Key takeaways

A montage maps channel names to physical locations on the scalp. It is needed for topographic plots, bad channel interpolation, and source localisation.
The 10-20 system is the original standard with 21 positions. The 10-10 and 10-05 systems extend it to 75 and 300+ positions, respectively. MNE includes all of these as built-in montages.
Use mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020") to create a montage and raw.set_montage(montage) to apply it.
If your channel names do not match the montage, rename them with raw.rename_channels() rather than ignoring the mismatch.
For non-standard electrode layouts, create a custom montage from a CSV file with x, y, z coordinates using mne.channels.make_dig_montage().
Setting the montage is quick and prevents hard-to-diagnose errors later. Do it as part of your standard loading workflow.

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
EEG amplifiers often record at high sampling rates: 1000, 2048, or even 5000 Hz. These rates are useful during recording because they capture the full bandwidth of the signal and allow you to detect very short-lived events. But for most analyses, you do not need that much temporal resolution.
If you are studying alpha oscillations (8–13 Hz), you do not need 5000 samples per second. A sampling rate of 256 Hz gives you more than enough resolution for frequencies up to 128 Hz (well above alpha). And working with lower sampling rates has real practical benefits:

Smaller file sizes: a 64-channel recording at 1000 Hz produces about 500 MB per hour. At 256 Hz, the same recording is about 125 MB. With large datasets, this difference matters.
Faster processing: filtering, ICA, and time-frequency analyses all run faster with fewer samples. ICA in particular can take much longer at high sampling rates because the number of time points directly affects computation time.
Reduced memory usage: if you are processing data in memory (as MNE does by default), lower sampling rates mean your arrays are smaller.

The trade-off is that resampling to a lower rate discards information above the new Nyquist frequency. If you resample to 256 Hz, you cannot analyse frequencies above 128 Hz. Make sure your target rate is high enough for the frequencies you care about.

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
The Nyquist theorem
The Nyquist theorem states that to faithfully represent a signal at frequency f, you need to sample at a rate of at least 2f. This minimum rate, 2f, is called the Nyquist rate. The maximum frequency that can be represented at a given sampling rate is called the Nyquist frequency, and it equals half the sampling rate.
For example:



Sampling rate
Nyquist frequency
Can represent up to




256 Hz
128 Hz
128 Hz


512 Hz
256 Hz
256 Hz


1000 Hz
500 Hz
500 Hz


2048 Hz
1024 Hz
1024 Hz



In practice, you want some margin above the highest frequency of interest. If you need to analyse gamma activity up to 100 Hz, a sampling rate of 256 Hz (Nyquist at 128 Hz) gives you a 28 Hz margin, which is enough for most filter designs to work well.

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
Anti-aliasing
If you simply throw away every other sample to halve the sampling rate (a process called decimation), any frequency above the new Nyquist frequency gets “folded back” into the lower frequency range. This phenomenon is called aliasing, and it creates false signals at frequencies where no real signal exists.
To prevent aliasing, you must apply a low-pass filter before reducing the sampling rate. This anti-aliasing filter removes all frequencies above the new Nyquist frequency so that there is nothing left to fold back. MNE’s resample() method does this automatically, so you do not need to apply a separate low-pass filter before resampling.
Here is a concrete example. Suppose your data is at 1000 Hz and you want to resample to 250 Hz. The new Nyquist frequency is 125 Hz. Before decimation, MNE applies a low-pass filter that removes everything above 125 Hz. Then it reduces the sampling rate. The result is a clean 250 Hz signal with no aliasing artifacts.

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
Using raw.resample() in MNE

Basic usage

import mne

# Load data (recorded at 1000 Hz, for example)
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)
print(f"Original sampling rate: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"Original number of samples: {raw.n_times}")

# Resample to 256 Hz
raw.resample(sfreq=256)
print(f"New sampling rate: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"New number of samples: {raw.n_times}")



With event handling
If your data has event markers (annotations or stim channels), resampling can shift event times slightly because the new time points may not align exactly with the old ones. MNE handles annotations automatically (it adjusts their onset times), but if you are working with events arrays, you should extract them before resampling and pass them to the events parameter:

# Extract events before resampling
events = mne.find_events(raw, stim_channel="Status")

# Resample data and events together
raw_resampled, events_resampled = raw.resample(
    sfreq=256,
    events=events
)

This ensures that event sample indices are adjusted to match the new sampling rate.


Full parameter control

raw.resample(
    sfreq=256,             # target sampling rate
    npad="auto",           # padding to reduce edge artifacts
    window="boxcar",       # window function for anti-aliasing
    events=None,           # events array to adjust (optional)
    pad="reflect_limited", # padding method
    verbose=True
)

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
Common target sampling rates
The choice of target sampling rate depends on what frequencies you need and what processing you plan to do. Here are the most common choices:









Target rate
Nyquist
Good for
Notes




250 Hz
125 Hz
Most ERP and oscillation studies
Common in BCI and clinical EEG


256 Hz
128 Hz
Same as 250 Hz
Power of 2, slightly faster FFT computation


500 Hz
250 Hz
Gamma studies, high temporal precision
Good compromise between speed and bandwidth


512 Hz
256 Hz
Same as 500 Hz
Power of 2


1000 Hz
500 Hz
Very high-frequency analysis
Rarely needed for scalp EEG



Powers of 2 (256, 512, 1024) are slightly more efficient for FFT-based analyses because the FFT algorithm is fastest when the number of samples is a power of 2. In practice, the difference is small, and you should not choose a sampling rate solely for this reason.
250 vs 256 Hz: both are common, and the choice rarely matters. Some labs prefer 256 because of the FFT advantage; others use 250 because it divides evenly into seconds (250 samples per second). Either is fine.

title: Resampling EEG data
section: When to resample in the pipeline
text:
When to resample in the pipeline
Resampling interacts with other preprocessing steps, so the order matters. Here is the recommended sequence:

Load data
Set channel types and montage
Filter (band-pass and/or notch): filter before resampling, not after. Filtering at the higher original sampling rate gives you better control over the filter design. If you filter after resampling, the lower Nyquist frequency constrains your filter options.
Resample: now that high-frequency content has been removed by the band-pass filter, you can safely reduce the sampling rate.
Run ICA, epoch, average, etc.

Some guides suggest resampling before filtering because it is faster (less data to filter). This can work if the anti-aliasing filter in resample() is sufficient for your needs, but the safer approach is to filter first so you have full control over the filter parameters.

Resampling after epoching
You can also resample epoched data. This is useful if you want to keep the full sampling rate for the continuous data (e.g., for accurate event detection) but reduce it for the epoched data (to speed up time-frequency analysis):

# Resample epochs
epochs = mne.Epochs(raw, events, event_id=1, tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.8)
epochs.resample(sfreq=256)

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
Working example

import numpy as np
import mne
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

# ── Create simulated data at 1000 Hz ────────────────────────
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sfreq = 1000
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Pink noise + 10 Hz alpha
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) / np.sqrt(freqs_fft), n=n_samples)
signal = pink * 20e-6 / pink.std()
signal += 5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Wrap in MNE Raw
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=["Oz"], sfreq=sfreq, ch_types=["eeg"])
raw = mne.io.RawArray(signal.reshape(1, -1), info)

# ── Compare original and resampled data ──────────────────────
raw_256 = raw.copy().resample(sfreq=256)

print(f"Original: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz, {raw.n_times} samples")
print(f"Resampled: {raw_256.info['sfreq']} Hz, {raw_256.n_times} samples")
print(f"Size reduction: {1 - raw_256.n_times / raw.n_times:.1%}")

# ── Compare PSDs ─────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

raw.compute_psd(fmax=200).plot(axes=axes[0], show=False)
axes[0].set_title(f"Original ({int(raw.info['sfreq'])} Hz)")

raw_256.compute_psd(fmax=120).plot(axes=axes[1], show=False)
axes[1].set_title(f"Resampled ({int(raw_256.info['sfreq'])} Hz)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

title: Resampling EEG data
text:
Key takeaways

Resample to reduce file size, speed up processing, and save memory. The most common target rates for EEG are 250 or 256 Hz (for studies up to ~100 Hz) and 500 or 512 Hz (for gamma studies).
The Nyquist theorem says you need at least 2 samples per cycle. Your sampling rate must be at least twice the highest frequency you want to analyse.
MNE’s resample() applies an anti-aliasing filter automatically, so frequencies above the new Nyquist frequency are removed before the sampling rate is reduced. You do not need to low-pass filter separately.
Filter before resampling in your pipeline. This gives you full control over filter design at the higher original sampling rate.
If your data has events, pass them to resample(events=events) so that event sample indices are adjusted to the new sampling rate.
Avoid resampling to a rate that is too low for your analysis. If you need gamma activity up to 80 Hz, do not resample below 200 Hz.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Running ICA is the easy part. The hard part is deciding which components are artifacts and which are brain activity. Every component you remove also removes some brain signal, because the separation is never perfect. Remove too few and your data stays contaminated. Remove too many and you distort the brain signals you care about.
This page covers the practical criteria for identifying artifact components: what to look for in the topography, time course, and spectrum, and how to use MNE’s automated detection methods to speed up the process.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Running ICA is the easy part. The hard part is deciding which components are artifacts and which are brain activity. Every component you remove also removes some brain signal, because the separation is never perfect. Remove too few and your data stays contaminated. Remove too many and you distort the brain signals you care about.
This page covers the practical criteria for identifying artifact components: what to look for in the topography, time course, and spectrum, and how to use MNE’s automated detection methods to speed up the process.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
The three views
When you inspect a component, you look at three things. Together, they give you a reliable picture of what the component represents.

Topography (spatial pattern): where on the scalp does the component project? This is the most reliable cue and usually sufficient on its own for clear cases.
Time course (waveform): what does the component look like over time? Intermittent sharp peaks suggest blinks. A regular rhythm suggests heartbeat. Sustained high-frequency bursts suggest muscle.
Power spectrum: which frequencies dominate the component? Low-frequency power points to eye artifacts. A broad high-frequency bump points to muscle. A clear peak at the alpha frequency (8-13 Hz) suggests a brain source.

MNE’s ica.plot_properties() shows all three views in a single figure, which makes the decision process easier.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Visual criteria by artifact type

Eye blinks
Blink components are usually the easiest to identify:

Topography: strong, symmetric frontal projection centred on Fp1 and Fp2. The pattern is positive at the front and drops off sharply toward posterior electrodes. The left-right symmetry distinguishes it from lateral eye movements.
Time course: intermittent large deflections lasting 200-400 ms, with long quiet periods in between. The deflections have a smooth, rounded shape.
Spectrum: dominated by low frequencies (below 5 Hz), with power falling off rapidly above that.

Confidence level: high. If the topography is clearly frontal and symmetric, and the time course shows intermittent sharp peaks, it is almost certainly a blink component. You will typically find one or two blink components.


Saccadic eye movements
Horizontal saccades produce a different pattern from blinks:

Topography: left-right asymmetric frontal pattern. One side of the frontal scalp (around F7 or F8) is positive while the other is negative. This reflects the horizontal displacement of the corneo-retinal dipole.
Time course: step-like transitions lasting 50-100 ms, often occurring in pairs (saccade and return). The steps are sharper and faster than blink deflections.
Spectrum: also dominated by low frequencies, but often with slightly more power in the 5-15 Hz range than blink components.

Vertical eye movements look more like attenuated blinks: frontal topography, but with smaller amplitude and a more sustained waveform.


Muscle artifacts
Muscle components come from the temporalis, frontalis, or neck muscles:

Topography: peripheral, concentrated at the edges of the electrode array. Temporalis muscle shows up at T7/T8 and F7/F8. Frontalis muscle appears at Fp1/Fp2 (but with a different spectral profile from blinks). Neck muscles project to posterior and temporal electrodes.
Time course: either sustained tonic activity (if the muscle is constantly tense) or intermittent bursts. The waveform looks irregular and noisy rather than smooth.
Spectrum: a broad spectral bump above 20 Hz, often extending to 40-50 Hz or higher. This high-frequency dominance is the strongest distinguishing feature. Brain components rarely have so much power above 30 Hz.

Muscle components can be tricky when they are intermittent, because a brief burst of muscle activity might look like a single event. The key is the spectrum: if a component’s power is concentrated above 20 Hz, it is very likely muscle.


Heartbeat (cardiac) artifacts
The heartbeat artifact appears when the electrical field of the heart reaches the scalp electrodes (which happens in all recordings, though it is sometimes too small to see):

Topography: broad, diffuse pattern without a clear focal point. It can vary between subjects depending on body build and electrode placement.
Time course: very regular peaks matching the heart rate (roughly 60-80 per minute, or once every 0.75-1 second). The QRS complex of the heartbeat appears as a sharp deflection, sometimes followed by a slower T-wave.
Spectrum: peaks at the heart rate frequency (around 1 Hz) with harmonics.

The regularity of the time course is the strongest identifier. If a component has a very regular, rhythmic pattern at about 1 Hz that does not look like brain oscillations (which are less regular and more sinusoidal), it is likely a cardiac component.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Decision flowchart
When inspecting a component, you can follow this sequence:

Look at the topography first. Is it frontal and symmetric? Likely a blink. Frontal and asymmetric? Likely a saccade. Peripheral (temporal or edge)? Likely muscle. Diffuse with no clear focal point? Could be heartbeat.
Check the spectrum. If power is concentrated below 5 Hz, it supports an eye artifact classification. If there is a broad bump above 20 Hz, it supports muscle. If you see a clear alpha peak (8-13 Hz) with a smooth topography, it is probably brain.
Look at the time course for confirmation. Intermittent sharp peaks = blinks. Step-like transitions = saccades. Regular rhythm at ~1 Hz = heartbeat. Sustained high-frequency noise = muscle.
When in doubt, keep the component. Removing a brain component is worse than keeping a mild artifact, because you cannot undo the removal.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Automated detection with find_bads_eog()
MNE can automatically identify blink and eye movement components by correlating them with an EOG (electrooculography) channel. If your recording includes dedicated EOG channels, this is fast and reliable.

import mne
from mne.preprocessing import ICA

# Fit ICA
ica = ICA(n_components=20, method="infomax",
          fit_params=dict(extended=True), random_state=42)
ica.fit(raw)

# Find components that correlate with the EOG channel
eog_indices, eog_scores = ica.find_bads_eog(raw)
print(f"EOG-related components: {eog_indices}")
print(f"Correlation scores: {eog_scores}")

# Mark them for exclusion
ica.exclude = eog_indices

# Plot the scores to see how clear the detection is
ica.plot_scores(eog_scores, title="EOG correlation scores")


Using a proxy channel
Many EEG setups do not include dedicated EOG channels. In that case, you can use a frontal EEG channel (like Fp1) as a proxy. The blink artifact is so large at frontal channels that they work well as a substitute.

# Use Fp1 as an EOG proxy
eog_indices, eog_scores = ica.find_bads_eog(raw, ch_name="Fp1")
print(f"EOG components (using Fp1 as proxy): {eog_indices}")

The method works by creating synthetic EOG epochs (time-locked to detected blink events), computing the average blink waveform for each component, and then correlating it with the average blink in the proxy channel. Components with a high correlation are flagged.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Automated detection with find_bads_ecg()
The same approach works for heartbeat artifacts:

# Find components that correlate with the ECG channel
ecg_indices, ecg_scores = ica.find_bads_ecg(raw)
print(f"ECG-related components: {ecg_indices}")

# If no ECG channel is available, MNE will try to use
# magnetometer channels (MEG) or create a synthetic ECG.
# For EEG-only data without an ECG channel, this may not work
# automatically. You might need to identify cardiac components
# by visual inspection instead.

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Combining automated and manual inspection
The automated methods are a good starting point, but they should not be the final word. A recommended workflow is:

Run find_bads_eog() and find_bads_ecg() to get initial candidates.
Plot the flagged components with ica.plot_properties() to verify that the detections make sense.
Browse the remaining components with ica.plot_sources() and ica.plot_components() to check for artifacts the automated methods may have missed.
Add or remove components from ica.exclude as needed.


# Step 1: Automated detection
eog_idx, _ = ica.find_bads_eog(raw, ch_name="Fp1")
ecg_idx, _ = ica.find_bads_ecg(raw)
ica.exclude = list(set(eog_idx + ecg_idx))  # combine, removing duplicates

# Step 2: Verify flagged components
ica.plot_properties(raw, picks=ica.exclude)

# Step 3: Browse all components
ica.plot_components()
ica.plot_sources(raw)

# Step 4: Adjust the exclude list if needed
# ica.exclude.append(7)   # add another artifact component
# ica.exclude.remove(3)   # un-flag a component that looks like brain

# Apply the correction
ica.apply(raw)

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Working example
The code below simulates data with both blink and heartbeat artifacts, fits ICA, and demonstrates how to identify each artifact type using the frontal loading (for blinks) and periodicity (for heartbeat) of the recovered components.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Parameters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 8
sfreq = 256
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

channel_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"]

# ── Source 1: Alpha oscillation (brain) ────────────────────────
alpha = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
alpha += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── Source 2: Blink artifact ──────────────────────────────────
blink = np.zeros(n_samples)
for bt in [0.8, 2.5, 4.1, 5.7, 7.3, 9.0]:
    idx = int(bt * sfreq)
    width = int(0.15 * sfreq)
    if idx + width < n_samples:
        t_b = np.arange(width) / sfreq
        blink[idx:idx + width] = 5 * np.sin(np.pi * t_b / (width / sfreq))

# ── Source 3: Heartbeat artifact ──────────────────────────────
heartbeat = np.zeros(n_samples)
heart_rate = 1.1  # beats per second (~66 bpm)
beat_times = np.arange(0.5, duration, 1 / heart_rate)
for bt in beat_times:
    idx = int(bt * sfreq)
    # QRS complex: sharp, brief spike
    qrs_width = int(0.04 * sfreq)
    if idx + qrs_width < n_samples:
        t_qrs = np.arange(qrs_width) / sfreq
        heartbeat[idx:idx + qrs_width] = 2 * np.sin(
            np.pi * t_qrs / (qrs_width / sfreq))

# ── Source 4: Background noise ─────────────────────────────────
noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── Mixing matrix ─────────────────────────────────────────────
# Blink: strong frontal. Heartbeat: diffuse, slightly stronger centrally.
mixing = np.array([
    [0.4, 1.0, 0.3, 0.4],   # Fp1
    [0.4, 0.95, 0.3, 0.4],  # Fp2
    [0.7, 0.3, 0.4, 0.3],   # F3
    [0.7, 0.25, 0.4, 0.3],  # F4
    [0.9, 0.05, 0.5, 0.3],  # C3
    [0.9, 0.05, 0.5, 0.3],  # C4
    [1.0, 0.02, 0.3, 0.2],  # O1
    [1.0, 0.02, 0.3, 0.2],  # O2
])

sources_true = np.vstack([alpha, blink, heartbeat, noise])
data = mixing @ sources_true
data *= 30e-6 / data.std()

# ── Fit ICA ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
ica = FastICA(n_components=4, random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
components = ica.fit_transform(data.T).T
ica_mixing = ica.mixing_

# ── Criterion 1: frontal loading (for blinks) ─────────────────
frontal_loading = np.abs(ica_mixing[:2, :]).mean(axis=0)
blink_ic = np.argmax(frontal_loading)

# ── Criterion 2: autocorrelation at heart rate lag ─────────────
heart_lag = int(sfreq / heart_rate)  # samples per heartbeat
autocorr_at_lag = np.zeros(4)
for i in range(4):
    c = components[i]
    c_norm = (c - c.mean()) / c.std()
    autocorr_at_lag[i] = np.abs(np.correlate(
        c_norm[:n_samples - heart_lag],
        c_norm[heart_lag:]
    )[0] / (n_samples - heart_lag))

cardiac_ic = np.argmax(autocorr_at_lag)

print(f"Blink component:     IC {blink_ic} "
      f"(frontal loading = {frontal_loading[blink_ic]:.4f})")
print(f"Heartbeat component: IC {cardiac_ic} "
      f"(autocorrelation = {autocorr_at_lag[cardiac_ic]:.4f})")

# ── Visualisation ──────────────────────────────────────────────
fig = plt.figure(figsize=(13, 8))
gs = fig.add_gridspec(2, 2, hspace=0.35, wspace=0.3)

# Top row: ICA component time courses
ax_top = fig.add_subplot(gs[0, :])
offset = 0
for i in range(4):
    trace = components[i] / np.max(np.abs(components)) + offset
    if i == blink_ic:
        colour, label_extra, lw = "#e74c3c", " (blink)", 1.0
    elif i == cardiac_ic:
        colour, label_extra, lw = "#3498db", " (heartbeat)", 1.0
    else:
        colour, label_extra, lw = "#2c3e50", "", 0.5
    ax_top.plot(times, trace, lw=lw, color=colour,
                label=f"IC {i}{label_extra}")
    offset -= 1.5
ax_top.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax_top.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax_top.set_title("ICA components")
ax_top.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax_top.set_xlim(0, duration)

# Bottom left: frontal loading bar chart
ax_bl = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 0])
colours_fl = ["#e74c3c" if i == blink_ic else "#95a5a6" for i in range(4)]
ax_bl.bar(range(4), frontal_loading, color=colours_fl)
ax_bl.set_xlabel("Component")
ax_bl.set_ylabel("Mean frontal loading")
ax_bl.set_title("Blink detection: frontal loading")
ax_bl.set_xticks(range(4))
ax_bl.set_xticklabels([f"IC {i}" for i in range(4)])

# Bottom right: autocorrelation at heart rate lag
ax_br = fig.add_subplot(gs[1, 1])
colours_ac = ["#3498db" if i == cardiac_ic else "#95a5a6" for i in range(4)]
ax_br.bar(range(4), autocorr_at_lag, color=colours_ac)
ax_br.set_xlabel("Component")
ax_br.set_ylabel("Autocorrelation at HR lag")
ax_br.set_title("Heartbeat detection: periodicity")
ax_br.set_xticks(range(4))
ax_br.set_xticklabels([f"IC {i}" for i in range(4)])

plt.show()

title: Identifying ICA components
text:
Key takeaways

Inspect three features of each component: topography (where it projects on the scalp), time course (what it looks like over time), and spectrum (which frequencies dominate).
Blinks: frontal, symmetric topography; intermittent sharp peaks; low-frequency spectrum.
Saccades: frontal, asymmetric (left-right) topography; step-like transitions; low-frequency spectrum.
Muscle: peripheral topography (temporal or edge electrodes); high-frequency spectral bump above 20 Hz; irregular, noisy waveform.
Heartbeat: diffuse topography; very regular rhythm at ~1 Hz; sharp QRS-like peaks.
Use ica.find_bads_eog() to detect blink/eye components automatically. If you have no dedicated EOG channel, use a frontal channel (like Fp1) as a proxy.
Use ica.find_bads_ecg() for heartbeat components. This requires an ECG channel or, for MEG data, magnetometer channels.
Always verify automated detections with visual inspection. The automated methods are a starting point, not a final answer.
When in doubt, keep the component. Removing brain signal is harder to correct than leaving a mild artifact in the data.

title: Preprocessing
text:
Raw EEG is noisy. It contains slow drifts from electrode impedance changes, high-frequency muscle activity, 50 or 60 Hz power line interference, and sometimes channels that stopped working mid-recording. Preprocessing cleans the signal so that later analysis steps (ICA, spectral analysis, connectivity) reflect brain activity rather than noise.
This module walks through the standard preprocessing pipeline in order: filtering, notch filtering, re-referencing, resampling, bad channel detection, interpolation, and segmentation into epochs. Each step has a clear rationale, and the order matters because some operations assume the data has already been cleaned in specific ways.

It contains slow drifts from electrode impedance changes, high-frequency muscle activity, 50 or 60 Hz power line interference, and sometimes channels that stopped working mid-recording. Preprocessing cleans the signal so that later analysis steps (ICA, spectral analysis, connectivity) reflect brain activity rather than noise.
This module walks through the standard preprocessing pipeline in order: filtering, notch filtering, re-referencing, resampling, bad channel detection, interpolation, and segmentation into epochs. Each step has a clear rationale, and the order matters because some operations assume the data has already been cleaned in specific ways.

title: Preprocessing
text:
Topics

Band-pass filtering
A band-pass filter keeps frequencies within a specified range and attenuates everything outside it. For EEG, a common choice is 0.1–40 Hz: the low cutoff removes slow drifts and the high cutoff removes muscle artifact and high-frequency noise.
MNE offers two types of filters:

FIR (finite impulse response): the default in MNE. FIR filters have a linear phase response, which means they do not distort the shape of ERP waveforms. They are slower to compute but safer for most applications.
IIR (infinite impulse response): faster but can introduce phase distortion. Useful for real-time applications or very long recordings where speed matters.

The choice of cutoff frequencies depends on what you plan to analyse. If you are interested in slow cortical potentials, you might lower the high-pass to 0.01 Hz. If you are studying gamma oscillations, you would raise the low-pass to 100 Hz or higher.
See Band-pass filtering for a detailed comparison of FIR and IIR filters, guidance on choosing cutoffs, and common pitfalls (like filtering too aggressively before ICA).
# Typical band-pass filter: keep 0.1 to 40 Hz
raw.filter(l_freq=0.1, h_freq=40.0)


Notch filtering
Power lines introduce a sharp peak at 50 Hz (Europe, Brazil, most of Asia) or 60 Hz (North America, parts of Asia). A notch filter removes this specific frequency and its harmonics (100, 150, 200 Hz, etc.) while leaving the rest of the spectrum intact.
MNE’s raw.notch_filter() can target multiple frequencies at once. It is usually applied after band-pass filtering, though if your low-pass cutoff is below 50 Hz, the band-pass filter will already have removed line noise.
See Notch filtering for examples and a discussion of when notch filtering is unnecessary.
# Remove 50 Hz and its harmonics
raw.notch_filter(freqs=[50, 100, 150])


Re-referencing
EEG measures voltage differences, so every recording has a reference electrode. The choice of reference affects the spatial distribution of the signal. Common re-referencing schemes include:

Average reference: subtracts the mean across all channels at each time point. Works well when you have many channels (32+) with good scalp coverage.
Linked mastoids: averages the signal at the two mastoid electrodes and uses that as the reference. Common in clinical EEG and older studies.
REST (reference electrode standardisation technique): a mathematical approach that estimates what the signal would look like with a reference at infinity.

Re-referencing is typically done after filtering and bad channel interpolation. If you re-reference before removing bad channels, the bad channel’s noise spreads to every other channel through the average.
See Re-referencing for worked examples of each scheme.
# Average reference
raw.set_eeg_reference(ref_channels="average")

# Linked mastoids (if M1 and M2 are in your montage)
raw.set_eeg_reference(ref_channels=["M1", "M2"])


Resampling
Many EEG amplifiers record at high sampling rates (1000, 2048, or even 5000 Hz). If your analysis only needs frequencies up to 40 Hz, you can safely downsample to 256 or 512 Hz. This makes all subsequent computations faster and reduces file sizes.
Resampling should be done after filtering (to avoid aliasing) but before epoching (because resampling epochs individually can introduce edge artifacts at epoch boundaries).
See Resampling for guidance on choosing a new sampling rate.
# Downsample from 1000 Hz to 256 Hz
raw.resample(sfreq=256)


Detecting and interpolating bad channels
A bad channel is one that records noise rather than brain activity. Common causes include high electrode impedance, a broken wire, or an electrode that lost contact with the scalp. Bad channels appear as flat lines, high-amplitude bursts, or signals that look nothing like their neighbours.
MNE provides several ways to detect bad channels:

Visual inspection: scroll through the data and click on bad channels.
Statistical methods: flag channels whose variance, correlation with neighbours, or spectral properties are outliers.
Automated tools: the autoreject package can detect bad channels and bad epochs simultaneously.

Once identified, bad channels are repaired by spherical spline interpolation, which estimates the missing signal from the surrounding good channels. This step should be done before re-referencing to average, so the bad channel does not contaminate the reference.
See Detecting and interpolating bad channels for a walkthrough of manual and automated detection.
# Mark bad channels
raw.info["bads"] = ["Cz", "F3"]

# Interpolate them
raw.interpolate_bads(reset_bads=True)


Segmentation into epochs
Many analyses require the data to be cut into short, equal-length segments called epochs. Each epoch is time-locked to an event (a stimulus onset, a button press, a marker in the recording). For resting-state analyses without events, you can cut the continuous data into fixed-length segments.
MNE creates epochs from a Raw object and an events array. The events array is a NumPy array with three columns: sample index, previous event value, and event ID.
See Segmentation into epochs for examples of event-locked and fixed-length epoching.
# Event-locked epochs: -0.2 to 0.5 seconds around each event
events = mne.find_events(raw, stim_channel="STI 014")
epochs = mne.Epochs(raw, events, event_id=1, tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.5,
                    baseline=(None, 0), preload=True)

# Fixed-length epochs for resting-state data
epochs = mne.make_fixed_length_epochs(raw, duration=2.0, preload=True)

title: Preprocessing
text:
The preprocessing pipeline in order
The order of preprocessing steps matters. Here is a typical pipeline and the reasoning behind the sequence:

Load data and set the montage.
Band-pass filter (e.g., 0.1–40 Hz). Filtering first removes slow drifts that can affect bad channel detection.
Notch filter (50 or 60 Hz). Remove line noise if it falls within your band-pass range.
Detect and interpolate bad channels. Do this before re-referencing.
Re-reference to average (or another scheme). Now that bad channels are repaired, the average is clean.
Resample if the sampling rate is higher than you need.
Segment into epochs (if your analysis requires it).
Artifact rejection / ICA (covered in Module 3).

title: Preprocessing
section: Working example: filter, notch, and re-reference
text:
Working example: filter, notch, and re-reference
The code below creates simulated EEG data, applies a band-pass filter, adds a notch filter, and re-references to average. It plots the power spectral density before and after filtering so you can see the effect.

import numpy as np
import mne

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# --- Create simulated raw data ---
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("biosemi64")
ch_names = montage.ch_names[:64]
sfreq = 512  # Hz (higher rate so we can see the 50 Hz peak)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
n_samples = int(10 * sfreq)
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Pink noise base
white = rng.standard_normal((len(ch_names), n_samples))
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
data = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)

# Add alpha rhythm (10 Hz) in posterior channels
alpha = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
posterior = [i for i, ch in enumerate(ch_names) if ch.startswith(("O", "P"))]
for idx in posterior:
    data[idx] += 3 * alpha

# Add 50 Hz line noise to all channels
line_noise = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * times)
data += line_noise

# Scale to realistic microvolts
data *= 20e-6 / data.std()

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
raw.set_montage(montage)

# --- Plot PSD before preprocessing ---
fig_before = raw.compute_psd(fmax=80).plot(
    average=True, picks="eeg",
)
fig_before.suptitle("Before preprocessing", fontsize=12)
fig_before.tight_layout()

# --- Preprocessing ---
# 1. Band-pass filter: 0.1 - 40 Hz
raw.filter(l_freq=0.1, h_freq=40.0)

# 2. Notch filter at 50 Hz (even though the band-pass already attenuated it,
#    this removes any residual leakage near the cutoff)
raw.notch_filter(freqs=50.0)

# 3. Re-reference to average
raw.set_eeg_reference(ref_channels="average")

# --- Plot PSD after preprocessing ---
fig_after = raw.compute_psd(fmax=80).plot(
    average=True, picks="eeg",
)
fig_after.suptitle("After preprocessing", fontsize=12)
fig_after.tight_layout()

text:
What comes next
With clean, filtered, re-referenced data, you are ready to deal with the remaining artifacts that filtering alone cannot remove: eye blinks, eye movements, muscle tension, and heartbeat. Move on to Module 3: Artifact rejection to learn about ICA and automated rejection methods.

title: Connectivity and metastability
text:
The previous modules treated each EEG channel independently: we filtered it, removed its artifacts, and measured its spectral content. But the brain is a network. Cognitive functions do not arise from isolated regions; they emerge from coordinated activity across distributed populations of neurones. To study this coordination, we need to measure how different brain regions communicate with each other.
This module covers phase-based connectivity and metastability. We start with the basics: what does it mean for two signals to be synchronised, and how do we measure that? Then we build up to the main topic: metastability, which quantifies how flexibly the brain switches between different coordination patterns over time. This concept is central to Natalia’s master’s project on metastability in Parkinson’s disease and Freezing of Gait.
The progression is:

Phase synchronisation and the Hilbert transform
Phase-locking value (PLV) and coherence
The Kuramoto order parameter
The relative phase alignment matrix
The dominant eigenvector and regional metastability
Group comparisons and relevance to Parkinson’s disease

title: Connectivity and metastability
text:

Cognitive functions do not arise from isolated regions; they emerge from coordinated activity across distributed populations of neurones. To study this coordination, we need to measure how different brain regions communicate with each other.
This module covers phase-based connectivity and metastability. We start with the basics: what does it mean for two signals to be synchronised, and how do we measure that? Then we build up to the main topic: metastability, which quantifies how flexibly the brain switches between different coordination patterns over time. Phase synchronisation and the Hilbert transform
Phase-locking value (PLV) and coherence
