Group comparison of regional metastability across 8 channels for three groups: healthy controls (HC), Parkinson’s disease without Freezing of Gait (PD-noFoG), and PD with Freezing of Gait (PD-FoG). Asterisks mark channels where ANOVA was significant after FDR correction.





Reading the group comparison output
The printed output walks through the three steps of the analysis:

ANOVA per channel: some channels show large F-statistics (indicating group differences) while others do not. Channels with small or absent effects (like O1 and O2 in this simulation) have high p-values.
Correction across channels: Bonferroni is conservative (it may miss channels with moderate effects), while FDR is more permissive. In practice, both methods are acceptable; FDR is often preferred in EEG research because it controls the expected proportion of false positives rather than the probability of any false positive.
Post-hoc pairwise t-tests: for each significant channel, we test all three pairs. The Bonferroni correction for 3 comparisons (multiplying each p-value by 3) is applied separately from the channel-level correction. Cohen’s d gives the effect size: values around 0.2 are small, 0.5 medium, and 0.8 large.

The bar chart shows the group means with standard error bars. Channels marked with an asterisk survived the FDR correction. The pattern we expect (HC > PD-noFoG > PD-FoG) is visible in channels with large simulated effects (C3, C4, P3, P4) but not in channels where the effect was small (O1, O2).
In Natalia’s real data, this analysis would use actual metastability values computed from the eigenvector pipeline in the first working example, with the channel names corresponding to the EEG montage used in the study.

title: Connectivity and metastability
text:
Summary of key formulas








Quantity
Formula
Interpretation




Instantaneous phase
\(\phi_k(t) = \arg\!\big(\text{Hilbert}(x_k(t))\big)\)
Where channel \(k\) is in its oscillatory cycle


Phase alignment matrix
\(A_{ij}(t) = \cos(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))\)
Pairwise phase similarity at time \(t\)


Kuramoto order parameter
\(R(t) = \frac{1}{N} \lvert \sum_k e^{i\phi_k(t)} \rvert\)
Global synchrony at time \(t\)


Dominant eigenvector
\(v(t) = \text{eigvec}_{max}(A(t))\)
Primary coordination pattern at time \(t\)


Regional metastability
\(\text{MS}_k = \text{Var}_t(v_k(t))\)
How flexibly region \(k\) changes its role


Global metastability
\(\text{MS}_{\text{global}} = \text{Var}_t(R(t))\)
How much overall synchrony fluctuates

title: Connectivity and metastability
text:
What comes next
This module introduced the theoretical and computational framework for measuring phase connectivity and metastability. The next steps are:

Apply this pipeline to real EEG data using MNE-Python for the preprocessing stages (filtering, artifact rejection, epoching) and the numpy/scipy code above for the metastability computation.
Explore different frequency bands (alpha, beta, theta) and compare the metastability patterns they reveal.
Run the group comparison analysis with proper statistical controls.
Consider additional connectivity measures (weighted PLV, imaginary coherence) as complementary analyses.

The exercises section will include practice problems where you modify the simulation parameters (number of channels, coupling strengths, noise levels) and observe how metastability changes.

title: Preprocessing: exercises
text: These exercises go with Module 2: Preprocessing. They walk you through the core preprocessing steps: removing line noise, applying band-pass filters, handling bad channels, re-referencing, and downsampling. Each exercise uses simulated data so you can see exactly what the processing does to a signal you control.

title: Preprocessing: exercises
section: Exercise 1: Remove 50 Hz line noise with a notch filter
text:
Exercise 1: Remove 50 Hz line noise with a notch filter
Create a simulated signal that contains a 10 Hz alpha oscillation mixed with 50 Hz line noise. Apply a notch filter at 50 Hz and plot the power spectral density (PSD) before and after to confirm the line noise is gone while the alpha peak survives.






TipHint





Build the signal by adding two sine waves: np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * t) for alpha and np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * t) for the line noise (make the line noise smaller, say half the alpha amplitude). Use raw.notch_filter(50) to remove the noise. Plot PSDs with raw.compute_psd().plot() (or raw.plot_psd() in older MNE versions).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

sfreq = 500
duration = 30
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

# Create a signal with 10 Hz alpha + 50 Hz line noise + background noise
ch_names = ["Oz"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

alpha = 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)      # 10 µV alpha
line_noise = 5e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 50 * times)   # 5 µV line noise
noise = np.random.randn(n_samples) * 2e-6             # 2 µV random noise
signal = (alpha + line_noise + noise).reshape(1, -1)

raw = mne.io.RawArray(signal, info)

# Plot PSD before filtering
fig_before = raw.compute_psd(fmax=80).plot(show=False)
fig_before.suptitle("PSD before notch filter")

# Apply notch filter at 50 Hz
raw_filtered = raw.copy().notch_filter(50)

# Plot PSD after filtering
fig_after = raw_filtered.compute_psd(fmax=80).plot(show=False)
fig_after.suptitle("PSD after notch filter")

You should see two peaks in the “before” plot (at 10 Hz and 50 Hz). After the notch filter, the 50 Hz peak disappears while the 10 Hz alpha peak remains.

title: Preprocessing: exercises
section: Exercise 2: Apply a band-pass filter (1–40 Hz)
text:
Exercise 2: Apply a band-pass filter (1–40 Hz)
Create simulated EEG data with multiple channels. Apply a band-pass filter between 1 and 40 Hz. Compare the PSD before and after to see which frequencies were kept and which were removed.






TipHint





Use raw.filter(l_freq=1, h_freq=40) for band-pass filtering. This combines a high-pass filter at 1 Hz (removes slow drifts) with a low-pass filter at 40 Hz (removes high-frequency noise). Plot the PSDs side by side to see the effect.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

sfreq = 500
duration = 60
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

# Create 8 channels with broadband noise plus a slow drift and
# a 10 Hz oscillation
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6

# Add a slow drift (0.1 Hz) to all channels
drift = 15e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.1 * times)
data += drift

# Add a 10 Hz alpha oscillation to occipital channels
alpha = 8e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
data[6] += alpha  # O1
data[7] += alpha  # O2

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Plot PSD before filtering
fig_before = raw.compute_psd(fmax=100).plot(show=False)
fig_before.suptitle("PSD before band-pass filter")

# Apply band-pass filter
raw_filtered = raw.copy().filter(l_freq=1, h_freq=40)

# Plot PSD after filtering
fig_after = raw_filtered.compute_psd(fmax=100).plot(show=False)
fig_after.suptitle("PSD after band-pass filter (1-40 Hz)")

# Compare a single channel in the time domain
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 6), sharex=True)
t_plot = slice(0, int(5 * sfreq))  # first 5 seconds

axes[0].plot(times[:int(5 * sfreq)], raw.get_data(picks="O1")[0, t_plot] * 1e6)
axes[0].set_title("O1 before filtering")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")

axes[1].plot(times[:int(5 * sfreq)], raw_filtered.get_data(picks="O1")[0, t_plot] * 1e6)
axes[1].set_title("O1 after band-pass filter (1-40 Hz)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

In the PSD plots, you should see that frequencies below 1 Hz and above 40 Hz are strongly attenuated after filtering. In the time-domain plots of O1, the slow drift visible in the unfiltered signal should be gone.

title: Preprocessing: exercises
section: Exercise 3: Mark a bad channel and interpolate it
text:
Exercise 3: Mark a bad channel and interpolate it
Create multi-channel simulated data with a standard montage. Deliberately corrupt channel "Fp1" by making it much noisier than the others. Mark it as bad, interpolate it, and compare the signal before and after interpolation.






TipHint





Set raw.info["bads"] = ["Fp1"] to mark the channel. Then call raw.interpolate_bads() to replace it with a weighted average of its neighbours. You need a montage set (so MNE knows which channels are neighbours); use mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020").









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sfreq = 500
duration = 20
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

# Use enough channels that interpolation has good neighbours
ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4",
    "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2", "F7", "F8",
    "T7", "T8", "P7", "P8", "Fz", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Generate clean data with a 10 Hz oscillation
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6
alpha = 8e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
for i in range(n_channels):
    data[i] += alpha

# Corrupt Fp1 (index 0): add large noise
fp1_idx = ch_names.index("Fp1")
data[fp1_idx] += np.random.randn(n_samples) * 100e-6  # very noisy

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Set montage (needed for interpolation)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Store the noisy Fp1 for comparison
fp1_before = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0].copy()

# Mark Fp1 as bad and interpolate
raw.info["bads"] = ["Fp1"]
print(f"Bad channels: {raw.info['bads']}")

raw.interpolate_bads()

fp1_after = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0]

# Compare before and after
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(12, 5), sharex=True)
t_slice = slice(0, int(2 * sfreq))  # first 2 seconds

axes[0].plot(times[:int(2 * sfreq)], fp1_before[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[0].set_title("Fp1 before interpolation (corrupted)")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")

axes[1].plot(times[:int(2 * sfreq)], fp1_after[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[1].set_title("Fp1 after interpolation")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Fp1 std before: {np.std(fp1_before) * 1e6:.1f} µV")
print(f"Fp1 std after:  {np.std(fp1_after) * 1e6:.1f} µV")

The interpolated Fp1 should have a much smaller amplitude range because it is now reconstructed from its (clean) neighbours. The standard deviation should drop from around 100 µV down to something close to the other channels (around 5–10 µV).

title: Preprocessing: exercises
text:
Exercise 4: Re-reference to average reference
Create simulated data and re-reference it to the average of all channels. Compare a frontal channel ("Fp1") and an occipital channel ("Oz") before and after re-referencing. Notice how the signals change.






TipHint





Use raw.set_eeg_reference("average") to apply the average reference. This subtracts the mean across all channels at each time point from every channel. The effect is usually more visible on channels that were far from the original reference.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sfreq = 500
duration = 10
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4",
    "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2", "Fz", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Create data: alpha oscillation mainly in occipital channels,
# frontal channels get a different pattern (slow wave)
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 3e-6

# Add alpha to occipital channels
alpha = 12e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
for name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += alpha

# Add a slow wave to frontal channels
slow = 8e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 1.5 * times)
for name in ["Fp1", "Fp2"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += slow

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Store pre-reref data
fp1_before = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0].copy()
oz_before = raw.get_data(picks="Oz")[0].copy()

# Re-reference to average
raw.set_eeg_reference("average", projection=False)

fp1_after = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0]
oz_after = raw.get_data(picks="Oz")[0]

# Plot comparison
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(14, 6), sharex=True)
t_slice = slice(0, int(3 * sfreq))
t_sec = times[:int(3 * sfreq)]

axes[0, 0].plot(t_sec, fp1_before[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[0, 0].set_title("Fp1 before re-referencing")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("µV")

axes[0, 1].plot(t_sec, oz_before[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[0, 1].set_title("Oz before re-referencing")

axes[1, 0].plot(t_sec, fp1_after[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[1, 0].set_title("Fp1 after average reference")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("µV")
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Time (s)")

axes[1, 1].plot(t_sec, oz_after[t_slice] * 1e6)
axes[1, 1].set_title("Oz after average reference")
axes[1, 1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

After average re-referencing, each channel’s signal is shifted by the mean of all channels at each time point. Because the occipital alpha is strong, it will “leak” slightly (inverted) into the frontal channels, and the frontal slow wave will leak into occipital channels. This is normal; the average reference does not remove real brain signals, it redistributes them.

title: Preprocessing: exercises
text:
Exercise 5: Downsample with anti-aliasing
Create simulated data at 1000 Hz. Apply an appropriate anti-aliasing low-pass filter, then downsample to 250 Hz. Compare the PSD of the original and the downsampled data to confirm that no aliased frequencies appear.






TipHint





Before downsampling, you must low-pass filter below the new Nyquist frequency (250 / 2 = 125 Hz) to prevent aliasing. MNE’s raw.resample() applies an anti-aliasing filter automatically, but for this exercise, do it manually with raw.filter() first so you can see the effect. Then use raw.resample(250) to change the sampling rate.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sfreq = 1000
duration = 30
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = ["C3", "C4", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Create data with content at multiple frequencies
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 3e-6

# Add a 10 Hz oscillation (should survive downsampling)
data += 8e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Add a 200 Hz oscillation (above new Nyquist, should be removed)
data += 4e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 200 * times)

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Plot PSD of the original (1000 Hz) data
fig_original = raw.compute_psd(fmax=400).plot(show=False)
fig_original.suptitle("PSD at original sampling rate (1000 Hz)")

# Step 1: Manual anti-aliasing filter (low-pass below new Nyquist)
raw_filtered = raw.copy().filter(l_freq=None, h_freq=120)

# Step 2: Downsample to 250 Hz
# (raw.resample also applies its own anti-aliasing filter internally,
# but we already filtered above to demonstrate the concept)
raw_downsampled = raw_filtered.copy().resample(250)

# Plot PSD of the downsampled data
fig_down = raw_downsampled.compute_psd(fmax=120).plot(show=False)
fig_down.suptitle("PSD after downsampling to 250 Hz")

print(f"Original sampling rate: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"Original n_samples: {raw.n_times}")
print(f"Downsampled sampling rate: {raw_downsampled.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"Downsampled n_samples: {raw_downsampled.n_times}")

In the original PSD, you should see peaks at 10 Hz and 200 Hz. After filtering and downsampling, the 200 Hz peak is gone (it was above the new Nyquist frequency of 125 Hz and was removed by the anti-aliasing filter). The 10 Hz peak remains intact because it is well within the passband.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
text: These exercises go with Module 4: Spectral and time-frequency analysis. They cover the practical side of frequency-domain analysis: computing power spectral density, extracting power in the standard EEG bands, tracking how spectral content changes over time, and comparing spectral features between groups. All exercises use simulated data so you always know the ground truth.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
section: Exercise 1: Compute PSD with Welch’s method and identify peaks
text:
Exercise 1: Compute PSD with Welch’s method and identify peaks
Create a simulated signal that combines a 10 Hz alpha oscillation, a 22 Hz beta oscillation, and pink (1/f) background noise. Compute the power spectral density using scipy.signal.welch and plot it. Identify the two spectral peaks and label them on the plot.






TipHint





Generate pink noise by filtering white noise in the frequency domain: take the FFT, scale each frequency bin by \(1/\sqrt{f}\) (to get a \(1/f\) power spectrum), then take the inverse FFT. Add two sine waves at 10 Hz and 22 Hz with different amplitudes (alpha is usually stronger than beta). For Welch’s method, use scipy.signal.welch(signal, fs=sfreq, nperseg=512). Plot on a log scale (ax.semilogy()) so both peaks are visible above the 1/f background.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Generate pink noise (1/f background)
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

# Add oscillatory components
alpha = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)   # 10 Hz alpha
beta = 0.7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 22 * times)    # 22 Hz beta (weaker)
eeg = pink + alpha + beta

# Compute PSD with Welch's method
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=512, noverlap=256)

# Plot
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1.2, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(10, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Alpha (10 Hz)")
ax.axvline(22, color="#3498db", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Beta (22 Hz)")
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Power spectral density")
ax.set_title("PSD of simulated EEG (alpha + beta + pink noise)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 50)
ax.legend()
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

You should see the characteristic 1/f slope of the pink noise with two peaks rising above it: a taller one at 10 Hz and a shorter one at 22 Hz. The log scale on the y-axis makes both peaks easy to spot, even though the alpha component has roughly twice the amplitude of the beta component.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
section: Exercise 2: Compute band power and relative power for the five standard bands
text:
Exercise 2: Compute band power and relative power for the five standard bands
Create a simulated signal with a strong alpha peak (similar to Exercise 1) and compute the absolute power in each of the five standard EEG frequency bands: delta (0.5–4 Hz), theta (4–8 Hz), alpha (8–13 Hz), beta (13–30 Hz), and gamma (30–45 Hz). Then compute the relative power of each band as a percentage of the total power across all bands. Print a table of results.






TipHint





After computing the PSD with scipy.signal.welch, use np.trapz() (or scipy.integrate.trapezoid()) to integrate the PSD over each frequency range. To select the right frequencies, create a boolean mask: mask = (freqs >= f_low) & (freqs < f_high). Relative power is simply band_power / total_power * 100. Total power is the sum of all five bands (or the integral over the full range).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Signal: pink noise + alpha oscillation + some beta
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()

alpha = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
beta = 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)
eeg = pink + alpha + beta

# Compute PSD
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)

# Define the standard EEG bands
bands = {
    "Delta": (0.5, 4),
    "Theta": (4, 8),
    "Alpha": (8, 13),
    "Beta":  (13, 30),
    "Gamma": (30, 45),
}

# Compute absolute band power by integrating the PSD
band_powers = {}
for name, (f_low, f_high) in bands.items():
    mask = (freqs_psd >= f_low) & (freqs_psd < f_high)
    band_powers[name] = np.trapz(psd[mask], freqs_psd[mask])

total_power = sum(band_powers.values())

# Print the results
print(f"{'Band':<8} {'Abs. power':>12} {'Rel. power (%)':>15}")
print("-" * 38)
for name, power in band_powers.items():
    rel = power / total_power * 100
    print(f"{name:<8} {power:>12.4f} {rel:>14.1f}%")
print("-" * 38)
print(f"{'Total':<8} {total_power:>12.4f} {'100.0%':>15}")

Alpha should dominate because we injected a strong 10 Hz oscillation. Delta will also have a fair share because the 1/f pink noise concentrates power at low frequencies. Beta and gamma should be low, and theta will be somewhere in between.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
section: Exercise 3: Visualise time-varying alpha power with a spectrogram
text:
Exercise 3: Visualise time-varying alpha power with a spectrogram
Create a 20-second signal where alpha power is strong in the first 10 seconds and weak (or absent) in the last 10 seconds, simulating an “eyes closed then eyes open” transition. Use scipy.signal.spectrogram to compute and plot the spectrogram. Verify that the alpha band (8–13 Hz) shows a clear drop at the midpoint.






TipHint





Build the signal in two halves: for the first half, add a large-amplitude 10 Hz sine wave to the noise; for the second half, use noise only (or add a much smaller sine wave). scipy.signal.spectrogram returns (frequencies, times, Sxx) where Sxx[i, j] is the power at frequencies[i] and times[j]. Plot it with ax.pcolormesh(times, frequencies, 10 * np.log10(Sxx)) for a dB scale. Use nperseg=256 and noverlap=128 for reasonable time-frequency resolution at 256 Hz sampling rate.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 20
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
midpoint = n_samples // 2

# Background noise for the full signal
noise = rng.standard_normal(n_samples) * 0.5

# Alpha oscillation: strong in first half, absent in second half
alpha = np.zeros(n_samples)
alpha[:midpoint] = 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times[:midpoint])

eeg = noise + alpha

# Compute the spectrogram
freqs_spec, times_spec, Sxx = signal.spectrogram(
    eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=256, noverlap=128
)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7))

# Top panel: time-domain signal
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, eeg, linewidth=0.3, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(10, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Transition")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Simulated EEG: strong alpha (0-10 s), then noise only (10-20 s)")
ax.legend()

# Bottom panel: spectrogram
ax = axes[1]
mesh = ax.pcolormesh(
    times_spec, freqs_spec, 10 * np.log10(Sxx),
    shading="gouraud", cmap="viridis"
)
ax.set_ylim(0, 40)
ax.axhline(8, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.axhline(13, color="white", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.7, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("Spectrogram (dB)")
fig.colorbar(mesh, ax=ax, label="Power (dB)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The spectrogram should show a bright horizontal band between 8 and 13 Hz in the first half of the recording, which disappears abruptly at the 10-second mark. The white dashed lines mark the alpha band boundaries. This is the spectral signature of alpha desynchronisation, which is what happens in real EEG when someone opens their eyes.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
section: Exercise 4: Compare PSD between two simulated groups
text:
Exercise 4: Compare PSD between two simulated groups
Simulate two “groups” of subjects. Group A has a strong alpha peak (10 Hz); Group B has a weak alpha peak. Generate 15 subjects per group, compute the alpha band power for each, and run an independent-samples t-test to determine whether the groups differ significantly. Plot the group-averaged PSDs and a box plot of alpha band power.






TipHint





For each subject, generate a fresh noise signal and add a 10 Hz sine wave with a group-specific amplitude (e.g., amplitude = 2.0 for Group A, amplitude = 0.5 for Group B, plus some between-subject variability drawn from a normal distribution). Compute the PSD for each subject with scipy.signal.welch, then integrate across the alpha band (8–13 Hz) to get one band-power value per subject. Use scipy.stats.ttest_ind for the t-test.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
n_subjects = 15

def simulate_subject(alpha_amp, rng):
    """Simulate one subject's EEG and return alpha band power."""
    # Pink noise
    white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
    pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
    pink = pink / pink.std()

    # Add alpha oscillation
    eeg = pink + alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

    # Compute PSD
    freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=1024, noverlap=512)
    return freqs_psd, psd

# Simulate both groups
alpha_powers_a = []
alpha_powers_b = []
psds_a = []
psds_b = []

for i in range(n_subjects):
    # Group A: strong alpha (mean amplitude 2.0, sd 0.3)
    amp_a = rng.normal(2.0, 0.3)
    freqs_psd, psd_a = simulate_subject(amp_a, rng)
    psds_a.append(psd_a)
    mask_alpha = (freqs_psd >= 8) & (freqs_psd < 13)
    alpha_powers_a.append(np.trapz(psd_a[mask_alpha], freqs_psd[mask_alpha]))

    # Group B: weak alpha (mean amplitude 0.5, sd 0.2)
    amp_b = rng.normal(0.5, 0.2)
    freqs_psd, psd_b = simulate_subject(amp_b, rng)
    psds_b.append(psd_b)
    alpha_powers_b.append(np.trapz(psd_b[mask_alpha], freqs_psd[mask_alpha]))

alpha_powers_a = np.array(alpha_powers_a)
alpha_powers_b = np.array(alpha_powers_b)

# T-test
t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(alpha_powers_a, alpha_powers_b)
print(f"Group A alpha power: mean = {alpha_powers_a.mean():.3f}, "
      f"sd = {alpha_powers_a.std():.3f}")
print(f"Group B alpha power: mean = {alpha_powers_b.mean():.3f}, "
      f"sd = {alpha_powers_b.std():.3f}")
print(f"t-test: t = {t_stat:.3f}, p = {p_value:.6f}")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 5))

# Left: group-averaged PSDs
ax = axes[0]
mean_psd_a = np.mean(psds_a, axis=0)
mean_psd_b = np.mean(psds_b, axis=0)
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, mean_psd_a, label="Group A (strong alpha)",
            color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.5)
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, mean_psd_b, label="Group B (weak alpha)",
            color="#3498db", linewidth=1.5)
ax.axvspan(8, 13, alpha=0.15, color="orange", label="Alpha band")
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("PSD")
ax.set_xlim(0, 45)
ax.set_title("Group-averaged PSD")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

# Right: box plot of alpha band power
ax = axes[1]
bp = ax.boxplot(
    [alpha_powers_a, alpha_powers_b],
    labels=["Group A\n(strong alpha)", "Group B\n(weak alpha)"],
    patch_artist=True
)
bp["boxes"][0].set_facecolor("#e74c3c")
bp["boxes"][1].set_facecolor("#3498db")
for box in bp["boxes"]:
    box.set_alpha(0.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Alpha band power (8-13 Hz)")
ax.set_title(f"Alpha power comparison (p = {p_value:.2e})")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

You should see a highly significant p-value (well below 0.05) because the two groups have very different alpha amplitudes by design. The PSD plot will show Group A with a tall alpha peak and Group B with a much smaller one. In real studies, the effect sizes are usually much smaller, but the analysis workflow is the same.

title: Spectral analysis: exercises
section: Exercise 5: Build a reusable band-power function
text:
Exercise 5: Build a reusable band-power function
Write a function compute_band_powers(data, sfreq) that takes a 2D NumPy array (channels x samples) and a sampling rate, and returns a dictionary where each key is a band name ("delta", "theta", "alpha", "beta", "gamma") and each value is a 1D array of band powers (one value per channel). Test it on a simulated multi-channel signal and print the results.






TipHint





Inside the function, loop over channels and compute the PSD for each one using scipy.signal.welch. Then, for each band, integrate the PSD between the band’s frequency limits using np.trapz. Return a dictionary of arrays. You could also compute the PSD for all channels at once by passing a 2D array to scipy.signal.welch (it operates along the last axis by default, so you may need to handle the axis parameter).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
from scipy import signal


BANDS = {
    "delta": (0.5, 4),
    "theta": (4, 8),
    "alpha": (8, 13),
    "beta":  (13, 30),
    "gamma": (30, 45),
}


def compute_band_powers(data, sfreq, nperseg=1024):
    """Compute band power for each channel in the standard EEG bands.

    Parameters
    ----------
    data : numpy.ndarray
        2D array of shape (n_channels, n_samples).
    sfreq : float
        Sampling frequency in Hz.
    nperseg : int
        Number of samples per Welch segment (controls frequency resolution).

    Returns
    -------
    band_powers : dict
        Keys are band names ('delta', 'theta', 'alpha', 'beta', 'gamma').
        Values are 1D arrays of shape (n_channels,) with the band power
        for each channel.
    """
    n_channels = data.shape[0]
    band_powers = {name: np.zeros(n_channels) for name in BANDS}

    for ch in range(n_channels):
        freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(
            data[ch], fs=sfreq, nperseg=nperseg, noverlap=nperseg // 2
        )
        for name, (f_low, f_high) in BANDS.items():
            mask = (freqs_psd >= f_low) & (freqs_psd < f_high)
            band_powers[name][ch] = np.trapz(psd[mask], freqs_psd[mask])

    return band_powers


# ── Test the function ──────────────────────────────────────────
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

sfreq = 256
duration = 30
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2", "Oz", "Pz"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)

# Simulate data: noise + alpha in occipital channels + beta in central
data = rng.standard_normal((n_channels, n_samples)) * 0.5

# Add alpha to O1, O2, Oz
for ch_name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz"]:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch_name)
    data[idx] += 2.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)

# Add beta to C3, C4
for ch_name in ["C3", "C4"]:
    idx = ch_names.index(ch_name)
    data[idx] += 1.0 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)

# Compute band powers
bp = compute_band_powers(data, sfreq)

# Print the results
print(f"{'Channel':<8}", end="")
for name in BANDS:
    print(f"{name:>10}", end="")
print()
print("-" * 58)
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"{ch_names[ch]:<8}", end="")
    for name in BANDS:
        print(f"{bp[name][ch]:>10.4f}", end="")
    print()

The occipital channels (O1, O2, Oz) should show high alpha power relative to the others. The central channels (C3, C4) should show higher beta power. Frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2) and Pz will only have noise, so their band powers should be roughly uniform and much lower.

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
text: These exercises go with Module 3: Artifact rejection. They cover the two main strategies for dealing with artifacts: rejecting contaminated segments outright, and using ICA to separate artifacts from brain signals. All exercises use simulated data so you can verify that the cleaning actually works (you know the ground truth).

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
section: Exercise 1: Reject epochs by peak-to-peak amplitude
text:
Exercise 1: Reject epochs by peak-to-peak amplitude
Create epoched data where some epochs contain large-amplitude bursts (simulating muscle artifacts). Reject any epoch where the peak-to-peak amplitude exceeds 100 µV. Report how many epochs were rejected and how many survived.






TipHint





Create a Raw object, add events with mne.make_fixed_length_events(), and build Epochs from them. To inject artifacts into some epochs, pick a few event times and add a large spike to the data at those times before epoching. Use the reject parameter in mne.Epochs(): pass reject=dict(eeg=100e-6) to reject epochs where any EEG channel exceeds 100 µV peak-to-peak. After creating the Epochs object, call epochs.drop_log to see which epochs were dropped.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

sfreq = 500
duration = 60
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "P3", "P4", "O1", "O2"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Create clean EEG-like data
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 10e-6

# Inject large artifacts at known times (simulating muscle bursts)
# Add a 200 µV spike lasting 100 ms at these times:
artifact_times = [5.0, 12.3, 25.7, 33.1, 41.5, 52.8]
for t_art in artifact_times:
    start = int(t_art * sfreq)
    end = start + int(0.1 * sfreq)  # 100 ms burst
    if end < n_samples:
        data[:, start:end] += 200e-6 * np.random.randn(n_channels, end - start)

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Create 2-second epochs
events = mne.make_fixed_length_events(raw, duration=2.0)

# Build epochs with peak-to-peak rejection at 100 µV
epochs = mne.Epochs(
    raw, events,
    tmin=0, tmax=2.0,
    baseline=None,
    reject=dict(eeg=100e-6),
    preload=True
)

# Report the results
n_total = len(events)
n_kept = len(epochs)
n_rejected = n_total - n_kept

print(f"Total epochs: {n_total}")
print(f"Kept: {n_kept}")
print(f"Rejected: {n_rejected}")

# Show the drop log (which epochs were dropped and why)
epochs.plot_drop_log()

The exact number of rejected epochs depends on where the artifacts fall relative to the epoch boundaries, but you should see roughly 6 epochs rejected (one per artifact burst). Epochs that did not overlap with any artifact time should survive.

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
section: Exercise 2: Run ICA and plot component topographies
text:
Exercise 2: Run ICA and plot component topographies
Run ICA with 15 components on simulated multi-channel data. Plot the component topographies to see how ICA decomposes the data.






TipHint





Create a Raw object with at least 20 channels and set a standard montage (ICA topography plots need channel positions). Use mne.preprocessing.ICA(n_components=15, random_state=42) and call ica.fit(raw). Then ica.plot_components() shows the scalp maps.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
from mne.preprocessing import ICA

sfreq = 500
duration = 120  # ICA works better with more data
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

# Use 20 channels so we have enough for 15 ICA components
ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "F7", "F8", "Fz",
    "C3", "C4", "Cz",
    "T7", "T8",
    "P3", "P4", "P7", "P8", "Pz",
    "O1", "O2", "Oz"
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Simulate data: mix of oscillations at different frequencies per region
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6

# Add alpha to occipital channels
alpha = 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
for name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += alpha

# Add beta to central channels
beta = 6e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)
for name in ["C3", "C4", "Cz"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += beta

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Set montage (required for topography plots)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Band-pass filter before ICA (1 Hz high-pass helps ICA converge)
raw.filter(l_freq=1, h_freq=40)

# Fit ICA
ica = ICA(n_components=15, random_state=42)
ica.fit(raw)

print(ica)

# Plot component topographies
ica.plot_components(title="ICA components")

Each component map shows a spatial pattern. With simulated data like this, you may see components that capture the occipital alpha pattern, the central beta pattern, and several noise components. With real data, you would look for components that match the spatial signature of known artifacts (blinks in frontal channels, lateral eye movements, etc.).

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
section: Exercise 3: Simulate and remove a blink artifact with ICA
text:
Exercise 3: Simulate and remove a blink artifact with ICA
Create data with a simulated blink artifact: a large, brief deflection on frontal channels ("Fp1", "Fp2") that repeats every 3 seconds. Run ICA, identify the blink component, exclude it, and apply the cleaning. Compare the frontal signal before and after.






TipHint





Create the blink as a Gaussian pulse (use scipy.signal.windows.gaussian() or just np.exp(-0.5 * ((t - t_blink) / width)**2)) with a large amplitude (say 80 µV) added mainly to Fp1 and Fp2 and with smaller contributions to nearby channels. After fitting ICA, use ica.find_blinks() or inspect the components manually with ica.plot_sources(raw). Exclude the blink component with ica.exclude = [component_index] and then ica.apply(raw).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
from mne.preprocessing import ICA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sfreq = 500
duration = 120
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "F7", "F8", "Fz",
    "C3", "C4", "Cz",
    "T7", "T8",
    "P3", "P4", "P7", "P8", "Pz",
    "O1", "O2", "Oz"
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Clean EEG: alpha oscillation plus noise
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6
alpha = 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
for name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz", "P3", "P4", "Pz"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += alpha

# Store a copy of clean data for comparison
data_clean = data.copy()

# Add blink artifacts every 3 seconds on frontal channels
blink_width = 0.15  # seconds (width of the Gaussian pulse)
blink_times = np.arange(1.5, duration - 1, 3.0)  # every 3 seconds

for t_blink in blink_times:
    # Gaussian pulse centred at t_blink
    pulse = np.exp(-0.5 * ((times - t_blink) / blink_width) ** 2)

    # Blink is strongest at Fp1/Fp2, weaker at F3/F4/Fz/F7/F8
    data[ch_names.index("Fp1")] += 80e-6 * pulse
    data[ch_names.index("Fp2")] += 80e-6 * pulse
    for name in ["F3", "F4", "Fz"]:
        data[ch_names.index(name)] += 30e-6 * pulse
    for name in ["F7", "F8"]:
        data[ch_names.index(name)] += 15e-6 * pulse

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Filter before ICA
raw.filter(l_freq=1, h_freq=40)

# Store Fp1 before ICA cleaning
fp1_before = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0].copy()

# Fit ICA
ica = ICA(n_components=15, random_state=42)
ica.fit(raw)

# Find the blink component automatically using EOG-like detection on Fp1
# (Fp1 acts as a proxy for an EOG channel here)
blink_indices, blink_scores = ica.find_bads_eog(
    raw, ch_name="Fp1", threshold=2.0
)
print(f"Blink component(s) found: {blink_indices}")

# Exclude the blink component(s) and apply
ica.exclude = blink_indices
ica.apply(raw)

fp1_after = raw.get_data(picks="Fp1")[0]

# Compare before and after
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(14, 6), sharex=True)
t_plot = slice(0, int(10 * sfreq))  # first 10 seconds
t_sec = times[:int(10 * sfreq)]

axes[0].plot(t_sec, fp1_before[t_plot] * 1e6)
axes[0].set_title("Fp1 before ICA blink removal")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")

axes[1].plot(t_sec, fp1_after[t_plot] * 1e6)
axes[1].set_title("Fp1 after ICA blink removal")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Amplitude (µV)")
axes[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The “before” plot should show clear blink-shaped bumps every 3 seconds on the Fp1 channel. After ICA cleaning, those bumps should be gone (or greatly reduced) while the background EEG signal is preserved.

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
section: Exercise 4: Compare PSD before and after ICA cleaning
text:
Exercise 4: Compare PSD before and after ICA cleaning
Using the blink-removal pipeline from Exercise 3, plot the PSD of the data before and after ICA cleaning. Pay attention to the low-frequency range (below 5 Hz), where blink artifacts contribute most of their power.






TipHint





Make a copy of the Raw object before applying ica.apply(). Then compute and plot the PSD for both copies using raw.compute_psd().plot(). Focus on the 0–40 Hz range. Blink artifacts are mostly low-frequency (below 3–4 Hz), so you should see a reduction in power in that range after cleaning.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
from mne.preprocessing import ICA
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

sfreq = 500
duration = 120
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = [
    "Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "F7", "F8", "Fz",
    "C3", "C4", "Cz",
    "T7", "T8",
    "P3", "P4", "P7", "P8", "Pz",
    "O1", "O2", "Oz"
]
n_channels = len(ch_names)
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Create data with alpha + blink artifacts
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6
alpha = 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
for name in ["O1", "O2", "Oz"]:
    data[ch_names.index(name)] += alpha

# Add blinks every 3 seconds
blink_width = 0.15
for t_blink in np.arange(1.5, duration - 1, 3.0):
    pulse = np.exp(-0.5 * ((times - t_blink) / blink_width) ** 2)
    data[ch_names.index("Fp1")] += 80e-6 * pulse
    data[ch_names.index("Fp2")] += 80e-6 * pulse
    for name in ["F3", "F4", "Fz"]:
        data[ch_names.index(name)] += 30e-6 * pulse

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)
raw.filter(l_freq=1, h_freq=40)

# Save a copy before ICA
raw_before = raw.copy()

# Fit ICA and remove blink components
ica = ICA(n_components=15, random_state=42)
ica.fit(raw)
blink_indices, _ = ica.find_bads_eog(raw, ch_name="Fp1", threshold=2.0)
ica.exclude = blink_indices
ica.apply(raw)

# Plot PSDs side by side
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(14, 5))

# Before ICA
psd_before = raw_before.compute_psd(fmax=40, picks="Fp1")
psd_before.plot(axes=axes[0], show=False)
axes[0].set_title("Fp1 PSD before ICA cleaning")

# After ICA
psd_after = raw.compute_psd(fmax=40, picks="Fp1")
psd_after.plot(axes=axes[1], show=False)
axes[1].set_title("Fp1 PSD after ICA cleaning")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The PSD of Fp1 before ICA cleaning should show elevated power in the low-frequency range (roughly 1–4 Hz) due to the blink artifacts. After cleaning, that low-frequency hump should be reduced. The alpha peak at 10 Hz (if visible on Fp1 at all) should remain unchanged because ICA separates the blink from the brain signal rather than filtering frequencies indiscriminately.

title: Artifact rejection: exercises
text:
Exercise 5: Threshold-based artifact detector
Write a function that scans a Raw object in fixed-length windows and flags any window where any channel exceeds a threshold of plus or minus 75 µV. Return a list of (start_time, end_time) tuples for the bad segments. Test it on simulated data with known artifacts.






TipHint





Use raw.get_data() to get the data matrix and work in NumPy. Divide the data into windows of, say, 1 second (i.e., sfreq samples). For each window, check whether np.max(np.abs(window)) exceeds 75e-6. If it does, record the start and end times. You can convert sample indices to times by dividing by sfreq.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne


def detect_artifacts(raw, threshold_uv=75, window_sec=1.0):
    """Find segments where any channel exceeds the amplitude threshold.

    Parameters
    ----------
    raw : mne.io.Raw
        The raw data to scan.
    threshold_uv : float
        Threshold in microvolts. Any window where a channel exceeds
        this value (positive or negative) is flagged.
    window_sec : float
        Length of each scanning window in seconds.

    Returns
    -------
    bad_segments : list of tuple
        Each tuple is (start_time, end_time) in seconds.
    """
    sfreq = raw.info["sfreq"]
    data = raw.get_data()  # shape: (n_channels, n_samples)
    threshold_v = threshold_uv * 1e-6  # convert µV to V

    window_samples = int(window_sec * sfreq)
    n_samples = data.shape[1]
    bad_segments = []

    for start in range(0, n_samples, window_samples):
        end = min(start + window_samples, n_samples)
        window = data[:, start:end]

        if np.max(np.abs(window)) > threshold_v:
            t_start = start / sfreq
            t_end = end / sfreq
            bad_segments.append((t_start, t_end))

    return bad_segments


# Test on simulated data
sfreq = 500
duration = 30
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
data = np.random.randn(len(ch_names), n_samples) * 10e-6  # ~10 µV noise

# Inject artifacts at known times
artifact_info = [
    (3.2, "Fp1"),   # blink at 3.2 s
    (10.5, "C3"),   # muscle artifact at 10.5 s
    (22.0, "O1"),   # movement at 22 s
]

for t_art, ch in artifact_info:
    ch_idx = ch_names.index(ch)
    sample = int(t_art * sfreq)
    # Add a 150 µV spike lasting 50 ms
    spike_len = int(0.05 * sfreq)
    data[ch_idx, sample:sample + spike_len] += 150e-6

raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Run the detector
bad_segs = detect_artifacts(raw, threshold_uv=75, window_sec=1.0)

print(f"Found {len(bad_segs)} bad segments:")
for start, end in bad_segs:
    print(f"  {start:.1f} - {end:.1f} s")

# Verify: we expect 3 bad segments (one per injected artifact)
# The exact window boundaries depend on where the artifact falls,
# but each artifact should flag exactly one 1-second window.

You should see three bad segments, one for each injected artifact. The start and end times will be rounded to 1-second window boundaries (e.g., the artifact at 3.2 seconds falls in the 3.0–4.0 second window). If you want finer resolution, reduce window_sec to 0.5 or 0.25 seconds.

title: EEG with Python
text: This site covers everything you need to analyse EEG data in Python, using MNE-Python as the main library. The content follows the structure of the EEGLAB tutorials, but translated to Python, with examples using simulated data you can run without needing real patient recordings.

title: EEG with Python
text:
Modules

1. Getting started
Installing MNE-Python, understanding the Raw and Epochs data structures, loading files, and visually inspecting the signal.


2. Preprocessing
Band-pass and notch filtering, re-referencing, resampling, bad channel detection, and interpolation.


3. Artifact rejection
Visual inspection, automated epoch rejection, and Independent Component Analysis (ICA) for removing blinks, eye movements, and muscle artifacts.


4. Spectral and time-frequency analysis
Power spectral density (PSD), time-frequency decomposition, topographic maps by band, and event-related potentials (ERPs).


5. Connectivity and metastability
Instantaneous phase via the Hilbert transform, relative phase alignment, dominant eigenvector, and regional metastability computation. The core module for the master’s project.

title: Metastability: exercises
text:
These exercises go with Module 5: Connectivity and metastability. They build up the metastability pipeline one step at a time, from extracting instantaneous phase with the Hilbert transform to running a full group comparison between simulated patient and control data. Each exercise adds a piece to the pipeline, so work through them in order.
This is the core of Natalia’s project, so the exercises are more detailed than in earlier modules. Take your time with each one and make sure you understand what every intermediate result means before moving on.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 1: Extract instantaneous phase with the Hilbert transform
text:
Exercise 1: Extract instantaneous phase with the Hilbert transform
Create a pure 10 Hz sine wave lasting 2 seconds. Apply the Hilbert transform to obtain the analytic signal, then extract the instantaneous amplitude (envelope) and instantaneous phase. Plot three things on separate subplots:

The original signal
The instantaneous amplitude (envelope) overlaid on the original signal
The instantaneous phase (in radians, ranging from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\))

Verify that the envelope is approximately constant (because a pure sine wave has constant amplitude) and that the phase increases linearly from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\) and wraps around.






TipHint





Use scipy.signal.hilbert() to compute the analytic signal. This function returns a complex array; the real part is the original signal and the imaginary part is the Hilbert transform. Use np.abs() to get the instantaneous amplitude and np.angle() to get the phase. For a pure sine wave, the envelope should be nearly flat (equal to the sine amplitude) and the phase should be a sawtooth pattern that increases linearly and wraps at \(\pm\pi\).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert

sfreq = 256
duration = 2.0
times = np.arange(int(sfreq * duration)) / sfreq

# Create a pure 10 Hz sine wave
freq = 10
amplitude = 1.0
x = amplitude * np.sin(2 * np.pi * freq * times)

# Hilbert transform
analytic = hilbert(x)
inst_amplitude = np.abs(analytic)
inst_phase = np.angle(analytic)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(10, 8), sharex=True)

# Panel 1: original signal
ax = axes[0]
ax.plot(times, x, color="#2c3e50", linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Original 10 Hz sine wave")

# Panel 2: signal with envelope overlay
ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(times, x, color="#2c3e50", linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.5, label="Signal")
ax.plot(times, inst_amplitude, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.5,
        label="Envelope (instantaneous amplitude)")
ax.plot(times, -inst_amplitude, color="#e74c3c", linewidth=1.5, alpha=0.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Signal with instantaneous amplitude envelope")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

# Panel 3: instantaneous phase
ax = axes[2]
ax.plot(times, inst_phase, color="#27ae60", linewidth=1)
ax.set_ylabel("Phase (radians)")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_title("Instantaneous phase")
ax.set_yticks([-np.pi, -np.pi/2, 0, np.pi/2, np.pi])
ax.set_yticklabels([r"$-\pi$", r"$-\pi/2$", "0", r"$\pi/2$", r"$\pi$"])
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

# Verify: envelope should be close to the amplitude
print(f"Expected envelope: {amplitude:.3f}")
print(f"Mean envelope: {inst_amplitude.mean():.3f}")
print(f"Std of envelope: {inst_amplitude.std():.6f}")

The envelope should be very close to 1.0 everywhere (the amplitude of the sine wave), with tiny deviations at the edges due to boundary effects of the Hilbert transform. The phase should look like a sawtooth: it increases linearly from \(-\pi\) to \(\pi\) and then wraps back. Each complete cycle of the sawtooth corresponds to one period of the 10 Hz oscillation, so you should see 20 teeth across the 2-second window.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 2: Verify phase difference between two channels
text:
Exercise 2: Verify phase difference between two channels
Create two channels, both oscillating at 10 Hz, but with a fixed phase offset of \(\pi/4\) radians between them. Extract the instantaneous phase of each channel using the Hilbert transform. Compute \(\cos(\phi_1(t) - \phi_2(t))\) at every time point and verify that it is approximately equal to \(\cos(\pi/4) \approx 0.707\).






TipHint





Generate the first channel as np.sin(2 * pi * 10 * t) and the second as np.sin(2 * pi * 10 * t + pi/4). Apply the Hilbert transform to each. Compute the phase difference and take the cosine. The result should hover around 0.707 with very small fluctuations (due to numerical precision and edge effects). To avoid edge artifacts, discard the first and last 0.5 seconds before computing the mean.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert

sfreq = 256
duration = 5.0
times = np.arange(int(sfreq * duration)) / sfreq

# Two channels with a known phase offset of pi/4
phase_offset = np.pi / 4
ch1 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
ch2 = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times + phase_offset)

# Extract instantaneous phase for each channel
phase1 = np.angle(hilbert(ch1))
phase2 = np.angle(hilbert(ch2))

# Compute cos(phase difference)
cos_phase_diff = np.cos(phase1 - phase2)

# Trim edges (0.5 s from each end) to avoid boundary artifacts
trim = int(0.5 * sfreq)
cos_trimmed = cos_phase_diff[trim:-trim]

expected = np.cos(phase_offset)
actual_mean = cos_trimmed.mean()

print(f"Phase offset: pi/4 = {phase_offset:.4f} radians")
print(f"Expected cos(phase_diff): {expected:.4f}")
print(f"Measured mean cos(phase_diff): {actual_mean:.4f}")
print(f"Difference from expected: {abs(actual_mean - expected):.6f}")

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 6))

ax = axes[0]
t_plot = times < 1  # show first second only
ax.plot(times[t_plot], ch1[t_plot], label="Channel 1", color="#2c3e50")
ax.plot(times[t_plot], ch2[t_plot], label="Channel 2 (offset pi/4)",
        color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude")
ax.set_title("Two 10 Hz oscillations with pi/4 phase offset")
ax.legend()

ax = axes[1]
ax.plot(times, cos_phase_diff, color="#27ae60", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(expected, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--",
           label=f"Expected: cos(pi/4) = {expected:.3f}")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("cos(phase difference)")
ax.set_title("Cosine of phase difference over time")
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

The cosine of the phase difference should sit very close to 0.707 across the entire recording. Small deviations at the start and end are normal: the Hilbert transform has edge effects where the filter does not have enough data on one side. In the interior of the signal, the measurement should be accurate to within a fraction of a percent. This exercise confirms that the Hilbert transform correctly recovers the known phase relationship we built into the data.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 3: Build a 4x4 phase alignment matrix
text:
Exercise 3: Build a 4x4 phase alignment matrix
Simulate 4 channels, each oscillating at 10 Hz with known phases. At a single time point, build the phase alignment matrix \(A_{ij} = \cos(\phi_i - \phi_j)\) and print it. Verify that:

The matrix is symmetric: \(A_{ij} = A_{ji}\)
The diagonal is all ones: \(A_{ii} = 1\)
Off-diagonal values match what you would compute by hand

Use these channel phases at the chosen time point: \(\phi_1 = 0\), \(\phi_2 = \pi/4\), \(\phi_3 = \pi/2\), \(\phi_4 = \pi\).






TipHint





You can construct the alignment matrix directly from a vector of phases. If phi is a 1D array of length 4, then phi[:, None] - phi[None, :] gives a 4x4 matrix of pairwise differences, and np.cos() of that matrix gives you \(A\). Check symmetry with np.allclose(A, A.T). The expected values can be computed by hand: for example, \(A_{12} = \cos(0 - \pi/4) = \cos(\pi/4) \approx 0.707\).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np

# Define the phases at a single time point
phi = np.array([0, np.pi / 4, np.pi / 2, np.pi])
channel_labels = ["Ch1 (0)", "Ch2 (pi/4)", "Ch3 (pi/2)", "Ch4 (pi)"]

# Build the phase alignment matrix
phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
A = np.cos(phase_diff)

# Print the matrix
print("Phase alignment matrix A:")
print()

# Header
print(f"{'':>14}", end="")
for label in channel_labels:
    print(f"{label:>14}", end="")
print()

# Rows
for i, label in enumerate(channel_labels):
    print(f"{label:>14}", end="")
    for j in range(len(phi)):
        print(f"{A[i, j]:>14.4f}", end="")
    print()

print()

# Verify properties
print("Checks:")
print(f"  Symmetric: {np.allclose(A, A.T)}")
print(f"  Diagonal all ones: {np.allclose(np.diag(A), 1.0)}")

# Verify specific entries by hand
print()
print("Spot checks:")
print(f"  A[0,1] = cos(0 - pi/4) = cos(-pi/4) = {np.cos(-np.pi/4):.4f} "
      f"(matrix: {A[0,1]:.4f})")
print(f"  A[0,3] = cos(0 - pi) = cos(-pi) = {np.cos(-np.pi):.4f} "
      f"(matrix: {A[0,3]:.4f})")
print(f"  A[1,2] = cos(pi/4 - pi/2) = cos(-pi/4) = {np.cos(-np.pi/4):.4f} "
      f"(matrix: {A[1,2]:.4f})")
print(f"  A[2,3] = cos(pi/2 - pi) = cos(-pi/2) = {np.cos(-np.pi/2):.4f} "
      f"(matrix: {A[2,3]:.4f})")

The matrix should be:




Ch1
Ch2
Ch3
Ch4




Ch1
1.0000
0.7071
0.0000
-1.0000


Ch2
0.7071
1.0000
0.7071
-0.7071


Ch3
0.0000
0.7071
1.0000
0.0000


Ch4
-1.0000
-0.7071
0.0000
1.0000



Reading this: channels 1 and 2 are mostly aligned (0.707), channels 1 and 3 are a quarter-cycle apart (0), and channels 1 and 4 are in perfect anti-phase (-1). The matrix is symmetric and has ones on the diagonal, as expected. This is one snapshot; in the full pipeline, you build this matrix at every time point and track how it changes.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 4: Extract and interpret the dominant eigenvector
text:
Exercise 4: Extract and interpret the dominant eigenvector
Take the 4x4 phase alignment matrix from Exercise 3 and compute its eigenvalues and eigenvectors using numpy.linalg.eigh. Identify the dominant eigenvector (the one with the largest eigenvalue). Explain what the elements of the dominant eigenvector tell you about the grouping of the four channels.






TipHint





numpy.linalg.eigh returns eigenvalues in ascending order, so the dominant eigenvector is the last column of the eigenvectors matrix. Look at the signs of the eigenvector elements: channels with the same sign are in the same “community” (oscillating together), and channels with opposite signs are in anti-phase communities. Given the phases you used (\(0, \pi/4, \pi/2, \pi\)), channels 1–3 should cluster together (they are all within a half-cycle of each other), while channel 4 (at \(\pi\)) should have the opposite sign.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np

# Reconstruct the phase alignment matrix from Exercise 3
phi = np.array([0, np.pi / 4, np.pi / 2, np.pi])
phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
A = np.cos(phase_diff)

# Eigendecomposition
eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)

print("Eigenvalues (ascending order):")
for i, val in enumerate(eigenvalues):
    print(f"  lambda_{i+1} = {val:.4f}")

print()
print("Dominant eigenvalue:", eigenvalues[-1])
dominant = eigenvectors[:, -1]  # last column = largest eigenvalue

print()
print("Dominant eigenvector:")
labels = ["Ch1 (phase=0)", "Ch2 (phase=pi/4)",
          "Ch3 (phase=pi/2)", "Ch4 (phase=pi)"]
for i, (label, val) in enumerate(zip(labels, dominant)):
    print(f"  {label}: v = {val:+.4f}")

print()
print("Interpretation:")
print("  Channels with the same sign are phase-aligned (in the same community).")
print("  Channels with opposite signs are in anti-phase communities.")

# The signs tell us the grouping
signs = np.sign(dominant)
group_positive = [labels[i] for i in range(len(labels)) if signs[i] > 0]
group_negative = [labels[i] for i in range(len(labels)) if signs[i] < 0]

print()
print(f"  Community 1 (positive): {group_positive}")
print(f"  Community 2 (negative): {group_negative}")

The dominant eigenvector should show channels 1, 2, and 3 with the same sign (they are within a half-cycle of each other, so they are more aligned than not) and channel 4 with the opposite sign (it is at \(\pi\), which is anti-phase with channel 1).
The magnitude of each element tells you how strongly that channel participates in the dominant pattern. Channel 1 (phase 0) and channel 4 (phase \(\pi\)) should have the largest magnitudes because they define the two extremes. Channel 3 (phase \(\pi/2\)) should have a smaller magnitude because it sits on the boundary between the two communities.
This is what the eigenvector decomposition does: it finds the primary axis of coordination in the network and tells you which channels are on which side of that axis.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 5: Full metastability pipeline on 8 channels
text:
Exercise 5: Full metastability pipeline on 8 channels
Implement the complete metastability pipeline on simulated data with 8 channels. Create two conditions and compute regional metastability for each:

Condition A (tightly coupled): all 8 channels are strongly coupled to a common reference oscillation. The phases stay close together, so the alignment matrix changes little over time. This should produce low metastability.
Condition B (time-varying coupling): the coupling strength between channels drifts over time (some channels synchronise and desynchronise periodically). The alignment matrix changes a lot, so metastability should be higher.

For each condition, run the full pipeline:

Generate 8 channels of band-limited oscillatory data
Extract instantaneous phase with the Hilbert transform
At each time point, build the 8x8 phase alignment matrix
Extract the dominant eigenvector
Compute regional metastability as the temporal variance of each eigenvector element

Compare the mean regional metastability between the two conditions and plot the results.






TipHint





For Condition A, use a high coupling strength (e.g., 0.95) for all channels. For Condition B, make the coupling vary sinusoidally over time: coupling(t) = 0.5 + 0.4 * sin(2 * pi * f_mod * t), where f_mod is a slow modulation frequency (e.g., 0.1 Hz). This makes channels periodically synchronise and desynchronise.
To generate coupled oscillatory data, create a reference oscillation and mix each channel’s signal as coupling * reference + (1 - coupling) * independent. Band-pass filter before applying the Hilbert transform.
For computational efficiency, compute the alignment matrix at a downsampled rate (e.g., every 10 ms rather than every sample). Remember to enforce sign continuity on the eigenvector: if \(v(t) \cdot v(t-1) < 0\), flip \(v(t)\).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Parameters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 8
sfreq = 256
duration = 60  # seconds
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
freq_osc = 10.0  # Hz

channel_names = [f"Ch{i}" for i in range(n_channels)]


def generate_coupled_data(coupling_array, rng):
    """Generate multi-channel oscillatory data with given coupling.

    Parameters
    ----------
    coupling_array : ndarray, shape (n_channels, n_samples)
        Coupling strength for each channel at each time point.
        Values between 0 (independent) and 1 (locked to reference).
    rng : numpy.random.Generator
        Random number generator.

    Returns
    -------
    data : ndarray, shape (n_channels, n_samples)
    """
    # Common reference oscillation with slow phase drift
    ref_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
                 + 0.3 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
    ref_signal = np.sin(ref_phase)

    data = np.zeros((n_channels, n_samples))
    for ch in range(n_channels):
        # Independent oscillation with its own phase drift
        ind_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
                     + 2.0 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
        ind_signal = np.sin(ind_phase)

        # Mix reference and independent, sample by sample
        c = coupling_array[ch]
        data[ch] = c * ref_signal + (1 - c) * ind_signal
        data[ch] += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

    return data


def compute_metastability(data, sfreq, lo=8.0, hi=13.0):
    """Run the full metastability pipeline.

    Returns
    -------
    regional_ms : ndarray, shape (n_channels,)
        Temporal variance of each eigenvector element.
    eigvec_series : ndarray, shape (n_channels, n_timepoints)
        Dominant eigenvector at each downsampled time point.
    """
    n_ch, n_samp = data.shape
    b, a = butter(4, [lo, hi], btype="band", fs=sfreq)

    # Extract instantaneous phase
    phases = np.zeros_like(data)
    for ch in range(n_ch):
        filtered = filtfilt(b, a, data[ch])
        phases[ch] = np.angle(hilbert(filtered))

    # Downsample to 100 Hz for the alignment matrix
    step = max(1, sfreq // 100)
    time_indices = np.arange(0, n_samp, step)
    n_tp = len(time_indices)

    eigvec_series = np.zeros((n_ch, n_tp))

    for ti, t in enumerate(time_indices):
        phi = phases[:, t]
        phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
        A = np.cos(phase_diff)

        eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
        dominant = eigenvectors[:, -1]

        # Sign continuity
        if ti > 0 and np.dot(dominant, eigvec_series[:, ti - 1]) < 0:
            dominant = -dominant

        eigvec_series[:, ti] = dominant

    regional_ms = np.var(eigvec_series, axis=1)
    return regional_ms, eigvec_series


# ── Condition A: tightly coupled (constant high coupling) ─────
coupling_a = np.full((n_channels, n_samples), 0.95)
data_a = generate_coupled_data(coupling_a, rng)
ms_a, eigvec_a = compute_metastability(data_a, sfreq)

# ── Condition B: time-varying coupling ────────────────────────
# Coupling oscillates between 0.1 and 0.9 at 0.1 Hz
coupling_b = np.zeros((n_channels, n_samples))
for ch in range(n_channels):
    # Each channel has a slightly different modulation phase
    mod_phase = 2 * np.pi * ch / n_channels
    coupling_b[ch] = 0.5 + 0.4 * np.sin(
        2 * np.pi * 0.1 * times + mod_phase
    )
data_b = generate_coupled_data(coupling_b, rng)
ms_b, eigvec_b = compute_metastability(data_b, sfreq)

# ── Report ────────────────────────────────────────────────────
print("Condition A (tightly coupled):")
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"  {channel_names[ch]}: MS = {ms_a[ch]:.6f}")
print(f"  Mean regional MS: {ms_a.mean():.6f}")

print()
print("Condition B (time-varying coupling):")
for ch in range(n_channels):
    print(f"  {channel_names[ch]}: MS = {ms_b[ch]:.6f}")
print(f"  Mean regional MS: {ms_b.mean():.6f}")

print()
print(f"Ratio (B / A): {ms_b.mean() / ms_a.mean():.2f}x")

# ── Plot ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

# Panel 1: eigenvector dynamics for condition A (first 15 s)
ax = axes[0]
step = max(1, sfreq // 100)
t_plot = np.arange(0, n_samples, step) / sfreq
for ch in range(n_channels):
    ax.plot(t_plot, eigvec_a[ch], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlim(0, 15)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("v_k(t)")
ax.set_title("A. Eigenvector (tight coupling)")

# Panel 2: eigenvector dynamics for condition B (first 15 s)
ax = axes[1]
for ch in range(n_channels):
    ax.plot(t_plot, eigvec_b[ch], linewidth=0.5, alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlim(0, 15)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("v_k(t)")
ax.set_title("B. Eigenvector (varying coupling)")

# Panel 3: comparison bar chart
ax = axes[2]
x = np.arange(n_channels)
width = 0.35
bars_a = ax.bar(x - width/2, ms_a, width, label="Condition A (tight)",
                color="#2c3e50", alpha=0.7)
bars_b = ax.bar(x + width/2, ms_b, width, label="Condition B (varying)",
                color="#e74c3c", alpha=0.7)
ax.set_xlabel("Channel")
ax.set_ylabel("Regional metastability")
ax.set_title("C. Regional MS comparison")
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(channel_names, fontsize=9)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Condition A (tight coupling) should show low metastability across all channels: the eigenvector elements stay nearly constant because all channels maintain the same phase relationship. Condition B (time-varying coupling) should show higher metastability: the eigenvector elements fluctuate because the coupling changes over time, causing different channels to move in and out of alignment.
The eigenvector dynamics plots make this visible. In panel A, the lines are nearly flat. In panel B, they oscillate, reflecting the slow modulation of the coupling strength. The bar chart in panel C should show a clear difference between conditions for every channel.
This is the core logic behind using metastability to study brain dynamics: if a brain region’s role in the coordination pattern is flexible (high metastability), it is participating in a dynamic, adaptive network. If it is rigid (low metastability), something may be constraining its dynamics, as is hypothesised in Parkinson’s disease.

title: Metastability: exercises
section: Exercise 6: Simulated Parkinson’s vs Control group comparison
text:
Exercise 6: Simulated Parkinson’s vs Control group comparison
This exercise puts the entire pipeline together in a realistic analysis scenario. Simulate two groups of “subjects”:

Control group (10 subjects): coupling parameters that produce moderate, flexible coordination (moderate metastability).
Parkinson’s group (10 subjects): coupling parameters that produce rigid, excessive synchronisation (low metastability), consistent with the pathological beta synchrony seen in PD.

For each subject, generate 8 channels of oscillatory data, run the full metastability pipeline, and store the mean regional metastability. Then run an independent-samples t-test to compare the groups and produce a publication-quality figure showing the results.






TipHint





For control subjects, use moderate coupling strengths drawn from a normal distribution with mean around 0.5 and standard deviation 0.1. For Parkinson’s subjects, use higher coupling (mean 0.85, sd 0.05), reflecting the excessive synchronisation seen in PD.
Add between-subject variability: each subject should have slightly different coupling strengths across channels (draw them from the group-level distribution). Compute the metastability pipeline for each subject separately and store one summary value per subject (the mean across all channels).
Use scipy.stats.ttest_ind for the group comparison. Since PD subjects should have higher coupling and therefore lower metastability, you expect the PD group to have significantly lower mean metastability than the controls.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt
from scipy.stats import ttest_ind

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Parameters ─────────────────────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 8
sfreq = 256
duration = 60
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq
freq_osc = 10.0
n_subjects = 10

channel_names = [f"Ch{i}" for i in range(n_channels)]


def generate_subject_data(mean_coupling, sd_coupling, rng):
    """Generate coupled oscillatory data for one subject.

    Each channel gets a coupling value drawn from N(mean_coupling, sd_coupling),
    clipped to [0.05, 0.99].
    """
    # Draw per-channel coupling strengths for this subject
    couplings = rng.normal(mean_coupling, sd_coupling, size=n_channels)
    couplings = np.clip(couplings, 0.05, 0.99)

    # Common reference oscillation
    ref_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
                 + 0.3 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
    ref_signal = np.sin(ref_phase)

    data = np.zeros((n_channels, n_samples))
    for ch in range(n_channels):
        ind_phase = (2 * np.pi * freq_osc * times
                     + 2.0 * np.cumsum(rng.standard_normal(n_samples) / sfreq))
        ind_signal = np.sin(ind_phase)
        data[ch] = (couplings[ch] * ref_signal
                    + (1 - couplings[ch]) * ind_signal
                    + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples))

    return data, couplings


def compute_regional_metastability(data, sfreq, lo=8.0, hi=13.0):
    """Compute regional metastability for all channels."""
    n_ch, n_samp = data.shape
    b, a = butter(4, [lo, hi], btype="band", fs=sfreq)

    phases = np.zeros_like(data)
    for ch in range(n_ch):
        filtered = filtfilt(b, a, data[ch])
        phases[ch] = np.angle(hilbert(filtered))

    step = max(1, sfreq // 100)
    time_indices = np.arange(0, n_samp, step)
    n_tp = len(time_indices)

    eigvec_series = np.zeros((n_ch, n_tp))

    for ti, t in enumerate(time_indices):
        phi = phases[:, t]
        phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
        A = np.cos(phase_diff)

        eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
        dominant = eigenvectors[:, -1]

        if ti > 0 and np.dot(dominant, eigvec_series[:, ti - 1]) < 0:
            dominant = -dominant

        eigvec_series[:, ti] = dominant

    regional_ms = np.var(eigvec_series, axis=1)
    return regional_ms


# ── Simulate both groups ──────────────────────────────────────
ms_controls = []         # mean MS per subject
ms_pd = []               # mean MS per subject
ms_controls_per_ch = []  # per-channel MS for each subject
ms_pd_per_ch = []

print("Simulating control subjects...")
for subj in range(n_subjects):
    data, couplings = generate_subject_data(
        mean_coupling=0.50, sd_coupling=0.10, rng=rng
    )
    ms = compute_regional_metastability(data, sfreq)
    ms_controls.append(ms.mean())
    ms_controls_per_ch.append(ms)
    print(f"  Control {subj+1:2d}: mean coupling = {couplings.mean():.3f}, "
          f"mean MS = {ms.mean():.6f}")

print()
print("Simulating Parkinson's subjects...")
for subj in range(n_subjects):
    data, couplings = generate_subject_data(
        mean_coupling=0.85, sd_coupling=0.05, rng=rng
    )
    ms = compute_regional_metastability(data, sfreq)
    ms_pd.append(ms.mean())
    ms_pd_per_ch.append(ms)
    print(f"  PD      {subj+1:2d}: mean coupling = {couplings.mean():.3f}, "
          f"mean MS = {ms.mean():.6f}")

ms_controls = np.array(ms_controls)
ms_pd = np.array(ms_pd)
ms_controls_per_ch = np.array(ms_controls_per_ch)  # (n_subjects, n_channels)
ms_pd_per_ch = np.array(ms_pd_per_ch)

# ── Statistical test ──────────────────────────────────────────
t_stat, p_value = ttest_ind(ms_controls, ms_pd)

print()
print("=" * 50)
print("Group comparison (independent-samples t-test)")
print("=" * 50)
print(f"Controls: mean MS = {ms_controls.mean():.6f} "
      f"(sd = {ms_controls.std():.6f})")
print(f"PD:       mean MS = {ms_pd.mean():.6f} "
      f"(sd = {ms_pd.std():.6f})")
print(f"t = {t_stat:.3f}, p = {p_value:.6f}")
if p_value < 0.05:
    print("Result: significant difference (p < 0.05)")
else:
    print("Result: no significant difference")

# ── Effect size (Cohen's d) ───────────────────────────────────
pooled_std = np.sqrt(
    (ms_controls.std()**2 + ms_pd.std()**2) / 2
)
cohens_d = (ms_controls.mean() - ms_pd.mean()) / pooled_std
print(f"Cohen's d = {cohens_d:.2f}")

# ── Visualisation ─────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 3, figsize=(15, 5))

# Panel 1: individual subject metastability values
ax = axes[0]
jitter_c = rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1, size=n_subjects)
jitter_p = rng.uniform(-0.1, 0.1, size=n_subjects)
ax.scatter(np.zeros(n_subjects) + jitter_c, ms_controls,
           color="#3498db", s=60, alpha=0.7, label="Controls", zorder=3)
ax.scatter(np.ones(n_subjects) + jitter_p, ms_pd,
           color="#e74c3c", s=60, alpha=0.7, label="Parkinson's", zorder=3)
# Group means
ax.plot([-0.2, 0.2], [ms_controls.mean()] * 2,
        color="#2c3e50", linewidth=2)
ax.plot([0.8, 1.2], [ms_pd.mean()] * 2,
        color="#2c3e50", linewidth=2)
ax.set_xticks([0, 1])
ax.set_xticklabels(["Controls", "Parkinson's"])
ax.set_ylabel("Mean regional metastability")
ax.set_title(f"A. Individual subjects (p = {p_value:.2e})")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

# Panel 2: box plot
ax = axes[1]
bp = ax.boxplot(
    [ms_controls, ms_pd],
    labels=["Controls", "Parkinson's"],
    patch_artist=True, widths=0.5
)
bp["boxes"][0].set_facecolor("#3498db")
bp["boxes"][1].set_facecolor("#e74c3c")
for box in bp["boxes"]:
    box.set_alpha(0.5)
ax.set_ylabel("Mean regional metastability")
ax.set_title(f"B. Group comparison (Cohen's d = {cohens_d:.2f})")

# Panel 3: per-channel comparison
ax = axes[2]
x = np.arange(n_channels)
width = 0.35
mean_c = ms_controls_per_ch.mean(axis=0)
sem_c = ms_controls_per_ch.std(axis=0) / np.sqrt(n_subjects)
mean_p = ms_pd_per_ch.mean(axis=0)
sem_p = ms_pd_per_ch.std(axis=0) / np.sqrt(n_subjects)

ax.bar(x - width/2, mean_c, width, yerr=sem_c,
       label="Controls", color="#3498db", alpha=0.7, capsize=3)
ax.bar(x + width/2, mean_p, width, yerr=sem_p,
       label="Parkinson's", color="#e74c3c", alpha=0.7, capsize=3)
ax.set_xlabel("Channel")
ax.set_ylabel("Regional metastability")
ax.set_title("C. Per-channel metastability")
ax.set_xticks(x)
ax.set_xticklabels(channel_names, fontsize=9)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

You should see a significant p-value (likely well below 0.01), with the control group showing higher metastability than the Parkinson’s group. This reflects the simulation design: PD subjects have higher coupling, which means their channels stay locked in a fixed coordination pattern (low metastability), while controls have moderate coupling that allows more flexible coordination (higher metastability).
The per-channel plot (panel C) should show the difference across all channels, since we used a global coupling difference between groups. In a real study with real EEG data, you would expect the effect to be region-specific (some channels showing larger group differences than others), which is why regional metastability is more informative than a single global number.
The Cohen’s d value tells you the effect size: how many standard deviations apart the two group means are. With the parameters used here, the effect is deliberately large (to make the exercise clear). In real clinical data, effect sizes tend to be smaller, and you need more subjects and careful statistical controls to detect them.
This exercise mirrors the analysis pipeline that Natalia will run on real EEG data from Parkinson’s patients and healthy controls. The key differences with real data are: (a) the data come from actual EEG recordings rather than simulations, (b) preprocessing (filtering, artifact rejection) is needed before the metastability computation, (c) there will be three groups (controls, PD without FoG, PD with FoG) rather than two, and (d) the analysis will use multiple frequency bands and a larger number of channels.
