title: Getting started: exercises
text:
These exercises go with Module 1: Getting started. They cover the building blocks of MNE-Python: creating Raw objects from scratch, reading metadata, simulating known signals, extracting time segments, and saving and reloading data. Work through them in order; each one adds a small piece to what you already know.
All exercises use simulated data so you do not need any external files.

title: Getting started: exercises
section: Exercise 1: Create a simulated Raw object
text:
Exercise 1: Create a simulated Raw object
Create a Raw object from scratch with:

32 EEG channels
a sampling rate of 500 Hz
60 seconds of random data

After creating it, set all channels to type "eeg" and apply the standard 10-20 montage. Print the Info object to confirm everything looks right.






TipHint





Use numpy.random.randn() to generate a (32, n_samples) array and mne.io.RawArray() to wrap it in a Raw object. Create the Info first with mne.create_info(), passing sfreq=500 and ch_types="eeg". For channel names, use the first 32 channels from mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020").ch_names.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

# Get 32 channel names from the standard 10-20 montage
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
ch_names = montage.ch_names[:32]

# Create the Info object
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=500, ch_types="eeg")

# Generate 60 seconds of random data (32 channels x 30000 samples)
# MNE expects data in volts, so scale to a realistic EEG amplitude (~20 µV)
n_samples = 500 * 60
data = np.random.randn(32, n_samples) * 20e-6

# Create the Raw object
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Apply the montage
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Check the result
print(raw.info)
print(f"Number of channels: {len(raw.ch_names)}")
print(f"Sampling rate: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")
print(f"Duration: {raw.times[-1]:.1f} seconds")

title: Getting started: exercises
text:
Exercise 2: Inspect the Info object
Load the MNE sample dataset (or create a synthetic Raw object with mixed channel types) and answer these questions by examining its Info object:

How many channels does it have?
What is the sampling rate?
What channel types are present, and how many of each?

Print each answer to the console.






TipHint





The Info object behaves like a dictionary. Use info['nchan'] for the channel count and info['sfreq'] for the sampling rate. To count channel types, try mne.channel_type(info, k) for each channel index, or use raw.get_channel_types() and count with a Counter or a simple loop.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
from collections import Counter

# Create a synthetic dataset with mixed channel types
# 20 EEG channels, 2 EOG channels, 1 stim channel
ch_names_eeg = [f"EEG{i:03d}" for i in range(1, 21)]
ch_names_eog = ["EOG1", "EOG2"]
ch_names_stim = ["STI 014"]
ch_names = ch_names_eeg + ch_names_eog + ch_names_stim
ch_types = ["eeg"] * 20 + ["eog"] * 2 + ["stim"] * 1

sfreq = 256
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types=ch_types)

# Generate random data (23 channels x 10 seconds)
data = np.random.randn(23, sfreq * 10) * 20e-6
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Answer the three questions
print(f"1. Number of channels: {raw.info['nchan']}")
print(f"2. Sampling rate: {raw.info['sfreq']} Hz")

type_counts = Counter(raw.get_channel_types())
print("3. Channel types:")
for ch_type, count in type_counts.items():
    print(f"   {ch_type}: {count}")

title: Getting started: exercises
section: Exercise 3: Simulate and plot a 12 Hz oscillation
text:
Exercise 3: Simulate and plot a 12 Hz oscillation
Create a Raw object that contains a known 12 Hz sine wave in a channel called "Oz". Include at least a few other channels with random noise so the data looks like a realistic (if simplified) recording. Plot the first 2 seconds of channel "Oz" and verify that you can see roughly 24 cycles (12 Hz times 2 seconds).






TipHint





Build a time vector with np.arange(0, duration, 1/sfreq), then create the 12 Hz sine with np.sin(2 * np.pi * 12 * times). Scale it to a realistic amplitude (say 10 µV = 10e-6 V). For the other channels, use np.random.randn() with a smaller amplitude. Use raw.plot() with duration=2 and picks=["Oz"] to zoom in on the channel of interest.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

sfreq = 500
duration = 10  # seconds
times = np.arange(0, duration, 1 / sfreq)
n_samples = len(times)

# Channel setup: Oz will carry the 12 Hz oscillation,
# the rest will have background noise
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2", "Oz"]
n_channels = len(ch_names)

# Random background noise for all channels (~5 µV)
data = np.random.randn(n_channels, n_samples) * 5e-6

# Add a 12 Hz sine wave to Oz (index 6) with amplitude 10 µV
oz_index = ch_names.index("Oz")
data[oz_index] += 10e-6 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 12 * times)

# Create the Raw object
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Apply a standard montage so MNE knows channel positions
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Plot channel Oz for the first 2 seconds
raw.plot(duration=2, picks=["Oz"], title="12 Hz oscillation in Oz")

You should see a clear sinusoidal pattern with about 24 full cycles across the 2-second window. The other channels will look like flat noise at this scale.

title: Getting started: exercises
text:
Exercise 4: Crop a 5-second segment
Starting from any Raw object (create one if you need to), extract a 5-second segment from the middle of the recording using raw.crop(). Print the duration of the cropped object to confirm it is 5 seconds, then plot the segment.






TipHint





raw.crop(tmin, tmax) modifies the object in place by default. If you want to keep the original, call raw.copy().crop(tmin, tmax) instead. For a 60-second recording, cropping from 27.5 to 32.5 seconds gives you a 5-second window from the middle.









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne

# Create a 60-second recording
sfreq = 500
ch_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "C3", "C4", "Pz", "O1", "O2", "Oz"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
data = np.random.randn(len(ch_names), sfreq * 60) * 20e-6
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

print(f"Original duration: {raw.times[-1]:.1f} seconds")

# Crop a 5-second segment from the middle (keep original intact)
raw_cropped = raw.copy().crop(tmin=27.5, tmax=32.5)

print(f"Cropped duration: {raw_cropped.times[-1]:.1f} seconds")

# Plot the segment
raw_cropped.plot(title="5-second cropped segment")

section: Exercise 5: Save and reload a FIF file
text:
Exercise 5: Save and reload a FIF file
Create a Raw object, save it to MNE’s native FIF format, reload it from disk, and verify that the data in the reloaded object matches the original. Use numpy.allclose() to compare the arrays numerically.






TipHint





Save with raw.save("filename_raw.fif", overwrite=True). Reload with mne.io.read_raw_fif("filename_raw.fif", preload=True). To compare the data arrays, use raw.get_data() on both objects and pass them to np.allclose(). MNE file names should end with _raw.fif for raw data (MNE will warn you otherwise).









NoteSolution






import numpy as np
import mne
import os

# Create a small Raw object
sfreq = 256
ch_names = ["C3", "C4", "Cz", "Pz", "Oz"]
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
data = np.random.randn(len(ch_names), sfreq * 10) * 15e-6
raw_original = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)

# Save to FIF
fif_path = "/tmp/test_raw.fif"
raw_original.save(fif_path, overwrite=True)

# Reload
raw_loaded = mne.io.read_raw_fif(fif_path, preload=True)

# Compare
data_original = raw_original.get_data()
data_loaded = raw_loaded.get_data()

if np.allclose(data_original, data_loaded):
    print("Data matches: the save/load round-trip preserved all values.")
else:
    print("Data mismatch! Something went wrong.")

# Check that metadata also matches
print(f"Original sfreq: {raw_original.info['sfreq']}")
print(f"Loaded sfreq:   {raw_loaded.info['sfreq']}")
print(f"Original channels: {raw_original.ch_names}")
print(f"Loaded channels:   {raw_loaded.ch_names}")

# Clean up
os.remove(fif_path)

title: Artifact rejection
text:
Even after filtering, EEG data still contains signals that come from sources other than the brain. Eye blinks produce large, slow deflections in frontal channels. Eye movements create step-like shifts. Muscle tension from clenching the jaw or furrowing the brow adds high-frequency bursts. The heartbeat generates a rhythmic artifact, especially in recordings with a small number of channels.
These non-brain signals are called artifacts. Removing them is one of the most important steps in any EEG analysis pipeline, because if artifacts remain in the data, they will contaminate your results. This module covers the main strategies for artifact rejection, from simple visual inspection to Independent Component Analysis (ICA).

title: Artifact rejection
text:
Even after filtering, EEG data still contains signals that come from sources other than the brain. Eye blinks produce large, slow deflections in frontal channels. Eye movements create step-like shifts. Muscle tension from clenching the jaw or furrowing the brow adds high-frequency bursts. The heartbeat generates a rhythmic artifact, especially in recordings with a small number of channels.
These non-brain signals are called artifacts. Removing them is one of the most important steps in any EEG analysis pipeline, because if artifacts remain in the data, they will contaminate your results. This module covers the main strategies for artifact rejection, from simple visual inspection to Independent Component Analysis (ICA).

title: Artifact rejection
text:
Topics

Types of artifacts
Artifacts fall into a few broad categories based on their source:









Type
Source
What it looks like
Affected channels




Ocular (blink)
Eyelid movement
Large, slow positive deflection (100–300 uV)
Fp1, Fp2, AF3, AF4


Ocular (saccade)
Eye movement
Step-like lateral shift
F7/F8 (horizontal), Fp1/Fp2 (vertical)


Muscular (EMG)
Jaw, neck, forehead muscles
High-frequency burst (> 20 Hz)
Temporal and frontal channels


Cardiac (ECG)
Heartbeat
Rhythmic sharp peaks (~1 Hz)
Can appear anywhere, often left temporal


Movement
Head or body movement
Slow, large-amplitude drift
All channels



See Types of EEG artifacts for example traces and topographies of each type.


Visual inspection and manual rejection
The simplest approach to artifact removal is to look at the data and mark bad segments or bad epochs by hand. MNE’s interactive plotting tools let you click on time segments in continuous data (raw.plot()) or on individual epochs (epochs.plot()) to mark them for exclusion.
Manual rejection is time-consuming for large datasets, but it is a useful skill to develop early on. It trains your eye to recognise what clean EEG looks like and what different artifacts look like, which helps you evaluate whether automated methods are working correctly later.
See Visual inspection and manual rejection for a guided walkthrough.
# Interactive epoch browser -- click on bad epochs to mark them
epochs.plot(n_epochs=10, n_channels=30, scalings={"eeg": 100e-6})

# After marking, drop the bad epochs
epochs.drop_bad()


Amplitude-based epoch rejection
A quick way to remove the worst artifacts is to reject any epoch where the peak-to-peak amplitude exceeds a threshold. This catches blinks (which can reach 200–300 uV) and large muscle bursts without requiring you to inspect every epoch individually.
You set the threshold when creating the Epochs object or afterwards with epochs.drop_bad(). A common starting point for EEG is 150 uV peak-to-peak, but the right value depends on your data, your participants, and your channels.
See Amplitude-based epoch rejection for guidance on choosing thresholds.
# Reject epochs where any EEG channel exceeds 150 uV peak-to-peak
reject = {"eeg": 150e-6}
epochs = mne.Epochs(raw, events, event_id=1, tmin=-0.2, tmax=0.5,
                    reject=reject, preload=True)
print(f"Kept {len(epochs)} of {len(events)} epochs")


Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
Amplitude-based rejection throws away entire epochs. If a participant blinks frequently, you might lose a large fraction of your data. ICA offers a better approach: it separates the mixed signal at each channel into statistically independent components, some of which correspond to brain activity and some to artifacts. You can then remove the artifact components and reconstruct the data without them.
The key idea is that the signal at each electrode is a weighted mixture of several underlying sources. ICA finds those sources. A blink component will have a frontal topography and a characteristic time course (sharp peaks coinciding with blinks). A brain component will have a more distributed topography and a time course that looks like neural oscillations.
ICA works best on data that has already been high-pass filtered (at least 1 Hz) and from which the worst segments have been removed. If the data is too noisy, ICA has trouble separating the components cleanly.
See ICA: theory and practice for the mathematical background and ICA in MNE-Python for the practical implementation.
# Fit ICA with 20 components
ica = mne.preprocessing.ICA(n_components=20, random_state=42)
ica.fit(raw)

# Plot the components
ica.plot_components()
ica.plot_sources(raw)


Identifying ICA components
After fitting ICA, you need to decide which components are artifacts and which are brain activity. MNE provides several tools for this:

Visual inspection: look at the component topography and time course. Blink components have a frontal topography; muscle components have a temporal topography with high-frequency content.
Correlation with EOG/ECG channels: if you recorded the electrooculogram (EOG) or electrocardiogram (ECG), MNE can correlate each component with those channels to find matches automatically.

See Identifying ICA components for detailed examples with annotated plots.
# Automatic detection using EOG channel
eog_indices, eog_scores = ica.find_bads_eog(raw, ch_name="Fp1")
ica.exclude = eog_indices

# Apply ICA to remove the identified components
ica.apply(raw)


Automated ICA labelling with ICLabel
Manually labelling ICA components is subjective and time-consuming. The ICLabel algorithm, originally developed for EEGLAB, classifies each component into one of seven categories: brain, muscle, eye, heart, line noise, channel noise, or other. The mne-icalabel package brings this to Python.
ICLabel uses a neural network trained on a large labelled dataset. It is not perfect, but it provides a good starting point. You can use its predictions as suggestions and override them when you disagree.
See Automated ICA labelling with ICLabel for installation and usage examples.
from mne_icalabel import label_components

# Label all ICA components
labels = label_components(raw, ica, method="iclabel")

# Exclude components classified as non-brain
ica.exclude = [
    i for i, label in enumerate(labels["labels"])
    if label not in ("brain", "other")
]
ica.apply(raw)


The autoreject approach
The autoreject package takes a different approach to artifact handling. Instead of using ICA, it works at the epoch level: it learns channel-specific rejection thresholds from the data, interpolates bad channels within individual epochs (so different epochs can have different bad channels), and rejects epochs that are too noisy to repair.
Autoreject can be used on its own or in combination with ICA. A common workflow is to run ICA first (to remove eye and heart artifacts), then run autoreject on the epoched data (to catch remaining bad epochs and channels).
See Automated artifact rejection with autoreject for a worked example.
from autoreject import AutoReject

ar = AutoReject(n_interpolate=[1, 2, 4], random_state=42, n_jobs=-1)
epochs_clean, reject_log = ar.fit_transform(epochs, return_log=True)
reject_log.plot("horizontal")

title: Artifact rejection
section: Working example: ICA on simulated data with blink artifact
text:
Working example: ICA on simulated data with blink artifact
The code below creates simulated EEG data, adds a synthetic blink artifact to the frontal channels, runs ICA, and identifies the blink component. This lets you see the full ICA workflow from start to finish on data where you know exactly what the artifact looks like.

import numpy as np
import mne

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# --- Create 32-channel simulated EEG ---
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("biosemi32")
ch_names = montage.ch_names[:32]
sfreq = 256
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")
n_samples = int(30 * sfreq)  # 30 seconds for enough blinks
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Pink noise base
white = rng.standard_normal((len(ch_names), n_samples))
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
data = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
data *= 20e-6 / data.std()

# --- Add synthetic blink artifacts ---
# Blinks are modelled as Gaussian bumps, occurring every 3-5 seconds,
# strongest at Fp1 and Fp2, decreasing toward posterior channels.
blink_times = np.arange(2, 28, 3.5)  # blink at these times (seconds)
blink_duration = 0.25  # seconds (half-width of the Gaussian)
blink_amplitude = 100e-6  # 100 uV (realistic blink amplitude)

# Weight by distance from frontal pole: Fp channels get full weight,
# posterior channels get almost none
frontal_channels = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "AF3", "AF4", "F3", "Fz", "F4"]
channel_weights = np.zeros(len(ch_names))
for i, ch in enumerate(ch_names):
    if ch in ("Fp1", "Fp2"):
        channel_weights[i] = 1.0
    elif ch in ("AF3", "AF4"):
        channel_weights[i] = 0.7
    elif ch in ("F3", "Fz", "F4", "F7", "F8"):
        channel_weights[i] = 0.4
    elif ch.startswith("FC") or ch.startswith("C"):
        channel_weights[i] = 0.15
    else:
        channel_weights[i] = 0.05

for bt in blink_times:
    blink_signal = blink_amplitude * np.exp(
        -0.5 * ((times - bt) / blink_duration) ** 2
    )
    data += np.outer(channel_weights, blink_signal)

# --- Build Raw and preprocess ---
raw = mne.io.RawArray(data, info)
raw.set_montage(montage)

# High-pass filter at 1 Hz (ICA works better with high-pass >= 1 Hz)
raw.filter(l_freq=1.0, h_freq=40.0)

# --- Fit ICA ---
n_components = 15
ica = mne.preprocessing.ICA(
    n_components=n_components,
    method="fastica",
    random_state=42,
    max_iter="auto",
)
ica.fit(raw)

# --- Identify the blink component ---
# Use Fp1 as a proxy EOG channel (since we added blinks there)
eog_indices, eog_scores = ica.find_bads_eog(
    raw, ch_name="Fp1", threshold=2.0
)
print(f"Blink component(s) identified: {eog_indices}")
print(f"Correlation scores: {eog_scores[eog_indices]}")

# Plot component topographies
fig_components = ica.plot_components(
    picks=range(min(n_components, 15)),
    title="ICA components",
)

# Plot the scores to show which component correlates with Fp1
fig_scores = ica.plot_scores(
    eog_scores,
    title="ICA component correlation with Fp1 (blink proxy)",
    labels="eog",
)

In the component topography plot, look for a component with strong frontal loading (high weights at Fp1 and Fp2, decreasing toward the back of the head). That is the blink component. The bar plot of scores confirms which component has the highest correlation with the Fp1 channel, which we used as a proxy for the EOG.
To actually remove the blink component from the data, you would run:
ica.exclude = eog_indices
raw_clean = ica.apply(raw.copy())
The .copy() call is important: ica.apply() modifies the data in place, so if you want to keep the original for comparison, work on a copy.

title: Artifact rejection
text:
Choosing between rejection strategies
Different strategies work best in different situations:








Strategy
Best for
Limitations




Manual rejection
Small datasets, learning
Subjective, slow


Amplitude threshold
Quick cleaning, removing extreme artifacts
Loses entire epochs, threshold is arbitrary


ICA
Blinks, eye movements, heartbeat
Needs enough data (~60+ seconds), can overfit with few channels


ICLabel
Large datasets, reproducibility
Not perfect; still needs human review


Autoreject
Channel-level noise, automated pipelines
Does not handle continuous artifacts like blinks



In practice, many researchers combine these approaches. A typical workflow is:

Remove the worst segments by visual inspection.
Run ICA to identify and remove blink, eye movement, and heart components.
Epoch the data.
Use amplitude-based rejection or autoreject to clean the remaining epochs.

title: Getting started
text: This module covers everything you need before you start analysing real EEG data. You will install MNE-Python, learn the main data structures that MNE uses to represent brain signals, practise loading files in several common formats, and create simulated EEG data so you can experiment without needing access to patient recordings. By the end of this module you should be able to open a raw EEG file, inspect it visually, and understand what you are looking at.

title: Getting started
text: This module covers everything you need before you start analysing real EEG data. You will install MNE-Python, learn the main data structures that MNE uses to represent brain signals, practise loading files in several common formats, and create simulated EEG data so you can experiment without needing access to patient recordings. By the end of this module you should be able to open a raw EEG file, inspect it visually, and understand what you are looking at.

title: Getting started
text:
Topics

Installing MNE-Python
MNE-Python can be installed with pip or conda. The conda-forge channel tends to handle compiled dependencies (like HDF5 for reading certain file formats) more smoothly, but pip works well for most setups. See the installation guide for step-by-step instructions covering both methods.
# pip
pip install mne

# conda (recommended for beginners)
conda install -c conda-forge mne
If you plan to use features like 3D source-space visualisation, you will also need PyVista and pyvistaqt. For the work in this site, the base mne package is enough.


MNE data structures
MNE organises EEG data into a small set of objects. Understanding these is the single most important step before doing any analysis, because every function in MNE expects one of them as input.








Object
What it holds
Typical use




Raw
Continuous recording (all channels, full duration)
Loading, filtering, visual inspection


Epochs
Short segments time-locked to events
Averaging, classification, connectivity


Evoked
Averaged signal across epochs for one condition
ERP plots, statistical comparisons


Info
Metadata: channel names, sampling rate, montage
Attached to every Raw/Epochs/Evoked object



See Understanding MNE data structures for a detailed walkthrough of each object and how they relate to one another.


Loading EEG data
Real EEG recordings come in many formats depending on the amplifier and software used during acquisition. MNE has dedicated readers for the most common ones:

EDF / EDF+ (European Data Format): mne.io.read_raw_edf(). Very common in clinical and research settings.
BDF (BioSemi Data Format): mne.io.read_raw_bdf(). Used with BioSemi ActiveTwo amplifiers.
BrainVision (.vhdr + .vmrk + .eeg): mne.io.read_raw_brainvision(). Used with BrainProducts amplifiers.
EEGLAB .set files: mne.io.read_raw_eeglab(). Useful if collaborators preprocessed data in EEGLAB/MATLAB.

All of these return a Raw object. The loading functions share a common interface, so once you know how to work with one format, switching to another is just a matter of changing the function name and file path. See Loading EEG data for examples of each format.
# Example: loading a BrainVision file
raw = mne.io.read_raw_brainvision("subject01.vhdr", preload=True)
print(raw.info)


Creating simulated EEG data
When you are learning, it helps to work with data you fully control. MNE’s mne.simulation module lets you create realistic multi-channel EEG signals with known properties. This means you can add a known artifact, remove it with ICA, and check whether the procedure worked, something you cannot do with real data where the “ground truth” is unknown.
See Simulating EEG data for the full details. Below is a working example that creates a 64-channel recording and plots it.


Setting channel locations (montages)
EEG channels have physical positions on the scalp. MNE needs to know these positions to draw topographic maps, to interpolate bad channels from their neighbours, and to compute average references correctly. A montage is a mapping from channel names to 3D coordinates.
MNE ships with standard montages like standard_1020 (the international 10-20 system) and biosemi64. You apply a montage to your data with raw.set_montage(). See Setting channel locations for worked examples.
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("standard_1020")
raw.set_montage(montage)


Visual inspection of raw data
Before any automated processing, you should always look at your data. MNE’s raw.plot() opens an interactive browser where you can scroll through the recording, mark bad channels, and annotate noisy segments. This step catches problems that no algorithm will flag: a loose electrode, a participant moving during the recording, or a channel that drifted steadily throughout the session.
See Visual inspection of raw data for tips on what to look for and how to annotate bad segments.
raw.plot(n_channels=30, scalings="auto", title="Raw EEG")


The BIDS format for EEG
The Brain Imaging Data Structure (BIDS) is a standard way to organise neuroimaging datasets, including EEG. BIDS specifies a folder hierarchy, file naming convention, and metadata files (JSON sidecars, *_channels.tsv, *_events.tsv) that make datasets self-documenting and shareable.
The mne-bids package reads and writes BIDS-formatted EEG datasets. If you are working with a public dataset, there is a good chance it follows BIDS. See The BIDS format for EEG for an introduction and examples of reading BIDS datasets with mne_bids.read_raw_bids().

title: Getting started
text:
Working example: simulated 64-channel EEG
The code below creates a 64-channel EEG recording lasting 10 seconds, adds some simulated brain activity, and plots it. You can run this without any external data files.

import numpy as np
import mne

# Reproducibility
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# Create a 64-channel montage and Info object
montage = mne.channels.make_standard_montage("biosemi64")
ch_names = montage.ch_names[:64]
sfreq = 256  # Hz
info = mne.create_info(ch_names=ch_names, sfreq=sfreq, ch_types="eeg")

# Generate 10 seconds of simulated data
# Mix of alpha (10 Hz) and pink noise to look roughly like resting-state EEG
n_samples = int(10 * sfreq)
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Pink noise (1/f): generate white noise and shape the spectrum
white = rng.standard_normal((len(ch_names), n_samples))
freqs = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)

# Add a 10 Hz alpha oscillation (stronger in posterior channels)
alpha = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
posterior = [i for i, ch in enumerate(ch_names) if ch.startswith(("O", "P"))]
for idx in posterior:
    pink[idx] += 3 * alpha

# Scale to realistic microvolts (roughly 20-50 uV peak-to-peak)
pink *= 20e-6 / pink.std()

# Build the Raw object
raw = mne.io.RawArray(pink, info)
raw.set_montage(montage)

# Plot a 5-second window
fig = raw.plot(
    duration=5,
    n_channels=20,
    scalings={"eeg": 50e-6},
    title="Simulated 64-channel EEG",
    show=True
)

Creating RawArray with float64 data, n_channels=64, n_times=2560
    Range : 0 ... 2559 =      0.000 ...     9.996 secs
Ready.
Using matplotlib as 2D backend.





Simulated 64-channel EEG data using the BioSemi montage.




The plot shows 20 channels over 5 seconds. Posterior channels (O1, O2, Oz, Pz, etc.) show a clear 10 Hz alpha rhythm, while frontal channels have mostly broadband noise. This is a rough approximation of what resting-state EEG looks like when a person sits with their eyes closed.
