What comes next
Once you are comfortable loading and inspecting raw data, move on to Module 2: Preprocessing, where you will learn how to filter the signal, remove line noise, and re-reference the channels.

title: Spectral and time-frequency analysis
text:
So far we have cleaned the EEG signal and removed artifacts. Now we can ask a quantitative question: what frequencies are present in the recording, and how does their power change over time?
Spectral analysis decomposes the EEG into its constituent oscillations. A resting-state recording with eyes closed will show a prominent peak around 10 Hz (alpha), while a person performing mental arithmetic will show stronger beta activity (13–30 Hz) and reduced alpha. These patterns are the backbone of EEG research, and measuring them precisely requires the right tools.
This module covers two complementary approaches. First, power spectral density (PSD) tells you the average frequency content of a recording. Second, time-frequency decomposition reveals how that content evolves over time, which is what you need when you want to link oscillatory changes to specific events or cognitive states.

title: Spectral and time-frequency analysis
text:
So far we have cleaned the EEG signal and removed artifacts. Now we can ask a quantitative question: what frequencies are present in the recording, and how does their power change over time?
Spectral analysis decomposes the EEG into its constituent oscillations. A resting-state recording with eyes closed will show a prominent peak around 10 Hz (alpha), while a person performing mental arithmetic will show stronger beta activity (13–30 Hz) and reduced alpha. These patterns are the backbone of EEG research, and measuring them precisely requires the right tools.
This module covers two complementary approaches. First, power spectral density (PSD) tells you the average frequency content of a recording. Second, time-frequency decomposition reveals how that content evolves over time, which is what you need when you want to link oscillatory changes to specific events or cognitive states.

title: Spectral and time-frequency analysis
text:
Topics

Power spectral density with Welch’s method
PSD estimates how much power (signal energy) is present at each frequency. Welch’s method is the standard approach: it splits the signal into overlapping windows, computes the Fourier transform of each window, and averages the resulting spectra. The averaging reduces noise and gives a smoother estimate than a single FFT of the entire recording.
The key parameters are:

Window length (n_fft): longer windows give better frequency resolution but worse time resolution. A 2-second window gives 0.5 Hz resolution (1/2 seconds).
Overlap: typically 50%. More overlap means more windows and a smoother estimate, at the cost of computation time.
Window function: a Hamming window is the default in MNE. It tapers the edges of each segment to reduce spectral leakage (artificial spreading of peaks into neighbouring frequencies).

In MNE, raw.compute_psd(method="welch") handles all of this. You can also use scipy.signal.welch() directly if you want more control. See Power spectral density (PSD) for the full treatment, including units, parameter choices, and comparisons between conditions.
# Compute PSD with Welch's method in MNE
psd = raw.compute_psd(method="welch", fmin=1, fmax=45, n_fft=512)
psd.plot()


EEG frequency bands
EEG oscillations are grouped into named bands. The exact boundaries vary across publications, but the most common convention is shown below. See EEG frequency bands for a deeper discussion of each band, including its neural generators and how to measure band power reliably.



Band
Frequency range
Typical association




Delta
0.5–4 Hz
Deep sleep, pathology


Theta
4–8 Hz
Drowsiness, memory encoding


Alpha
8–13 Hz
Relaxed wakefulness, eyes closed


Beta
13–30 Hz
Active thinking, motor planning


Gamma
30–100 Hz
Perception, binding, attention



Alpha is usually the most prominent rhythm in healthy adults during rest. It is strongest over posterior (occipital and parietal) regions and attenuates when the person opens their eyes or starts a cognitive task. This suppression is called alpha desynchronisation and is one of the most reliable findings in EEG research.
Beta activity is associated with active cortical processing. It is prominent over motor cortex during motor planning and attenuates just before and during movement (beta desynchronisation), then rebounds after movement ends (beta rebound).
Gamma oscillations are faster and lower in amplitude. They are harder to measure with scalp EEG because high-frequency signals are attenuated by the skull, and muscle artifact overlaps with the gamma range. Many gamma findings from scalp EEG have been questioned for this reason.


Topographic maps by band
A topographic map shows how power is distributed across the scalp at a given frequency or band. MNE can plot band-power topographies directly from a PSD object. See Topographic maps for a deeper discussion of interpolation, normalisation, colour maps, and common pitfalls.
# Plot topographic maps for each band
psd.plot_topomap(bands={"Delta": (0.5, 4), "Theta": (4, 8),
                        "Alpha": (8, 13), "Beta": (13, 30)},
                 normalize=True)
These maps let you see spatial patterns at a glance. For instance, alpha power concentrated over occipital regions confirms that the posterior alpha rhythm is present. Asymmetric patterns (more power on one side) can indicate lateralised cortical processing or, in clinical settings, focal abnormalities.
When comparing topographies across conditions or groups, normalising the power values (dividing by total power) is important. Otherwise, differences in overall signal amplitude (due to electrode impedance, skull thickness, etc.) can mask the actual spatial pattern.


Time-frequency decomposition
PSD gives you the average spectrum over a time window, but many interesting phenomena in EEG are transient. An event-related desynchronisation might last only a few hundred milliseconds. To capture this, you need time-frequency decomposition: a method that estimates power at each frequency at each time point. See Time-frequency decomposition for a detailed comparison of wavelet and multitaper approaches, including guidance on choosing parameters.
Morlet wavelets are the most common approach in EEG. A Morlet wavelet is a short sinusoid tapered by a Gaussian envelope. You convolve the signal with wavelets of different frequencies, and the amplitude of the result at each time-frequency point tells you how much power is present there.
The number of cycles in the wavelet controls the trade-off between time and frequency resolution. Fewer cycles (e.g., 3) give better time resolution but smear across frequencies. More cycles (e.g., 7) give sharp frequency peaks but blur short-lived events. A common compromise is to scale the number of cycles linearly with frequency: for example, n_cycles = freqs / 2.
# Time-frequency decomposition with Morlet wavelets in MNE
freqs = np.arange(4, 40, 1)
power = mne.time_frequency.tfr_morlet(
    epochs, freqs=freqs, n_cycles=freqs / 2,
    return_itc=False, average=True
)
power.plot([0])  # plot for the first channel
Multitaper methods offer an alternative. Instead of a single taper (window), multitaper applies several orthogonal tapers (Slepian sequences) to each time window and averages the results. This gives a smoother spectral estimate with better control over frequency resolution. The bandwidth parameter controls how many tapers are used: wider bandwidth means more tapers and smoother estimates, at the cost of frequency resolution.
# Multitaper time-frequency decomposition
power_mt = mne.time_frequency.tfr_multitaper(
    epochs, freqs=freqs, n_cycles=freqs / 2,
    time_bandwidth=4.0, return_itc=False, average=True
)


Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
ERSP measures how oscillatory power changes relative to a baseline period. It is the time-frequency equivalent of an event-related potential (ERP): instead of looking at the average voltage waveform, you look at the average power change across trials. See Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP) for the full treatment of baseline correction modes, ERD/ERS interpretation, and statistical testing.
The standard procedure is:

Compute the time-frequency representation for each epoch.
Average the power across epochs.
Convert to a baseline-relative measure (typically percent change or decibels relative to a pre-stimulus interval).

In MNE, you can apply baseline correction to the AverageTFR object:
power.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent")
power.plot([0], title="ERSP: percent change from baseline")
Positive values indicate an increase in power relative to baseline (event-related synchronisation, ERS), and negative values indicate a decrease (event-related desynchronisation, ERD). A typical motor task shows beta ERD during movement preparation and beta ERS (rebound) after movement ends.


Band power extraction for statistical comparison
For group-level statistics, you often need a single number per participant per condition, not an entire time-frequency map. The common approach is to extract average band power in a specific time-frequency window of interest. See Group-level statistics for EEG for a full walkthrough of statistical testing, multiple comparisons correction, and cluster-based permutation tests.
Steps:

Define the frequency band (e.g., alpha: 8–13 Hz).
Define the time window (e.g., 0.2–0.5 seconds post-stimulus).
Average power across frequencies and time points within that window.
Do this for each epoch (or each participant’s average) and each condition.
Feed the resulting values into a statistical test (t-test, ANOVA, mixed-effects model).

# Extract alpha power (8-13 Hz) in a time window (0.2-0.5 s)
alpha_power = power.copy().crop(tmin=0.2, tmax=0.5)
alpha_data = alpha_power.data[:, 4:9, :]  # channels x freq indices x time
alpha_mean = alpha_data.mean(axis=(1, 2))  # one value per channel
Choosing the time-frequency window is a critical step. If you select the window based on the data (e.g., picking the time and frequency with the strongest effect), you inflate your false-positive rate. The window should ideally be defined a priori, based on previous literature or a separate pilot dataset.


Event-related potentials (ERPs)
While spectral analysis focuses on oscillatory power, another way to analyse EEG is to look at the average voltage waveform time-locked to an event. This is the event-related potential, or ERP. You epoch the continuous recording around each event (stimulus onset, response, etc.), then average across trials. Because noise is random and the brain response is consistent, the averaging cancels out the noise and reveals the underlying signal.
ERPs are one of the oldest and most widely used tools in cognitive neuroscience. Classic components include the P300 (a positive deflection around 300 ms after a rare or surprising stimulus), the N400 (a negative deflection related to semantic processing), and the N170 (associated with face perception).
In MNE, computing an ERP is simple once you have epochs:
# Average across epochs to get the ERP
evoked = epochs["stimulus"].average()
evoked.plot()

# Plot topographic maps at specific time points
evoked.plot_topomap(times=[0.1, 0.2, 0.3])
You can also compare ERPs between conditions by computing a difference wave: subtract the evoked response in one condition from another. This isolates the part of the brain response that differs between conditions.
See Event-related potentials (ERPs) for the full treatment, including the signal-to-noise logic behind averaging, classic ERP components, difference waves, and grand averages across participants.

title: Spectral and time-frequency analysis
section: Working example: PSD of simulated data with alpha and beta oscillations
text:
Working example: PSD of simulated data with alpha and beta oscillations
The code below creates a simulated EEG signal containing two known oscillations: a 10 Hz alpha rhythm and a 20 Hz beta rhythm, on top of pink noise. It then computes the PSD using Welch’s method and plots it. You should see two clear peaks at 10 and 20 Hz.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy import signal

# Set up parameters
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
sfreq = 256          # sampling frequency in Hz
duration = 30        # seconds (longer recording gives smoother PSD)
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

# Generate pink noise (1/f background)
white = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)
freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_samples, d=1 / sfreq)
freqs_fft[0] = 1  # avoid division by zero
pink_filter = 1 / np.sqrt(freqs_fft)
pink = np.fft.irfft(np.fft.rfft(white) * pink_filter, n=n_samples)
pink = pink / pink.std()  # normalise

# Add oscillations
alpha = 1.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)   # 10 Hz alpha
beta = 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 20 * times)    # 20 Hz beta (weaker)
eeg = pink + alpha + beta

# Compute PSD with Welch's method
freqs_psd, psd = signal.welch(eeg, fs=sfreq, nperseg=512, noverlap=256)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(12, 4))

# Left panel: time-domain signal (first 2 seconds)
ax = axes[0]
mask = times < 2
ax.plot(times[mask], eeg[mask], linewidth=0.5, color="#2c3e50")
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Simulated EEG signal (first 2 seconds)")

# Right panel: PSD
ax = axes[1]
ax.semilogy(freqs_psd, psd, linewidth=1.2, color="#2c3e50")
ax.axvline(10, color="#e74c3c", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Alpha (10 Hz)")
ax.axvline(20, color="#3498db", linestyle="--", alpha=0.7, label="Beta (20 Hz)")
ax.set_xlabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_ylabel("Power spectral density")
ax.set_title("PSD (Welch's method)")
ax.set_xlim(0, 45)
ax.legend()

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Power spectral density of simulated EEG with alpha (10 Hz) and beta (20 Hz) oscillations.




The left panel shows the raw time-domain signal. You can see the oscillatory structure, but it is hard to tell the exact frequencies just by looking. The right panel makes the frequency content explicit: the 1/f background slopes downward, and the two injected oscillations appear as clear peaks at 10 and 20 Hz. The alpha peak is taller because we gave it a larger amplitude.
This is the basic logic of spectral analysis: decompose a complex signal into its frequency components, then quantify how much power each component carries.

title: Spectral and time-frequency analysis
text:
What comes next
With the ability to measure oscillatory power in hand, the next module moves to connectivity and metastability. Instead of asking “how much alpha is present in this channel?”, we will ask “are the alpha oscillations in different channels synchronised with each other?” That question leads to phase-based connectivity measures and, ultimately, to the concept of metastability. See Module 5: Connectivity and metastability.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
PSD tells you how much power sits at each frequency, averaged over the entire recording (or over a long segment). But the brain’s spectral profile is not static. Alpha power increases when you close your eyes and decreases when you open them. Beta power drops just before a movement and rebounds afterwards. Gamma bursts last only tens of milliseconds. If you average over these changes, you lose them entirely.
Time-frequency decomposition solves this problem by estimating power at each frequency and each time point simultaneously. Instead of a one-dimensional PSD curve, you get a two-dimensional map with time on the x-axis and frequency on the y-axis. Colour indicates power. These maps reveal the temporal dynamics of oscillatory activity that PSD cannot capture.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
PSD tells you how much power sits at each frequency, averaged over the entire recording (or over a long segment). But the brain’s spectral profile is not static. Alpha power increases when you close your eyes and decreases when you open them. Beta power drops just before a movement and rebounds afterwards. Gamma bursts last only tens of milliseconds. If you average over these changes, you lose them entirely.
Time-frequency decomposition solves this problem by estimating power at each frequency and each time point simultaneously. Instead of a one-dimensional PSD curve, you get a two-dimensional map with time on the x-axis and frequency on the y-axis. Colour indicates power. These maps reveal the temporal dynamics of oscillatory activity that PSD cannot capture.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
The intuition: trading resolution
The fundamental challenge in time-frequency analysis is the uncertainty principle: you cannot have perfect resolution in both time and frequency simultaneously. A short analysis window gives you good temporal resolution (you know when something happened) but poor frequency resolution (you cannot tell apart nearby frequencies). A long window gives you good frequency resolution but poor temporal resolution.
Every time-frequency method navigates this trade-off differently. The two most common approaches in EEG research are Morlet wavelets and the multitaper method.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Morlet wavelets
A Morlet wavelet is a short sinusoidal oscillation multiplied by a Gaussian envelope. It looks like a brief burst of a particular frequency, which makes it a natural tool for detecting oscillatory bursts in neural data.
The wavelet for frequency \(f_0\) is:
\[w(t, f_0) = A \, \exp\!\left(-\frac{t^2}{2\sigma_t^2}\right) \exp(i \, 2\pi f_0 \, t)\]
where \(\sigma_t\) controls the width of the Gaussian envelope. The number of cycles \(n\) in the wavelet is related to \(\sigma_t\) by \(n = 2\pi f_0 \sigma_t\). This parameter controls the time-frequency trade-off:

Fewer cycles (e.g., \(n = 3\)): the wavelet is short, giving good temporal resolution but poor frequency resolution. Good for detecting brief events.
More cycles (e.g., \(n = 7\)): the wavelet is longer, giving better frequency resolution at the cost of temporal precision. Good for sustained oscillations.

A common choice is \(n = 7\) for frequencies above 8 Hz and fewer cycles for lower frequencies. Some researchers use a linearly increasing number of cycles (e.g., \(n\) proportional to frequency), so that relative frequency resolution is constant across the spectrum.

How the computation works
Time-frequency decomposition with wavelets involves convolving the signal with each wavelet. At each time point, you slide the wavelet along the signal, compute the dot product, and record the result. The squared magnitude of the result gives the instantaneous power at that frequency and time point.
In practice, the convolution is done in the frequency domain (multiply FFTs, then inverse FFT) because it is much faster.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
The multitaper method
The multitaper method (Thomson, 1982) takes a different approach. Instead of using a single window at each time point, it uses several orthogonal tapers (typically discrete prolate spheroidal sequences, or DPSS tapers) and averages the spectra across tapers. This reduces spectral leakage and variance at the cost of some frequency resolution.
For time-frequency analysis, the multitaper method is applied to short, overlapping time windows (similar to short-time Fourier transform, but with multiple tapers per window). MNE implements this via tfr_multitaper().
The multitaper method is particularly useful when you need reliable power estimates and are willing to sacrifice some frequency resolution. It tends to produce smoother time-frequency maps than the wavelet approach.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Computing time-frequency representations in MNE
MNE provides two main functions for time-frequency decomposition:

Using Morlet wavelets

import mne
import numpy as np

# Load data and create epochs
raw = mne.io.read_raw_edf("recording.edf", preload=True)
raw.filter(l_freq=0.5, h_freq=45.0)

events = mne.find_events(raw)
epochs = mne.Epochs(raw, events, tmin=-0.5, tmax=1.5, baseline=None,
                    preload=True)

# Define frequencies of interest
freqs = np.arange(4, 40, 1)  # 4 to 39 Hz in 1 Hz steps
n_cycles = freqs / 2.0       # adaptive: more cycles at higher frequencies

# Compute time-frequency representation
tfr = epochs.compute_tfr(method="morlet", freqs=freqs, n_cycles=n_cycles,
                         return_itc=False, average=True)

# tfr is an AverageTFR object: shape (n_channels, n_freqs, n_times)

The n_cycles parameter controls the time-frequency trade-off. Setting n_cycles = freqs / 2.0 means that each wavelet has a duration of half a cycle per Hz, which gives a good balance for most EEG data.


Using the multitaper method

# Multitaper time-frequency
tfr_mt = epochs.compute_tfr(method="multitaper", freqs=freqs,
                            n_cycles=n_cycles, return_itc=False,
                            average=True, time_bandwidth=4.0)

The time_bandwidth parameter controls the spectral smoothing. Higher values give more smoothing (more tapers, smoother estimates) at the cost of frequency resolution. A value of 4.0 is a common default.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Plotting time-frequency maps

# Basic TFR plot for a single channel
tfr.plot(picks="Cz", baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent",
         title="Time-frequency: Cz")

# Topographic TFR plot (scalp maps at selected time-frequency windows)
tfr.plot_topo(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent")

# Joint plot: TFR + topographies at selected times
tfr.plot_joint(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent",
               timefreqs={(0.3, 10): "Alpha", (0.5, 25): "Beta"})

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Baseline correction
Raw time-frequency power values are difficult to interpret because different frequencies have very different absolute power levels (the 1/f spectrum). Baseline correction removes this frequency-dependent scaling by expressing post-stimulus power relative to a pre-stimulus baseline period.
MNE supports several baseline modes:








Mode
Formula
Interpretation




"mean"
\(P - P_{\text{baseline}}\)
Absolute change from baseline


"ratio"
\(P / P_{\text{baseline}}\)
Ratio relative to baseline


"logratio"
\(\log(P / P_{\text{baseline}})\)
Log ratio (symmetric around 0)


"percent"
\((P - P_{\text{baseline}}) / P_{\text{baseline}} \times 100\)
Percentage change


"zscore"
\((P - \mu_{\text{baseline}}) / \sigma_{\text{baseline}}\)
z-score relative to baseline



The "percent" mode is the most commonly reported in the EEG literature. It is easy to interpret: a value of 50 means power increased by 50% relative to baseline, and -30 means power decreased by 30%.

# Apply baseline correction in-place
tfr.apply_baseline(baseline=(-0.5, 0), mode="percent")

The baseline period should be a time interval before the event of interest where you do not expect any task-related changes. A common choice is -500 to 0 ms (the 500 ms before stimulus onset).

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP)
Event-related spectral perturbation (ERSP; Makeig, 1993) is the name for the baseline-corrected, trial-averaged time-frequency map. It is essentially what you get when you compute the TFR across trials, average them, and apply baseline correction. The term is used mainly in the EEGLAB literature, but the concept is the same across toolboxes.
An ERSP map typically shows:

Event-related desynchronisation (ERD): a decrease in power relative to baseline, often seen in the alpha and beta bands during motor preparation or cognitive engagement.
Event-related synchronisation (ERS): an increase in power relative to baseline, such as the beta rebound after movement or gamma bursts during stimulus processing.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Working example
The code below creates simulated epoched data with a clear alpha desynchronisation after stimulus onset, computes the time-frequency representation using Morlet wavelets, and plots the result.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Simulation parameters ──────────────────────────────────
sfreq = 256
n_trials = 80
tmin, tmax = -0.5, 1.5
n_times = int((tmax - tmin) * sfreq)
times = np.linspace(tmin, tmax, n_times)

# ── Generate simulated epochs ──────────────────────────────
# Each trial: pink noise + alpha oscillation that desynchronises after t=0
epochs_data = np.zeros((n_trials, n_times))

for trial in range(n_trials):
    # Pink noise background
    white = rng.standard_normal(n_times)
    freqs_fft = np.fft.rfftfreq(n_times, d=1 / sfreq)
    freqs_fft[0] = 1
    pink = np.fft.irfft(
        np.fft.rfft(white) / np.sqrt(freqs_fft), n=n_times
    )
    pink = pink / pink.std()

    # Alpha oscillation with amplitude modulation
    # Strong before stimulus (t<0), suppressed after (t>0.2)
    alpha_amp = np.ones(n_times)
    suppress_idx = times > 0.2
    alpha_amp[suppress_idx] = 0.3  # 70% reduction
    # Gradual recovery
    recovery_idx = times > 1.0
    alpha_amp[recovery_idx] = 0.3 + 0.7 * (
        (times[recovery_idx] - 1.0) / (tmax - 1.0)
    )
    phase_jitter = rng.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi)
    alpha = alpha_amp * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times + phase_jitter)

    epochs_data[trial] = 2.0 * pink + 3.0 * alpha

# ── Wavelet convolution ───────────────────────────────────
freqs_analysis = np.arange(2, 35, 0.5)
n_freqs = len(freqs_analysis)
tfr_power = np.zeros((n_freqs, n_times))

for fi, freq in enumerate(freqs_analysis):
    # Create Morlet wavelet
    n_cycles = max(3, freq / 2.0)
    sigma = n_cycles / (2 * np.pi * freq)
    wavelet_nsamples = int(6 * sigma * sfreq)
    if wavelet_nsamples % 2 == 0:
        wavelet_nsamples += 1
    t_wav = np.arange(-wavelet_nsamples // 2,
                       wavelet_nsamples // 2 + 1) / sfreq
    wavelet = np.exp(2j * np.pi * freq * t_wav) * np.exp(
        -t_wav**2 / (2 * sigma**2)
    )
    wavelet = wavelet / np.sqrt(np.sum(np.abs(wavelet)**2))

    # Convolve each trial and average power
    trial_power = np.zeros((n_trials, n_times))
    for trial in range(n_trials):
        conv = np.convolve(epochs_data[trial], wavelet, mode="same")
        trial_power[trial] = np.abs(conv) ** 2

    tfr_power[fi] = trial_power.mean(axis=0)

# ── Baseline correction (percent change) ───────────────────
baseline_mask = (times >= -0.5) & (times <= 0)
baseline_power = tfr_power[:, baseline_mask].mean(axis=1, keepdims=True)
tfr_pct = (tfr_power - baseline_power) / baseline_power * 100

# ── Plot ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

im = ax.pcolormesh(
    times, freqs_analysis, tfr_pct,
    cmap="RdBu_r", vmin=-80, vmax=80, shading="auto"
)
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Frequency (Hz)")
ax.set_title("Time-frequency decomposition (Morlet wavelets, % change)")
ax.axvline(0, color="black", linestyle="--", linewidth=0.8,
           label="Stimulus onset")
ax.axhline(8, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.axhline(13, color="grey", linestyle=":", linewidth=0.5)
ax.legend(fontsize=9)

cbar = plt.colorbar(im, ax=ax, label="Power change (%)")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Time-frequency decomposition of simulated EEG. The map shows alpha (8-13 Hz) desynchronisation (power decrease, blue) starting around 200 ms after stimulus onset, followed by a gradual return to baseline. This pattern mimics the classic event-related desynchronisation seen in visual and motor tasks.




The map shows the simulated alpha desynchronisation clearly: the 8–13 Hz band shows a power decrease (blue) after stimulus onset at time 0, reaching its maximum suppression around 200–1000 ms. Power then begins to recover towards baseline after 1 second. Below and above the alpha band, there is no systematic change because our simulation only modulated alpha amplitude.
In real data, you would typically see more complex patterns: alpha desynchronisation accompanied by beta suppression before movement, theta increases during memory encoding, and possibly gamma bursts during perceptual processing.

title: Time-frequency decomposition
text:
Key takeaways

Time-frequency decomposition estimates power at each frequency and time point, revealing the temporal dynamics that PSD averages away.
Morlet wavelets are the most common method in EEG research. The n_cycles parameter controls the trade-off between temporal precision (fewer cycles) and frequency precision (more cycles).
The multitaper method uses multiple orthogonal tapers to reduce variance, producing smoother maps at the cost of some frequency resolution.
In MNE, use epochs.compute_tfr(method="morlet", ...) or epochs.compute_tfr(method="multitaper", ...). The returned object has built-in plot(), plot_topo(), and plot_joint() methods.
Baseline correction is necessary to remove the 1/f power scaling and express post-stimulus power relative to a pre-stimulus period. The "percent" mode is the most commonly reported.
ERSP (event-related spectral perturbation) is the term for the baseline-corrected, trial-averaged time-frequency map. It reveals event-related desynchronisation (ERD, power decrease) and event-related synchronisation (ERS, power increase).

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Computing metastability is the easy part. Interpreting the numbers is harder. What does it mean if a participant’s global metastability is 0.003? Is that high or low? What if one channel has a metastability of 0.01 and another has 0.001? And how much do your preprocessing choices (epoch length, frequency band, number of channels) affect these values?
This page provides practical guidance for interpreting metastability values, understanding what they tell you about brain dynamics, and reporting them properly in research.

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Computing metastability is the easy part. Interpreting the numbers is harder. What does it mean if a participant’s global metastability is 0.003? Is that high or low? What if one channel has a metastability of 0.01 and another has 0.001? And how much do your preprocessing choices (epoch length, frequency band, number of channels) affect these values?
This page provides practical guidance for interpreting metastability values, understanding what they tell you about brain dynamics, and reporting them properly in research.

title: Interpreting metastability values
section: The spectrum from order to disorder
text:
The spectrum from order to disorder
Metastability describes where a system falls on a spectrum between two extremes:

Low metastability: order and rigidity
At one end, \(\text{MS} \approx 0\). The system is locked into a single coordination pattern that never changes. Every brain region maintains the same role, the same community membership, the same participation strength, time point after time point.
This is like an orchestra where every musician plays exactly the same note forever. There is perfect order, but nothing interesting happens. The system cannot adapt, respond, or process new information.
In neural terms, low metastability corresponds to excessive synchronisation: all regions are locked in step, leaving no room for flexible reconfiguration. This is the pattern associated with pathological states like Parkinson’s disease (excessive beta synchrony) and certain types of epileptic activity.


Very high metastability: disorder and instability
At the other end, metastability is very high. The coordination pattern changes wildly from one time point to the next. There is no stable structure at all.
This is like an orchestra where every musician plays random notes with no coordination. There is no order, and the system cannot sustain any coherent function.
In neural terms, very high metastability could indicate noise-driven dynamics, where the phase alignment matrix fluctuates randomly rather than reflecting meaningful brain state transitions. This can happen with very short epochs, noisy recordings, or when the signal-to-noise ratio is low.


The “sweet spot”: moderate-high metastability
The interesting region is in between. Moderate-to-high metastability means the system transitions between different coordination states in a structured way. It dwells in one pattern for a while, then transitions to another, then another.
This is like an orchestra performing a symphony: the musicians coordinate in different patterns for each movement, maintaining coherence within each section while transitioning between sections. There is both structure (within a dwelling state) and flexibility (between states).
This middle ground is where the healthy brain is thought to operate. High enough metastability for flexibility, but not so high that the system is chaotic.

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
The criticality hypothesis
The idea that the brain operates at a “sweet spot” connects to a broader theoretical framework: the criticality hypothesis.
In physics, a system is at its critical point when it sits at the boundary between two phases (like water at exactly 100C, between liquid and gas). At the critical point, the system shows maximum fluctuations, long-range correlations, and sensitivity to small perturbations.
Applied to the brain, the criticality hypothesis proposes that healthy neural dynamics operate near the critical point between full synchrony (order) and full desynchrony (disorder). At this point:

Information transmission is maximised.
The system has the widest repertoire of possible states.
Small inputs can produce large, coordinated responses.
The system is flexible but not unstable.

Metastability is one signature of near-critical dynamics. A system at criticality shows fluctuations between more synchronised and less synchronised states, producing moderate-to-high metastability. A system pushed away from criticality (towards too much order or too much disorder) shows reduced metastability.
This is a theoretical framework, not a proven fact. But it provides useful intuition for interpreting metastability values: higher metastability (within a healthy range) suggests the brain is operating in a more flexible, near-critical regime.

title: Interpreting metastability values
section: What metastability tells you about Parkinson’s disease
text:
What metastability tells you about Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease is characterised by excessive beta-band synchronisation in the basal ganglia-cortical circuits. From a metastability perspective, this means:

The coordination pattern involving motor regions is abnormally stable (low metastability in beta).
The brain cannot easily transition away from this pattern.
Motor symptoms (bradykinesia, rigidity, freezing of gait) may reflect this inability to switch between coordination states.

Dopaminergic medication and deep brain stimulation both reduce pathological beta synchrony and may increase metastability, restoring some of the brain’s dynamic flexibility.
For Natalia’s project, the prediction is that:

Healthy controls will show the highest regional metastability (most flexible).
PD patients without Freezing of Gait will show reduced metastability (moderately rigid).
PD patients with Freezing of Gait will show the lowest metastability (most rigid), particularly in frontal and motor regions.

These are testable hypotheses. The actual values will depend on the frequency band, the specific channels, and the preprocessing pipeline.

title: Interpreting metastability values
section: Other conditions associated with altered metastability
text:
Other conditions associated with altered metastability

Disorders of consciousness
Patients in vegetative state or minimally conscious state show markedly reduced metastability compared to healthy controls. The brain is locked into a limited set of coordination patterns and cannot transition between them. The degree of metastability reduction correlates with the level of consciousness (Demertzi et al., 2019).


Epilepsy
Seizures are a dramatic example of pathological synchronisation: large populations of neurones fire in lockstep, producing the characteristic high-amplitude, rhythmic EEG patterns. During a seizure, metastability drops sharply as the brain is trapped in a single, highly synchronised state.
Between seizures, some epilepsy patients show altered metastability at rest, suggesting that their brains operate further from the critical point than healthy brains.


Ageing
Healthy ageing is associated with changes in metastability, though the direction depends on the frequency band and the brain region. Some studies report decreased metastability in older adults, particularly in frontal regions, which may relate to age-related declines in cognitive flexibility.


Psychiatric conditions
Schizophrenia, depression, and attention deficit disorders have all been linked to altered brain dynamics, though the metastability literature in these areas is still developing. The general pattern is that conditions involving cognitive rigidity tend to show reduced metastability, while conditions involving instability or disorganisation may show altered (not necessarily reduced) metastability patterns.

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Practical considerations

Epoch length
The length of the data epoch affects metastability estimates. Shorter epochs provide fewer time points over which to compute the variance, leading to noisier estimates. Very short epochs (under 10 seconds) may produce unreliable metastability values.
As a rule of thumb, use at least 30 seconds of clean data. For resting-state studies, 2-5 minutes is typical. If you have multiple epochs per participant, you can compute metastability within each epoch and then average, or concatenate epochs before computing (but be cautious about edge effects at concatenation points).


Frequency band
Metastability values are frequency-band specific. Beta-band metastability and alpha-band metastability can tell you different things about the same brain.
For Parkinson’s disease research, beta (13-30 Hz) is the primary band of interest because of the well-established pathological beta synchrony. But alpha (8-13 Hz) and theta (4-8 Hz) are also worth examining, as PD affects multiple frequency bands.
Always report which frequency band you analysed. Never compute metastability from broadband (unfiltered) data, because the instantaneous phase is not meaningful for broadband signals.


Number of channels
More channels generally give you a richer picture of regional metastability, but they also increase computational cost and the severity of multiple comparisons correction. With 16 channels, you need to correct for 16 comparisons. With 64 channels, you need to correct for 64.
There is no “correct” number of channels. It depends on your research question. If you are interested in broad regional differences (frontal vs parietal vs occipital), 16-32 channels may suffice. If you need fine spatial resolution, you need more.


Noise and artefacts
Noisy data inflates metastability artificially. If the phase estimates are noisy, the eigenvector fluctuates randomly, producing high variance that has nothing to do with brain dynamics.
This is why thorough preprocessing (filtering, artefact rejection, ICA) is important before computing metastability. A “clean” recording with moderate metastability is more informative than a noisy recording with high metastability.


Reference choice
The choice of EEG reference affects phase estimates and therefore metastability. Common references (average reference, linked mastoids, Cz) produce different phase relationships between channels. Always report your reference choice, and be cautious when comparing metastability values across studies that used different references.

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Guidelines for reporting metastability
When reporting metastability in a paper or thesis, include the following information:

Both global and regional metastability. Global metastability (variance of the Kuramoto order parameter) gives the overall picture. Regional metastability (variance of each eigenvector element) gives the spatial detail. Report both.
Frequency band. State the band (e.g., beta, 13-30 Hz) and the filter specifications (filter order, type, implementation).
Epoch length. How many seconds of data per participant? How were epochs selected?
Preprocessing steps. Filtering, artefact rejection, ICA, re-referencing. Any of these can affect the results.
Number of channels and their locations. Which montage? Which channels were included?
Sign convention for eigenvectors. Did you use the continuity fix? How did you initialise it?
Statistical tests and corrections. What test (ANOVA, permutation)? What correction for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni, FDR)? Applied across channels, across frequency bands, or both?

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Working example: comparing “healthy” and “rigid” networks
Let us simulate two networks with different coupling strengths and compare their metastability profiles.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from scipy.signal import hilbert, butter, filtfilt

np.random.seed(42)

def simulate_network_metastability(n_channels, n_timepoints, coupling_strength,
                                    freq=10, fs=256, noise_std=1.0):
    """Simulate a network and compute regional metastability.

    Parameters
    ----------
    n_channels : int
        Number of channels.
    n_timepoints : int
        Number of time points.
    coupling_strength : float
        How tightly coupled the oscillators are.
    freq : float
        Natural frequency in Hz.
    fs : int
        Sampling rate in Hz.
    noise_std : float
        Standard deviation of phase noise.

    Returns
    -------
    regional_ms : array of shape (n_channels,)
    v_dominant : array of shape (n_timepoints, n_channels)
    """
    dt = 1 / fs
    t = np.arange(n_timepoints) * dt

    # Simulate Kuramoto-like phases with all-to-all coupling
    phases = np.zeros((n_channels, n_timepoints))
    # Random initial phases
    phases[:, 0] = np.random.uniform(0, 2 * np.pi, n_channels)
    # Slightly different natural frequencies
    omegas = 2 * np.pi * (freq + np.random.uniform(-0.5, 0.5, n_channels))

    for tp in range(1, n_timepoints):
        mean_phase = np.angle(np.mean(np.exp(1j * phases[:, tp - 1])))
        for ch in range(n_channels):
            coupling_term = coupling_strength * np.sin(mean_phase - phases[ch, tp - 1])
            phases[ch, tp] = (phases[ch, tp - 1] +
                              omegas[ch] * dt +
                              coupling_term * dt +
                              noise_std * np.sqrt(dt) * np.random.randn())

    # Compute phase alignment matrix and dominant eigenvector
    v_dominant = np.zeros((n_timepoints, n_channels))
    for tp in range(n_timepoints):
        phi = phases[:, tp]
        phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
        A = np.cos(phase_diff)
        eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
        v_dominant[tp] = eigenvectors[:, -1]

    # Sign continuity fix
    if v_dominant[0, np.argmax(np.abs(v_dominant[0]))] < 0:
        v_dominant[0] *= -1
    for tp in range(1, n_timepoints):
        if np.dot(v_dominant[tp], v_dominant[tp - 1]) < 0:
            v_dominant[tp] *= -1

    regional_ms = np.var(v_dominant, axis=0)
    return regional_ms, v_dominant

# Simulate both networks
n_ch = 12
n_tp = 1000

ms_healthy, v_healthy = simulate_network_metastability(
    n_ch, n_tp, coupling_strength=2.0, noise_std=1.5
)
ms_rigid, v_rigid = simulate_network_metastability(
    n_ch, n_tp, coupling_strength=15.0, noise_std=0.5
)

# Plot
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(12, 7))
t = np.arange(n_tp) / 256

# Top left: healthy eigenvector dynamics
for ch in [0, 3, 6, 9]:
    axes[0, 0].plot(t, v_healthy[:, ch], linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.8, label=f"Ch{ch}")
axes[0, 0].set_title("'Healthy' network: eigenvector dynamics")
axes[0, 0].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
axes[0, 0].set_ylabel("v_k(t)")
axes[0, 0].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")

# Top right: rigid eigenvector dynamics
for ch in [0, 3, 6, 9]:
    axes[0, 1].plot(t, v_rigid[:, ch], linewidth=0.8, alpha=0.8, label=f"Ch{ch}")
axes[0, 1].set_title("'Rigid' network: eigenvector dynamics")
axes[0, 1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
axes[0, 1].set_ylabel("v_k(t)")
axes[0, 1].legend(fontsize=8, loc="upper right")

# Make y-axis limits the same for comparison
y_min = min(axes[0, 0].get_ylim()[0], axes[0, 1].get_ylim()[0])
y_max = max(axes[0, 0].get_ylim()[1], axes[0, 1].get_ylim()[1])
axes[0, 0].set_ylim(y_min, y_max)
axes[0, 1].set_ylim(y_min, y_max)

# Bottom: regional metastability comparison
x = np.arange(n_ch)
width = 0.35
axes[1, 0].bar(x - width/2, ms_healthy, width, label="Healthy", color="steelblue",
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
axes[1, 0].bar(x + width/2, ms_rigid, width, label="Rigid", color="indianred",
               edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
axes[1, 0].set_xlabel("Channel")
axes[1, 0].set_ylabel("Regional metastability")
axes[1, 0].set_title("Regional metastability by channel")
axes[1, 0].set_xticks(x)
axes[1, 0].set_xticklabels([f"Ch{i}" for i in range(n_ch)], fontsize=8)
axes[1, 0].legend()

# Bottom right: summary
axes[1, 1].bar(["Healthy\n(moderate coupling)", "Rigid\n(strong coupling)"],
               [np.mean(ms_healthy), np.mean(ms_rigid)],
               color=["steelblue", "indianred"], edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
axes[1, 1].set_ylabel("Mean metastability")
axes[1, 1].set_title("Global comparison")

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Healthy network - mean MS: {np.mean(ms_healthy):.6f}, "
      f"range: [{np.min(ms_healthy):.6f}, {np.max(ms_healthy):.6f}]")
print(f"Rigid network   - mean MS: {np.mean(ms_rigid):.6f}, "
      f"range: [{np.min(ms_rigid):.6f}, {np.max(ms_rigid):.6f}]")




Comparison of metastability between a ‘healthy’ network (moderate coupling, higher metastability) and a ‘rigid’ network (strong coupling, lower metastability). Left: eigenvector dynamics over time. Right: regional metastability bar chart.




Healthy network - mean MS: 0.071866, range: [0.057746, 0.089247]
Rigid network   - mean MS: 0.002436, range: [0.000042, 0.011992]


The “healthy” network (moderate coupling) shows higher metastability: the eigenvector elements fluctuate more because the network reconfigures over time. The “rigid” network (strong coupling) shows lower metastability: the oscillators are locked in step and the coordination pattern barely changes.
This is a simplified simulation, but it captures the core logic. In real EEG data, the differences between groups may be subtler and concentrated in specific channels or frequency bands.

title: Interpreting metastability values
text:
Key takeaways

Low metastability means rigidity: the brain is locked in one coordination pattern. This is associated with pathological states like PD.
Moderate-to-high metastability means flexibility: the brain transitions between different coordination states. This is associated with healthy function.
Very high metastability may indicate noise or instability rather than meaningful flexibility. Context and preprocessing quality matter.
The criticality hypothesis suggests the healthy brain operates near the boundary between order and disorder, where metastability is high.
Epoch length, frequency band, number of channels, and noise all affect metastability estimates. Always account for these in your analysis.
When reporting, include both global and regional metastability, the frequency band, epoch length, preprocessing steps, and statistical corrections.
Compare values within a study, not across studies with different methods. Absolute metastability values are not standardised.

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
The phase alignment matrix tells you how every pair of channels is related at a single moment in time. But an \(N \times N\) matrix is hard to interpret directly, especially when \(N\) is 16 or 32 or 64 channels. You need a way to summarise the dominant pattern of coordination across the entire network in a single, interpretable vector.
That is what eigendecomposition does. The dominant eigenvector of the phase alignment matrix captures the primary pattern of phase alignment at each time point. Tracking how this vector changes over time is the basis for computing regional metastability, the core measure in Natalia’s project.

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
The phase alignment matrix tells you how every pair of channels is related at a single moment in time. But an \(N \times N\) matrix is hard to interpret directly, especially when \(N\) is 16 or 32 or 64 channels. You need a way to summarise the dominant pattern of coordination across the entire network in a single, interpretable vector.
That is what eigendecomposition does. The dominant eigenvector of the phase alignment matrix captures the primary pattern of phase alignment at each time point. Tracking how this vector changes over time is the basis for computing regional metastability, the core measure in Natalia’s project.

title: The dominant eigenvector
section: What eigendecomposition does to the phase alignment matrix
text:
What eigendecomposition does to the phase alignment matrix
The phase alignment matrix \(A(t)\) at time \(t\) is a real, symmetric \(N \times N\) matrix with entries \(A_{ij}(t) = \cos(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))\). Because it is symmetric, it has \(N\) real eigenvalues \(\lambda_1 \leq \lambda_2 \leq \dots \leq \lambda_N\) and \(N\) corresponding orthogonal eigenvectors \(v_1, v_2, \dots, v_N\).
Eigendecomposition factorises the matrix as:
\[A(t) = \sum_{k=1}^{N} \lambda_k \, v_k \, v_k^\top\]
Each eigenvalue-eigenvector pair captures one “mode” of the matrix. The largest eigenvalue \(\lambda_N\) and its eigenvector \(v_N\) capture the strongest pattern of pairwise alignment. The second-largest pair captures the next strongest pattern that is orthogonal to the first, and so on.
In practice, the largest eigenvalue typically accounts for a substantial fraction of the total variance in \(A(t)\), meaning that the dominant eigenvector is a good summary of the whole matrix.

title: The dominant eigenvector
section: Why the largest eigenvalue’s eigenvector captures the dominant coordination pattern
text:
Why the largest eigenvalue’s eigenvector captures the dominant coordination pattern
The eigenvector associated with the largest eigenvalue is the direction in channel space along which the phase alignment matrix has the most “spread”. In concrete terms:

If all channels are perfectly in phase, the alignment matrix is all ones. It has one large eigenvalue (\(\lambda_N = N\)) with an eigenvector \(v_N = (1/\sqrt{N}, \dots, 1/\sqrt{N})\), and all other eigenvalues are zero.
If channels form two anti-phase groups, the dominant eigenvector has positive values for one group and negative values for the other.
If channels are completely desynchronised, the eigenvalues are spread out and the dominant eigenvector accounts for only a small fraction of the total variance.

The dominant eigenvector answers the question: “What is the main pattern of coordination at this moment?” It tells you which channels are working together and which are in opposing communities.

title: The dominant eigenvector
section: Interpreting the elements of the dominant eigenvector
text:
Interpreting the elements of the dominant eigenvector
Each element \(v_k(t)\) of the dominant eigenvector corresponds to one channel (brain region). Two properties matter:

Sign = community membership
Channels with the same sign (both positive or both negative) are in the same phase community: they are aligned with each other. Channels with opposite signs are in anti-phase communities: when one group is at its peak, the other is at its trough.
For example, if \(v(t) = (0.3, 0.4, 0.35, -0.25, -0.3, -0.28, \dots)\), then channels 1-3 form one community and channels 4-6 form another. The two communities are in anti-phase with each other.


Magnitude = participation strength
The absolute value \(|v_k(t)|\) tells you how strongly channel \(k\) participates in the dominant pattern. A channel with \(|v_k| = 0.45\) is a strong participant. A channel with \(|v_k| = 0.05\) is barely involved: it is not well aligned with either community.
This means the dominant eigenvector gives you a complete picture of network organisation at one moment: who belongs to which community, and how strongly each member participates.


A concrete interpretation
Imagine you have 16 EEG channels and the dominant eigenvector at time \(t\) is:



Channel
Region

Fp2

C4

-0.38

O2

This tells you that frontal regions are synchronised with each other but in anti-phase with central regions. Occipital regions are not strongly involved in this particular pattern. One second later, the eigenvector might look completely different, with different communities and different participation levels.

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
The sign ambiguity problem
Eigenvectors have a fundamental ambiguity: if \(v\) is an eigenvector, then so is \(-v\). Multiplying an eigenvector by \(-1\) does not change its mathematical meaning; it just swaps which community is “positive” and which is “negative”.
This is not a problem at a single time point, because the community structure is the same regardless of the overall sign. But when you track \(v(t)\) over time, a random sign flip between adjacent time points creates a spurious jump that has nothing to do with real changes in brain dynamics.

The continuity fix
The standard solution is simple. At each time point \(t\), compute the inner product between \(v(t)\) and \(v(t-1)\):
\[\text{if} \quad v(t) \cdot v(t-1) < 0, \quad \text{flip:} \quad v(t) \leftarrow -v(t)\]
If the inner product is negative, the eigenvector has flipped sign relative to the previous time point, so you multiply it by \(-1\) to restore continuity. This ensures that the time series of eigenvector elements changes smoothly when the underlying coordination pattern changes smoothly.
You must initialise the process by choosing a sign convention for the first time point. A common choice is to ensure that the element with the largest absolute value is positive.
# Sign continuity fix
for t in range(1, n_timepoints):
    if np.dot(v_dominant[t], v_dominant[t - 1]) < 0:
        v_dominant[t] *= -1

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
Tracking v(t) over time
Once you have the sign-corrected dominant eigenvector at each time point, you have a time series \(v_k(t)\) for each channel \(k\). This time series describes how channel \(k\)’s role in the network changes over time.

Stable v(t) = rigid system
If \(v_k(t)\) stays approximately constant, then channel \(k\) always plays the same role in the dominant coordination pattern. It is always in the same community, with the same participation strength. The network configuration is rigid.
At the network level, if the entire vector \(v(t)\) is nearly constant, the brain is stuck in one coordination pattern. This is what we expect to see in conditions characterised by pathological rigidity, such as Parkinson’s disease with excessive beta synchrony.


Variable v(t) = flexible system
If \(v_k(t)\) fluctuates, then channel \(k\) switches between communities, or its participation strength changes over time. The network is reconfiguring, exploring different coordination patterns.
At the network level, variable \(v(t)\) means the brain transitions between different states. This flexibility is associated with healthy brain function, cognitive adaptability, and the ability to respond to changing demands.

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
Connection to metastability
The variability of \(v_k(t)\) over time is exactly what regional metastability measures:
\[\text{MS}_k = \text{Var}_t\!\big(v_k(t)\big)\]
A channel with high \(\text{MS}_k\) has a highly variable eigenvector element: it frequently changes its community membership or participation strength. A channel with low \(\text{MS}_k\) is locked into a fixed role.
This provides a spatial map of flexibility across the brain. You can ask: which regions are most flexible? Which are most rigid? Do patients and controls differ in specific regions?

title: The dominant eigenvector
section: Relationship to PCA and dimensionality reduction
text:
Relationship to PCA and dimensionality reduction
If you are familiar with Principal Component Analysis (PCA), eigendecomposition of the phase alignment matrix will feel familiar. PCA decomposes a covariance matrix into eigenvectors (principal components) that capture the main directions of variance. The dominant eigenvector of the phase alignment matrix serves a similar role: it captures the main pattern of coordination.
The differences are:

PCA operates on a covariance matrix computed over time (each entry summarises a time-averaged relationship). The phase alignment matrix is computed at a single time point (each entry is an instantaneous phase relationship).
PCA gives you static components. Eigendecomposition of \(A(t)\) gives you time-varying components.
In PCA, the first component explains the most variance. Here, the dominant eigenvector captures the strongest pattern of phase alignment.

The key conceptual link: both methods use the eigenvector of a matrix to find the most important pattern in a high-dimensional dataset. If you understand one, the other is a short step away.

title: The dominant eigenvector
section: Working example: eigendecomposition and eigenvector dynamics
text:
Working example: eigendecomposition and eigenvector dynamics
Let us build a phase alignment matrix from simulated phases, compute its eigendecomposition, and visualise the eigenvector. Then we will track how the eigenvector changes over time.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

np.random.seed(42)

# Parameters
n_channels = 12
n_timepoints = 500
fs = 256
freq = 10  # Hz

# Simulate phases with community structure
# Channels 0-5: community A (coupled together)
# Channels 6-11: community B (coupled together, anti-phase with A)
t = np.arange(n_timepoints) / fs

# Base phase that advances at 10 Hz
base_phase = 2 * np.pi * freq * t

# Generate phases with coupling
phases = np.zeros((n_channels, n_timepoints))
for ch in range(n_channels):
    if ch < 6:
        # Community A: base phase + small noise
        phases[ch] = base_phase + 0.3 * np.cumsum(np.random.randn(n_timepoints)) / fs
    else:
        # Community B: base phase + pi (anti-phase) + small noise
        phases[ch] = base_phase + np.pi + 0.3 * np.cumsum(np.random.randn(n_timepoints)) / fs

    # Add time-varying perturbation to make it dynamic
    phases[ch] += 0.5 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 0.2 * t + ch * 0.5)

# Compute phase alignment matrix and dominant eigenvector at each time point
v_dominant = np.zeros((n_timepoints, n_channels))

for tp in range(n_timepoints):
    # Build phase alignment matrix
    phi = phases[:, tp]
    phase_diff = phi[:, None] - phi[None, :]
    A = np.cos(phase_diff)

    # Eigendecomposition
    eigenvalues, eigenvectors = np.linalg.eigh(A)
    v = eigenvectors[:, -1]  # dominant eigenvector

    v_dominant[tp] = v

# Sign continuity fix
for tp in range(1, n_timepoints):
    if np.dot(v_dominant[tp], v_dominant[tp - 1]) < 0:
        v_dominant[tp] *= -1

# Ensure first eigenvector has its largest element positive
if v_dominant[0, np.argmax(np.abs(v_dominant[0]))] < 0:
    v_dominant[0] *= -1

# Re-run sign fix after initialisation
for tp in range(1, n_timepoints):
    if np.dot(v_dominant[tp], v_dominant[tp - 1]) < 0:
        v_dominant[tp] *= -1

# --- Plot ---
fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 1, figsize=(10, 7), gridspec_kw={"height_ratios": [1, 1.5]})

# Top: bar chart of dominant eigenvector at t=0
colours = ["steelblue" if v > 0 else "indianred" for v in v_dominant[0]]
axes[0].bar(range(n_channels), v_dominant[0], color=colours, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_xlabel("Channel")
axes[0].set_ylabel("Eigenvector element")
axes[0].set_title("Dominant eigenvector at t = 0")
axes[0].axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)
axes[0].set_xticks(range(n_channels))
axes[0].set_xticklabels([f"Ch{i}" for i in range(n_channels)], fontsize=8)

# Bottom: eigenvector elements over time for 4 channels
selected = [0, 3, 6, 9]
labels = [f"Ch{i} (community {'A' if i < 6 else 'B'})" for i in selected]
colours_line = ["steelblue", "cornflowerblue", "indianred", "salmon"]

for i, ch in enumerate(selected):
    axes[1].plot(t, v_dominant[:, ch], label=labels[i], color=colours_line[i], linewidth=1.2)

axes[1].set_xlabel("Time (s)")
axes[1].set_ylabel("Eigenvector element v_k(t)")
axes[1].set_title("Eigenvector dynamics over time")
axes[1].legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=9)
axes[1].axhline(0, color="grey", linewidth=0.5)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()




Top: the dominant eigenvector at a single time point, showing two communities (positive and negative values). Bottom: eigenvector elements over time for four selected channels, showing how their roles in the network change.




In the top panel, you can see the community structure: channels 0-5 have positive eigenvector values (community A) and channels 6-11 have negative values (community B). The bar heights show participation strength.
In the bottom panel, you can see how the eigenvector elements change over time. Community A channels (blue lines) stay positive and community B channels (red lines) stay negative, but the magnitudes fluctuate. The variance of each channel’s time series is its regional metastability.

# Compute regional metastability
regional_ms = np.var(v_dominant, axis=0)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4))
colours_bar = ["steelblue" if i < 6 else "indianred" for i in range(n_channels)]
ax.bar(range(n_channels), regional_ms, color=colours_bar, edgecolor="white", linewidth=0.5)
ax.set_xlabel("Channel")
ax.set_ylabel("Metastability (variance of v_k)")
ax.set_title("Regional metastability")
ax.set_xticks(range(n_channels))
ax.set_xticklabels([f"Ch{i}" for i in range(n_channels)], fontsize=8)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

print(f"Global metastability (mean across channels): {np.mean(regional_ms):.6f}")
print(f"Min regional metastability: {np.min(regional_ms):.6f} (Ch{np.argmin(regional_ms)})")
print(f"Max regional metastability: {np.max(regional_ms):.6f} (Ch{np.argmax(regional_ms)})")




Regional metastability for each channel, computed as the variance of the dominant eigenvector element over time. All channels show similar metastability because the simulation uses uniform coupling within each community.




Global metastability (mean across channels): 0.000156
Min regional metastability: 0.000082 (Ch7)
Max regional metastability: 0.000227 (Ch2)

title: The dominant eigenvector
text:
Key takeaways

Eigendecomposition of the phase alignment matrix extracts the dominant pattern of coordination at each time point.
The dominant eigenvector (associated with the largest eigenvalue) summarises which channels are aligned and which are in anti-phase.
Each element’s sign indicates community membership; its magnitude indicates participation strength.
The sign ambiguity (eigenvectors can flip sign arbitrarily) must be fixed using a continuity check: flip \(v(t)\) if \(v(t) \cdot v(t-1) < 0\).
Tracking \(v_k(t)\) over time reveals whether a region’s role is stable (low metastability, rigid) or variable (high metastability, flexible).
Regional metastability is simply \(\text{Var}_t(v_k(t))\): the variance of the eigenvector element over time.
The approach is conceptually similar to PCA, but applied to instantaneous (not time-averaged) coordination matrices.

title: Automated artifact rejection with autoreject
text:
The standard approach to epoch rejection is to set a single amplitude threshold (say, 100 microvolts) and drop any epoch where any channel exceeds it. This works, but it has two problems.
First, the threshold is the same for all channels. A frontal channel near the eyes will naturally have larger voltage swings than an occipital channel, so a single threshold is either too strict for some channels (dropping clean epochs) or too lenient for others (keeping contaminated ones).
Second, the threshold is the same for all recordings. What counts as “too large” depends on the participant, the electrode impedances, the recording setup, and even the time of day. A threshold that works well for one participant may drop half the epochs for another.
The autoreject package (Jas et al., 2017) addresses both problems by learning channel-specific thresholds from the data itself. It tries many different thresholds for each channel, evaluates how well each one separates clean from noisy epochs, and picks the combination that produces the best overall result.

text:
