When we study the brain, we usually ask people to do something: respond to a stimulus, memorise a list, press a button. The brain’s response to these tasks tells us about the neural processes involved. But the brain is also active when you are not doing anything in particular. Even with your eyes closed and your mind wandering, billions of neurones are firing in coordinated patterns.
Resting-state EEG measures this spontaneous activity. It turns out that these “idle” patterns are not random. They reflect the brain’s intrinsic organisation, its default wiring, and its capacity for flexible coordination. For clinical populations (ageing, Parkinson’s disease, disorders of consciousness), resting-state measures can reveal dysfunction that task-based paradigms might miss, because patients may struggle with the tasks themselves.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
What resting-state EEG is
A resting-state EEG recording is collected while the participant sits quietly without performing any specific task. The participant is typically seated in a comfortable chair in a quiet, dimly lit room, with EEG electrodes placed on the scalp.
There are two standard protocols:

Eyes closed (EC)
The participant closes their eyes for a fixed period (typically 2–5 minutes). This is the simpler condition and produces the largest alpha oscillations. With the eyes closed, the visual cortex is not processing external input, and alpha oscillations (8–13 Hz) in occipital and parietal regions become prominent.
Eyes-closed resting state is easy for participants and produces reliable, high-amplitude signals. It is used in most clinical EEG protocols and is the standard baseline for many research studies.


Eyes open (EO)
The participant keeps their eyes open, usually fixating on a small cross or dot on a screen. This suppresses alpha oscillations (a phenomenon called alpha suppression or alpha blocking) and produces a different spectral profile with more beta activity.
Eyes-open resting state is more representative of waking brain activity, since we spend most of our day with eyes open. But it introduces more noise sources: eye movements, blinks, and visual processing of the fixation point and surrounding environment.


Combined protocol
Many studies record both conditions in alternating blocks (e.g., 2 minutes eyes closed, 2 minutes eyes open, repeated 2–3 times). This allows measurement of alpha reactivity, the change in alpha power between EC and EO conditions, which is itself a clinically informative variable.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
Why resting-state EEG is used

Minimising task confounds
Task-based paradigms require participants to understand instructions, stay motivated, and perform at a certain level. These requirements introduce confounds: differences between groups might reflect differences in task performance rather than differences in brain function.
Resting-state recordings avoid this problem. Everyone can sit still with their eyes closed. This makes resting-state EEG particularly valuable for:

Clinical populations who may have difficulty with cognitive tasks (e.g., patients with severe Parkinson’s disease, dementia, or disorders of consciousness).
Cross-group comparisons where groups differ in age, education, or cognitive ability.
Longitudinal studies where you want a stable baseline that is not affected by learning effects or changing task strategies.



Capturing intrinsic brain dynamics
The brain’s resting-state activity is not “noise” waiting for a task to impose structure. It reflects the brain’s intrinsic functional organisation: the set of networks that are active by default and that provide the scaffolding for task-related activity.
In fMRI research, resting-state recordings led to the discovery of the default mode network and other resting-state networks. EEG captures similar information, but with much higher temporal resolution (milliseconds rather than seconds). This makes it better suited for studying the dynamics of brain coordination, including the rapid transitions between states that metastability measures capture.


Practical advantages
Resting-state EEG is also simpler to collect than task-based EEG:

No stimulus presentation system is needed.
No response devices are required.
Recording sessions are shorter (5–10 minutes vs 30–60 minutes for complex tasks).
Data analysis does not require event-locked averaging or trial sorting.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
What resting-state EEG reveals

Spectral power
The most basic analysis of resting-state EEG is the power spectrum: how much energy is present at each frequency. Healthy adults show characteristic spectral features:

A 1/f background: power decreases with increasing frequency, reflecting the scale-free dynamics of cortical networks.
An alpha peak at 8–13 Hz, most prominent in posterior regions with eyes closed. The peak frequency and amplitude vary with age, arousal, and neurological condition.
A beta peak at 13–30 Hz, more prominent with eyes open or during alert wakefulness.

Changes in spectral power are associated with many clinical conditions. Alzheimer’s disease is characterised by a slowing of the alpha peak (shifting to lower frequencies) and increased theta power. Parkinson’s disease shows increased beta power in motor regions. Depression has been linked to frontal alpha asymmetry.


Alpha reactivity
The ratio of alpha power in the eyes-closed condition to the eyes-open condition is called alpha reactivity:
\[\text{Alpha reactivity} = \frac{\text{Alpha power (EC)}}{\text{Alpha power (EO)}}\]
or sometimes expressed as a percentage change. In healthy adults, closing the eyes approximately doubles the occipital alpha power.
Reduced alpha reactivity has been reported in Alzheimer’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, and disorders of consciousness. It suggests that the brain’s ability to modulate its intrinsic oscillatory activity is impaired.


Functional connectivity
Beyond spectral power, resting-state EEG can reveal the functional connectivity between brain regions. Phase-based measures (PLV, coherence) computed during rest show reproducible spatial patterns that correspond to known brain networks.
These connectivity patterns are not static: they change over time, with the brain transitioning between different coordination states. Metastability analysis captures this temporal structure and quantifies how flexibly the brain explores different states.

title: Resting-state EEG
section: The default mode network in EEG
text:
The default mode network in EEG
The default mode network (DMN) was first identified in fMRI as a set of brain regions (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate, precuneus, lateral temporal regions) that are more active during rest than during tasks. It is associated with self-referential thinking, mind wandering, and memory retrieval.
EEG cannot measure the DMN as directly as fMRI, because its spatial resolution is lower and it is limited to the cortical surface. However, EEG studies have found correlates of the DMN:

Alpha and beta oscillations in midline and posterior regions show patterns consistent with DMN activity.
Source-localised EEG (using inverse solutions like eLORETA) can estimate activity in DMN regions and compute connectivity between them.
EEG-fMRI studies have confirmed that alpha oscillations correlate with DMN activity measured in fMRI.

For Natalia’s project, the DMN is relevant because resting-state dynamics are partly driven by DMN activity. Altered DMN connectivity has been reported in Parkinson’s disease, and metastability analysis may reveal dynamic aspects of DMN function that static connectivity measures miss.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
Relevance for clinical populations

Ageing
Normal ageing is associated with:

A slowing of the alpha peak frequency (from around 10 Hz in young adults to 8–9 Hz in older adults).
Reduced alpha power and alpha reactivity.
Increased theta power.
Altered connectivity patterns, with some connections strengthening and others weakening.

These changes are gradual and variable across individuals. Resting-state EEG can track them longitudinally and may help distinguish normal ageing from early neurodegeneration.


Parkinson’s disease
Parkinson’s disease shows several resting-state EEG signatures:

Increased theta power in frontal and central regions, especially in patients with cognitive impairment.
Slowing of the alpha peak, similar to ageing but more pronounced.
Altered beta connectivity: excessive beta synchronisation in motor networks, which may reflect the pathological rigidity of the motor system.
Reduced metastability: preliminary evidence suggests that the brain’s dynamic flexibility is reduced in PD, particularly in motor-related regions.

For Natalia’s project, resting-state EEG from PD patients (both with and without Freezing of Gait) will be compared to healthy controls. The key question is whether metastability, measured from resting-state alpha or beta oscillations, differs between these groups and relates to the severity of motor symptoms.


Disorders of consciousness
In patients with severe brain injury who are in a vegetative state or minimally conscious state, resting-state EEG is one of the few tools available for assessing brain function. These patients cannot perform tasks, so resting-state measures provide the only window into their brain dynamics.
Reduced spectral complexity, lower alpha power, and decreased connectivity have been reported in patients with disorders of consciousness, with some measures showing correlation with the level of awareness.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
Practical considerations for resting-state recordings
Recording good resting-state EEG requires attention to several practical details:

Duration: at least 5 minutes per condition (EC and EO). Longer is better for connectivity and metastability analyses, which need enough data to estimate temporal variability reliably. Ten minutes is common in research protocols.
Vigilance: participants may become drowsy during prolonged eyes-closed recordings, especially older adults and patients. Drowsiness changes the spectral profile (increased theta, decreased alpha) and should be monitored. Some protocols include periodic checks (“Are you still awake?”).
Instruction wording: tell participants to relax and let their mind wander, but not to fall asleep. For eyes open, provide a fixation point to reduce eye movements.
Environmental control: minimise auditory and visual distractions. A quiet, dimly lit room is standard.
Electrode impedance: check impedances before recording. High impedance channels introduce noise that is particularly problematic in resting-state analysis because there are no events to average across.

title: Resting-state EEG
text:
Key takeaways

Resting-state EEG records the brain’s spontaneous activity while the participant sits quietly. It captures intrinsic brain dynamics without the confounds of task performance.
The two standard conditions are eyes closed (EC), which produces strong alpha oscillations, and eyes open (EO), which suppresses alpha. Both are typically recorded for 2–5 minutes each.
Alpha reactivity (the change in alpha power between EC and EO) is a clinically informative measure that is reduced in several neurological conditions.
Resting-state EEG reveals the brain’s intrinsic functional organisation through spectral power, functional connectivity, and dynamic coordination patterns.
For clinical populations, resting-state measures are especially valuable because they do not require task performance. This makes them suitable for patients with Parkinson’s disease, cognitive impairment, or disorders of consciousness.
Metastability analysis of resting-state EEG can quantify the brain’s dynamic flexibility, providing information that static measures of power or connectivity do not capture.
Practical considerations include recording duration (at least 5 minutes per condition), monitoring vigilance, providing clear instructions, and controlling the recording environment.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Filtering removes noise based on frequency: you can get rid of slow drifts and high-frequency muscle artifact because they occupy different frequency bands than the brain signals you care about. But some artifacts sit right on top of the frequencies of interest. Eye blinks produce large deflections that overlap with delta and theta frequencies. Heartbeat artifacts show up across a broad range. Horizontal eye movements contaminate frontal channels in the alpha and beta bands.
ICA separates these artifacts from brain activity based on their statistical independence, not their frequency. It works even when artifacts and brain signals share the same frequencies, which makes it one of the most powerful tools in the EEG preprocessing pipeline.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Filtering removes noise based on frequency: you can get rid of slow drifts and high-frequency muscle artifact because they occupy different frequency bands than the brain signals you care about. But some artifacts sit right on top of the frequencies of interest. Eye blinks produce large deflections that overlap with delta and theta frequencies. Heartbeat artifacts show up across a broad range. Horizontal eye movements contaminate frontal channels in the alpha and beta bands.
ICA separates these artifacts from brain activity based on their statistical independence, not their frequency. It works even when artifacts and brain signals share the same frequencies, which makes it one of the most powerful tools in the EEG preprocessing pipeline.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
The cocktail party problem
The classic analogy for ICA is the cocktail party problem. Imagine you are at a party with three people speaking at the same time. You have three microphones placed around the room. Each microphone picks up a different mixture of the three voices, depending on its distance from each speaker.
Your EEG electrodes are like the microphones. Each channel records a mixture of signals from different brain sources and artifacts. ICA tries to “unmix” these signals, recovering the original sources from the mixtures.
Formally, we assume that the recorded data \(\mathbf{x}(t)\) is a linear mixture of independent source signals \(\mathbf{s}(t)\):
\[\mathbf{x}(t) = \mathbf{A} \, \mathbf{s}(t)\]
where \(\mathbf{A}\) is the mixing matrix. ICA estimates the unmixing matrix \(\mathbf{W} = \mathbf{A}^{-1}\) so that:
\[\mathbf{s}(t) = \mathbf{W} \, \mathbf{x}(t)\]
The recovered sources \(\mathbf{s}(t)\) are the independent components. Each component has a time course (how it varies over time) and a spatial pattern (how it projects onto the scalp, given by the corresponding column of \(\mathbf{A}\)).

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Key assumptions
ICA relies on two assumptions:

Statistical independence: the source signals are independent of each other. Brain activity in different cortical patches and artifact sources (blinks, heartbeat, muscle) are generated by different physiological mechanisms, so this assumption is generally reasonable.
Linear mixing: each electrode records a weighted sum of the sources. This is a simplification (volume conduction is not perfectly linear), but it works well enough for scalp EEG.

There is also a mathematical requirement: at most one source can be Gaussian (normally distributed). Since EEG sources and most artifacts are non-Gaussian (they have skewed or heavy-tailed distributions), this requirement is usually satisfied.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
FastICA vs Infomax
Two ICA algorithms are commonly used in EEG:

FastICA
FastICA (Hyvarinen, 1999) finds independent components by maximising negentropy, a measure of how far a signal’s distribution is from Gaussian. It is fast, converges in few iterations, and is the default in many software packages.
Pros: fast computation, well understood mathematically. Cons: results can vary slightly between runs (sensitive to initialisation), and it may not separate all sources as cleanly as Infomax for EEG data.


Infomax
Infomax (Bell and Sejnowski, 1995) finds independent components by maximising the information transfer through a neural network model. The extended version (Lee et al., 1999) can handle both sub-Gaussian and super-Gaussian sources.
Pros: more stable results across runs, generally considered the gold standard for EEG. Cons: slower than FastICA, especially with many channels.
MNE-Python supports both algorithms through its mne.preprocessing.ICA class. The default is FastICA, but you can switch to Infomax by setting method="infomax". For research analysis, Infomax (or its extended variant, method="infomax" with fit_params=dict(extended=True)) is the safer choice.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
section: How to choose the number of components
text:
How to choose the number of components
ICA decomposes the data into as many components as there are channels (if you have 64 channels, you get 64 components). But you can ask for fewer components by setting n_components to a smaller number.
There are a few approaches:

Use all components: set n_components = n_channels. This gives ICA the most freedom to separate sources. It is the default and usually the best choice when you have clean data with no rank deficiencies.
Match the data rank: if you have already removed bad channels and re-referenced to average, the data rank is reduced by at least one. Setting n_components to the data rank avoids numerical problems. MNE can detect this automatically.
Use fewer components: setting n_components to, say, 25 when you have 64 channels means ICA only extracts the 25 “most independent” components. This can speed up computation, but you risk missing some artifact sources.

A practical guideline: start with the data rank as your number of components. If ICA has trouble converging or produces unstable results, try reducing by a few.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Identifying artifact components
After running ICA, you have a set of components. Some represent brain activity, and others represent artifacts. The task is to identify which is which, so you can remove the artifacts and keep the brain signals.

Blink components
Eye blinks produce a characteristic pattern:

Spatial pattern (topography): strong frontal projection, centred around Fp1 and Fp2, with a symmetric left-right distribution. This is the most reliable identifier.
Time course: occasional large deflections lasting about 200–400 ms, with long quiet periods between them.
Spectrum: dominated by low frequencies (below 5 Hz).



Eye movement components
Horizontal eye movements have a distinctive left-right asymmetry in the topography: one side of the frontal scalp is positive while the other is negative. Vertical eye movements look similar to blinks but are smaller and more sustained.


Muscle components
Muscle artifact (from jaw clenching, neck tension, or scalp muscles) shows:

Topography: peripheral, often concentrated at temporal or frontal electrodes.
Spectrum: dominated by high frequencies (above 20 Hz), with a broad spectral bump rather than a clear peak.
Time course: either sustained (tonic contraction) or burst-like (phasic activity).



Heartbeat components
The cardiac artifact has a regular time course matching the heart rate (roughly once per second). Its topography varies but often has a broad, diffuse pattern.


Automated detection
MNE-Python provides automated methods to identify artifact components:

ica.find_bads_eog(): correlates components with EOG (eye) channels to find blinks and eye movements.
ica.find_bads_ecg(): correlates components with ECG (heart) channels to find cardiac artifacts.

These methods work well when you have dedicated EOG and ECG channels. If you do not, you can use frontal EEG channels as proxies for EOG.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
section: Removing components and reconstructing clean data
text:
Removing components and reconstructing clean data
Once you have identified the artifact components, removing them is a simple matrix operation. ICA reconstructs the data using only the non-artifact components:
\[\mathbf{x}_{\text{clean}}(t) = \mathbf{A}_{\text{brain}} \, \mathbf{s}_{\text{brain}}(t)\]
In MNE, you mark artifact components by adding their indices to ica.exclude, then call ica.apply() to reconstruct the cleaned data.
A word of caution: each component you remove also removes some brain signal, because the separation is never perfect. Remove only components you are confident are artifacts. If you are unsure about a component, it is usually better to keep it.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Working example
The code below simulates multi-channel data containing brain-like oscillations, an eye-blink artifact, and noise. It runs ICA, identifies the blink component, and reconstructs clean data.

import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from sklearn.decomposition import FastICA

rng = np.random.default_rng(42)

# ── Simulation parameters ──────────────────────────────────────
n_channels = 8
sfreq = 256
duration = 10
n_samples = sfreq * duration
times = np.arange(n_samples) / sfreq

channel_names = ["Fp1", "Fp2", "F3", "F4", "C3", "C4", "O1", "O2"]

# ── Create source signals ─────────────────────────────────────
# Source 1: Alpha oscillation (brain)
alpha_source = np.sin(2 * np.pi * 10 * times)
alpha_source += 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# Source 2: Theta oscillation (brain)
theta_source = 0.8 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * 6 * times + 0.5)
theta_source += 0.2 * rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# Source 3: Eye blink artifact
blink_source = np.zeros(n_samples)
blink_times = [1.2, 3.5, 5.1, 6.8, 8.3, 9.7]  # blinks at these times
for bt in blink_times:
    blink_idx = int(bt * sfreq)
    blink_width = int(0.15 * sfreq)  # 150 ms blink duration
    if blink_idx + blink_width < n_samples:
        t_blink = np.arange(blink_width) / sfreq
        blink_shape = np.sin(np.pi * t_blink / (blink_width / sfreq))
        blink_source[blink_idx:blink_idx + blink_width] = 5 * blink_shape

# Source 4: Background noise
noise_source = rng.standard_normal(n_samples)

# ── Mixing matrix (how sources project to channels) ───────────
# Rows = channels, columns = sources
# Blink artifact projects strongly to frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2)
mixing = np.array([
    [0.5, 0.3, 1.0, 0.4],   # Fp1: strong blink
    [0.5, 0.3, 0.9, 0.4],   # Fp2: strong blink
    [0.7, 0.5, 0.3, 0.3],   # F3: moderate blink
    [0.7, 0.5, 0.2, 0.3],   # F4: moderate blink
    [0.9, 0.4, 0.05, 0.3],  # C3: weak blink
    [0.9, 0.4, 0.05, 0.3],  # C4: weak blink
    [1.0, 0.2, 0.02, 0.2],  # O1: almost no blink
    [1.0, 0.2, 0.02, 0.2],  # O2: almost no blink
])

sources = np.vstack([alpha_source, theta_source,
                      blink_source, noise_source])

# ── Mix the sources into channel data ─────────────────────────
data = mixing @ sources

# Scale to realistic amplitudes
data *= 30e-6 / data.std()

print(f"Data shape: {data.shape} ({n_channels} channels x {n_samples} samples)")

# ── Run ICA ───────────────────────────────────────────────────
ica = FastICA(n_components=4, random_state=42, max_iter=1000)
components = ica.fit_transform(data.T).T  # shape: (n_components, n_samples)
unmixing = ica.components_                 # unmixing matrix W
ica_mixing = ica.mixing_                   # estimated mixing matrix A

print(f"Extracted {components.shape[0]} independent components")

# ── Identify the blink component ──────────────────────────────
# The blink component should have the largest projection to frontal
# channels (Fp1, Fp2 = indices 0, 1)
frontal_loading = np.abs(ica_mixing[:2, :]).mean(axis=0)
blink_component = np.argmax(frontal_loading)
print(f"Blink component identified: IC {blink_component} "
      f"(frontal loading = {frontal_loading[blink_component]:.4f})")

# ── Reconstruct clean data (exclude blink component) ─────────
clean_components = components.copy()
clean_components[blink_component] = 0  # zero out the blink component
data_clean = ica_mixing @ clean_components

# ── Visualisation ─────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(13, 9))

# Panel 1: Original data (two frontal channels)
ax = axes[0]
offset = 0
for i, ch in enumerate([0, 1, 6, 7]):  # Fp1, Fp2, O1, O2
    trace = data[ch] / np.max(np.abs(data)) + offset
    ax.plot(times, trace, linewidth=0.5, label=channel_names[ch])
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Original data (with blink artifact)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

# Panel 2: ICA components
ax = axes[1]
offset = 0
for i in range(4):
    trace = components[i] / np.max(np.abs(components)) + offset
    colour = "#e74c3c" if i == blink_component else "#2c3e50"
    lw = 1.0 if i == blink_component else 0.5
    label = f"IC {i}" + (" (blink)" if i == blink_component else "")
    ax.plot(times, trace, linewidth=lw, color=colour, label=label)
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Independent components")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

# Panel 3: Cleaned data
ax = axes[2]
offset = 0
for i, ch in enumerate([0, 1, 6, 7]):
    trace = data_clean[ch] / np.max(np.abs(data_clean)) + offset
    ax.plot(times, trace, linewidth=0.5, label=channel_names[ch])
    offset -= 1.5
ax.set_xlabel("Time (s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Amplitude (a.u.)")
ax.set_title("Cleaned data (blink component removed)")
ax.legend(loc="upper right", fontsize=8, ncol=4)
ax.set_xlim(0, duration)

plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()

Data shape: (8, 2560) (8 channels x 2560 samples)
Extracted 4 independent components
Blink component identified: IC 3 (frontal loading = 0.0000)





ICA decomposition of simulated EEG. The blink artifact (Component 0) is identified by its large frontal projection and removed. The cleaned signal no longer shows the blink deflections.




In the top panel, you can see the large blink deflections in the frontal channels (Fp1, Fp2) while the occipital channels (O1, O2) are barely affected. The middle panel shows the four independent components: ICA successfully isolates the blink artifact into a single component (highlighted in red), with its characteristic sharp, intermittent waveform. The bottom panel shows the reconstructed data after removing the blink component. The frontal channels are now free of blink artifacts, while the underlying brain oscillations are preserved.

title: Independent Component Analysis (ICA)
text:
Key takeaways

ICA separates mixed signals into statistically independent sources. For EEG, this means separating brain activity from artifacts like blinks, eye movements, muscle tension, and heartbeat.
The method assumes that the sources are statistically independent and that the mixing is linear. Both assumptions hold reasonably well for scalp EEG.
Infomax is the recommended algorithm for EEG because it produces stable, reproducible results. FastICA is faster but can vary between runs.
Set the number of components to match the data rank (number of channels minus any rank reductions from re-referencing or bad channel removal).
Identify artifact components by inspecting their topography (spatial pattern), time course, and spectrum. Blinks have a strong frontal projection and intermittent large deflections. Muscle artifacts have peripheral topography and high-frequency spectra.
Remove only components you are confident are artifacts. Each removed component takes some brain signal with it, so conservative removal is preferable to aggressive cleaning.
MNE-Python’s ica.find_bads_eog() and ica.find_bads_ecg() can automate artifact component detection when dedicated EOG and ECG channels are available.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
If you want to understand how the brain works as a network, you need a way to measure whether two regions are coordinating their activity. Phase synchronisation is one of the most widely used approaches. It looks at the timing of oscillations, not their size, and asks a simple question: do these two signals maintain a consistent phase relationship over time?
This page covers the conceptual foundations of phase synchronisation, the different types that exist, and the theoretical framework that connects synchronisation to neural communication. These ideas underpin the connectivity measures (PLV, coherence, the phase alignment matrix) and the metastability analysis that Natalia will use in her project.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
If you want to understand how the brain works as a network, you need a way to measure whether two regions are coordinating their activity. Phase synchronisation is one of the most widely used approaches. It looks at the timing of oscillations, not their size, and asks a simple question: do these two signals maintain a consistent phase relationship over time?
This page covers the conceptual foundations of phase synchronisation, the different types that exist, and the theoretical framework that connects synchronisation to neural communication. These ideas underpin the connectivity measures (PLV, coherence, the phase alignment matrix) and the metastability analysis that Natalia will use in her project.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
What synchronisation means for oscillations
Two oscillations are synchronised when their phase relationship is consistent over time. The key word is “consistent”. The phases do not need to be identical; they just need to maintain a stable relationship.
Think of two people walking side by side. If they always step with their left foot at the same time, they are in phase. If one person’s left foot always hits the ground when the other’s right foot does, they are in anti-phase. If one person consistently steps half a beat behind the other, they have a stable phase lag. In all three cases, the relationship is predictable. That is synchronisation.
Now think of two people walking at different paces, with no particular relationship between their steps. Sometimes one is ahead, sometimes the other. The phase difference drifts randomly. That is desynchronisation.
For neural oscillations, synchronisation means that the phase difference between two signals, \(\Delta\phi(t) = \phi_1(t) - \phi_2(t)\), stays approximately constant (or at least has a preferred value) rather than wandering uniformly around the circle.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
Types of phase synchronisation

In-phase synchronisation
Two signals are in phase when \(\Delta\phi \approx 0\). They peak at the same time and trough at the same time. This is the simplest form of synchronisation.
In-phase synchronisation between two brain regions suggests that they are doing similar things at similar times. For example, two motor cortex regions that are both active during a movement task might show in-phase synchronisation in the beta band.


Anti-phase synchronisation
Two signals are in anti-phase when \(\Delta\phi \approx \pi\) (half a cycle apart). When one signal is at its peak, the other is at its trough.
Anti-phase synchronisation is not “the opposite of synchronisation”. It is still a stable, consistent relationship. It often occurs between regions that have an inhibitory or competitive relationship. For instance, regions on opposite sides of a functional boundary (one active, one suppressed) may show anti-phase coupling.


Constant phase lag
A constant phase lag means \(\Delta\phi \approx c\) for some fixed value \(c\) that is neither 0 nor \(\pi\). The signals are synchronised but offset by a fixed delay.
Phase lags are common in EEG because signals take time to propagate between regions. A consistent lag of, say, 20 milliseconds at 10 Hz corresponds to a phase difference of about \(0.4\pi\) radians. This is still meaningful synchronisation; it just reflects a transmission delay.


Summary








Type
Phase difference
Interpretation




In-phase
\(\Delta\phi \approx 0\)
Regions co-activate simultaneously


Anti-phase
\(\Delta\phi \approx \pi\)
Regions alternate (one up, one down)

title: Phase synchronisation
section: Why phase matters more than amplitude
text:
Why phase matters more than amplitude
EEG amplitude varies for many reasons that have nothing to do with neural communication: electrode impedance, scalp thickness, distance from the cortex, and reference choice all affect how large the signal appears at each electrode. Two regions could have very different amplitudes but still communicate effectively.
Phase, by contrast, is less affected by these physical factors. The timing of the oscillation (when it peaks and troughs) reflects the underlying neural dynamics more directly than the size of the signal. This is why most EEG connectivity measures focus on phase rather than amplitude.
There is a second reason. The brain appears to use phase as a mechanism for communication. If a region sends a burst of activity that arrives at a target region during the target’s excitable phase (near the trough for some cell types, near the peak for others), the message gets through. If it arrives during the refractory phase, it does not. Phase alignment determines whether communication is effective.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
The communication through coherence hypothesis
Fries (2005, 2015) formalised this idea as the communication through coherence (CTC) hypothesis. The core claim is:

Effective communication between two neural populations requires that their oscillations are coherent (phase-aligned) in the relevant frequency band.

The logic runs as follows:

Neural populations oscillate, alternating between excitable and non-excitable phases.
A sending population produces output at a particular phase of its cycle.
The receiving population is most sensitive to input at a particular phase of its own cycle.
If the two oscillations are coherent, the output of the sender arrives during the receiver’s excitable window, and information is transmitted.
If they are not coherent, the output arrives at random phases and is not effectively processed.

This means that the brain can route information by changing which pairs of regions are phase-aligned. To connect A with B, synchronise their oscillations. To disconnect them, desynchronise. This provides a flexible mechanism for selective communication without changing the physical wiring.
The CTC hypothesis is influential but not universally accepted. Some researchers argue that communication can occur through other mechanisms (amplitude correlations, broadband activity). Nonetheless, it provides a strong theoretical motivation for measuring phase synchronisation in EEG.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
Frequency-specific synchronisation
Different frequency bands support different types of communication:

Theta (4–8 Hz): long-range communication, particularly between frontal and temporal regions. Important for memory encoding, spatial navigation, and cognitive control.
Alpha (8–13 Hz): often interpreted as a “gating” mechanism. Regions that are alpha-synchronised may be jointly suppressed (functional inhibition), allowing other regions to process information without interference.
Beta (13–30 Hz): associated with motor coordination and sensorimotor communication. In Parkinson’s disease, excessive beta synchronisation between the basal ganglia and cortex is a hallmark finding.
Gamma (30–100 Hz): local processing and binding. Gamma synchronisation between nearby regions is thought to support feature integration (e.g., binding the colour, shape, and motion of an object into a unified percept).

Because different frequency bands carry different types of information, you should always analyse phase synchronisation within a specific frequency band. Mixing frequencies (or using broadband signals) produces uninterpretable results, because the instantaneous phase of a broadband signal does not correspond to any single oscillation.
This is why band-pass filtering must come before the Hilbert transform: you first isolate the frequency band of interest, then extract the phase within that band.

title: Phase synchronisation
section: Measuring synchronisation: an overview of methods
text:
Measuring synchronisation: an overview of methods
Several methods exist for quantifying phase synchronisation. They differ in what exactly they measure and how they handle noise and volume conduction.

Cross-correlation
The simplest approach. Compute the correlation between two time series. High correlation means the signals go up and down together. This captures both amplitude and phase similarity, making it less specific than phase-based measures. It also does not distinguish between different types of synchronisation (in-phase vs anti-phase).


Phase-locking value (PLV)
PLV measures the consistency of the phase difference over time:
\[\text{PLV} = \left| \frac{1}{T} \sum_{t=1}^{T} e^{i\Delta\phi(t)} \right|\]
PLV = 1 means perfect phase locking (constant phase difference); PLV = 0 means no phase locking (uniformly distributed phase difference). PLV ignores amplitude entirely, focusing only on phase. See the PLV topic page for details.


Coherence
Coherence is the normalised cross-spectral density. It captures both phase and amplitude relationships between two signals in the frequency domain. Coherence and PLV often give similar results, but coherence retains amplitude information while PLV discards it.


Phase alignment matrix
For multi-channel analysis, you can compute \(A_{ij}(t) = \cos(\phi_i(t) - \phi_j(t))\) at each time point to get a full matrix of pairwise phase relationships. This is the starting point for eigendecomposition and metastability analysis. See the phase alignment matrix topic page for details.

title: Phase synchronisation
text:
Functional connectivity vs effective connectivity
Phase synchronisation measures fall under the umbrella of functional connectivity: they detect statistical relationships between signals. Two signals that are phase-synchronised have a functional connection.
But functional connectivity does not tell you about the direction of influence. If A and B are synchronised, it could be because A drives B, B drives A, both are driven by a common source C, or some combination of these. Functional connectivity is symmetric: \(\text{PLV}_{AB} = \text{PLV}_{BA}\).
Effective connectivity, by contrast, attempts to infer the direction and causal structure of neural interactions. Methods like Granger causality, dynamic causal modelling (DCM), and transfer entropy estimate whether one signal predicts or causes changes in another.
For Natalia’s project, we focus on functional connectivity (specifically, phase-based measures and metastability). Effective connectivity methods are more complex and require stronger assumptions, but they are worth knowing about as context.
